a-agile-contracts.title: Agile procurement and contracting techniques
a-agile-contracts.notes: Manifesto value 'customer collaboration over contract negotiation'; win-lose contract perspectives increase risk; aim for shared risk and reward. Techniques: multi-tiered structure (fixed items like warranties and arbitration in a master agreement; changeable items like rates and product descriptions in a schedule of services; dynamic scope, schedule and budget in a lightweight statement of work); emphasise value delivered (milestones and payment tied to value-driven deliverables rather than phase gates on intermediate artefacts); fixed-price increments (decompose scope into fixed-price micro-deliverables such as user stories - customer controls spend, supplier limits over-commitment risk); not-to-exceed time and materials (cap the budget; new ideas replace original work within capacity; optional contingency hours); graduated time and materials (shared financial risk - higher hourly rate for early delivery, reduced rate for late delivery; quality is part of done); early cancellation option (customer may stop once enough value is delivered, paying a cancellation fee); dynamic scope option (fixed budget, customer may vary scope at specified points); team augmentation (supplier services embedded in the customer organisation; funding teams rather than scope - the most collaborative); favour full-service suppliers (avoid splitting work so each supplier does one thing, creating dependencies; prefer engagements delivering complete feature sets). Agile contracts rely on collaboration and trust: supplier delivers value early and often, customer gives timely feedback.

a-agile-measurements.title: Measurements in agile projects: empirical metrics, burndown/burnup, velocity, flow metrics, kanban board, feature charts, agile earned value, cumulative flow
a-agile-measurements.notes: Predictive status (e.g., '90% done', traffic lights) often hides reality - the 'watermelon project' (green outside, red inside) turns red with little warning because there is no empirical data until late. Agile measures what the team delivers, not what it predicts: finished features are better than surrogate measures like percent done; qualitative measures (business satisfaction, team morale) can complement quantitative ones. Estimation is limited to the next few weeks; with low variability and no multitasking, capacity stabilises; smaller chunks of work are more likely to be delivered. Forecasting: with reliable velocity (average story points per iteration) or average cycle time - e.g., 500 remaining points at 50 points per iteration = about 10 iterations; 30 stories at 3 days cycle time = 90 business days (about 4-5 months); show variability with hurricane-style charts. Story points rate relative work, risk and complexity; they are team-specific, so velocity cannot be compared or summed across teams. Burndown (Fig 5-1) shows remaining story points against a planned line (example: 37 points planned, at risk by Day 3); burnup (Fig 5-2) shows completed work from the same data and makes scope change visible; burndowns can dispirit a team and expose multitasking, oversized stories or absences. Velocity = sum of story point sizes of features actually completed in the iteration; it may take four to eight iterations to stabilise. Flow metrics: lead time (from adding an item to the board until it is completed/delivered), cycle time (time to process an item, from starting work to completion), response time (time an item waits before work starts; PDF 874 calls the similar measure 'reaction time' - ready to first column - lessons will note both names). Kanban board (Fig 5-3): columns Ready, Develop and Unit Test, Dev-Done, System Test, Done; WIP limits per column; when a column is at its limit the team cannot pull, and instead works from the right-most full column ('what do we do as a team to move this work?'); the Ready column can be reordered at any time. Burnups/burndowns are capacity measures; lead and cycle time are predictability measures. Measuring story points without finished features measures capacity, not finished work, violating 'working software is the primary measure of progress'. When depending on external groups: cycle time shows the team's own work, lead time exposes external dependencies. Feature chart (Fig 5-4): features complete, features remaining and total features over time - shows requirements growth. Product backlog burnup (Fig 5-5) shows completed against total expected work by iteration. Agile earned value (Fig 5-6, rendered): left axis scope in points, right axis spend; SPI = completed features / planned features (e.g., 25 of 30 planned points = 0.83); CPI = earned value (value of completed features) / actual costs (e.g., $2.2M / $2.8M = 0.79, i.e., 79 cents of value per dollar). Cumulative flow diagram (Fig 5-7, rendered): coloured bands Queue, Analysis, Development, Test, Deploy against months; vertical thickness shows work in queue, remaining work and completed work, horizontal distance shows response, cycle and lead time; a swelling band (e.g., test) signals a bottleneck; high WIP delays delivery.

a-apg-purpose-scope.title: Agile Practice Guide: purpose, joint PMI-Agile Alliance origin, scope and structure
a-apg-purpose-scope.notes: Chartered jointly by PMI and Agile Alliance (Agile Alliance co-funded it and does not endorse any methodology or certification) to equip teams with tools, situational guidelines and understanding of agile techniques; agile is used well beyond software (manufacturing, education, healthcare); there are multiple ways to succeed and teams should choose approaches that fit the project and culture. Written in a more informal style than PMI standards, with tips, sidebars and case studies; a bridge from predictive to agile approaches - many activities (e.g., planning) occur in both but are handled differently. Why now: exponential technology advances and customer demand for faster value; agile handles disruptive technologies; the first agile principle prioritises customer satisfaction; social media gives rapid, transparent feedback, so organisations must focus outward on customer experience. Disruptive technology (e.g., cloud computing with pay-as-you-go models and iterative releases) lowers barriers to entry; mature organisations risk being slow and complex versus startups, driving them to adopt an agile mindset. Sidebars: agile-based learning in education; disruptive technology. Scope (Table 1-1): in scope - agile at project or team level; most popular approaches per industry surveys; suitability factors; mapping agile to PMBOK Guide processes and Knowledge Areas; agile beyond software; guidance and techniques for implementation; definitions of generally accepted terms. Out of scope - organisation-wide agile or agile programs; niche, company-specific or incomplete approaches; recommending a particular approach; changing PMBOK Guide processes; removing software influence; prescriptive step-by-step instructions; new terms. Organisational change management is essential but out of scope (see Managing Change in Organizations). Audience: teams in the 'messy middle-ground' between predictive and agile. Structure: Section 2 introduction to agile (manifesto, mindset, definable vs high-uncertainty work, lean and Kanban); 3 life cycle selection (suitability filters, tailoring, combinations); 4 creating an agile environment (servant leadership, team composition); 5 delivering in an agile environment (practices, measurements); 6 organisational considerations (culture, readiness, business practices, PMO); 7 call to action; annexes are mandatory information too long for the body, appendixes are nonmandatory supplements; references, bibliography, glossary.

a-call-to-action.title: Agile Practice Guide call to action
a-call-to-action.notes: Agile adoption has grown sharply since the 2001 Manifesto and is no longer limited to IT or particular organisation sizes; inspection, adaptation and transparency remain constant truths; readers are invited to experiment, give feedback and engage with PMI and Agile Alliance communities ('inspection without adaptation is wasted effort'). Short orientation only - no examinable detail beyond reinforcing inspect-adapt-transparency.

a-charter-practices.title: Delivering in agile: chartering the project and team, retrospectives, backlog preparation and refinement, daily standups, demonstrations, iteration planning, technical execution practices, troubleshooting (Table 5-1)
a-charter-practices.notes: Chartering: every project needs a project charter (why it matters, direction, objective); agile teams also need norms - a team charter. Minimum: project vision or purpose and clear working agreements. An agile project charter answers: why are we doing this (vision); who benefits and how; what does done mean for the project (release criteria); how will we work together (intended flow of work). A servant leader may facilitate. Team charter / social contract ideas: team values (sustainable pace, core hours); working agreements (definition of 'ready' to take in work, definition of 'done' to judge completeness, respecting the timebox, WIP limits); ground rules (one person talks at a time); group norms (how meeting times are treated). Retrospectives - the single most important practice: the team learns, improves and adapts its process (Manifesto principle 12); 2-week iterations prompt a demo and retrospective, but retrospect also when a release ships (however small), when more than a few weeks have passed, when the team seems stuck and work isn't flowing, or at any milestone. Allocate enough time to gather data, process it and decide experiments; not about blame; use qualitative (feelings) and quantitative (measurements) data to find root causes, design countermeasures and action plans; limit action items to the team's capacity - completing fewer improvements beats starting many; decide how to measure each improvement's outcome and validate it next period; a facilitator helps rank items and the team picks how many to take on. Backlog preparation: the backlog is the ordered list of all the team's work in story form; create only enough stories to understand the first release broadly and the next iteration; product owners (or a product owner value team) may produce a product roadmap showing the anticipated sequence of deliverables, replanned as the team delivers. Backlog refinement: in iteration-based agile the product owner and team refine stories for the next iteration mid-iteration so the team understands them and their relative size; continuum - just-in-time refinement in flow (take the next card and discuss it); a timeboxed 1-hour discussion mid-way through a 2-week iteration; several sessions when new to the product or domain; tip: impact mapping shows how the product fits together; the product owner leads, a servant leader can facilitate; the product owner may ask the team to spike a feature to understand risks; approaches: triads (developer, tester, business analyst/product owner) writing stories; presenting a concept the team splits into stories; exploring together so stories are small enough for a steady flow - aim to complete a story at least once a day; goal of no more than 1 hour per week refining - more suggests over-preparation or missing skills. Daily standups: micro-commitments, uncover problems, keep work flowing; timebox 15 minutes; walk the kanban or task board; anyone can facilitate. Iteration-based questions (round-robin): what did I complete since the last standup; what do I plan to complete before the next; what are my impediments (risks, problems)? Flow-based questions (board right to left): what do we need to do to advance this work; is anyone working on anything not on the board; what do we need to finish as a team; any bottlenecks or blockers? Antipatterns: turning into status meetings (common for teams from predictive backgrounds) and solving problems in the standup - log them in a parking lot and solve afterwards; encourage any team member, not the PM, to facilitate; decide consciously whether the work needs standups. Demonstrations/reviews: the team demonstrates working product; the product owner accepts or declines stories; iteration-based - all completed work at iteration end; flow-based - when a coherent set has accumulated; guideline: demonstrate working product at least every 2 weeks; frequent delivery of working product is fundamental to agility - a team that doesn't demo or release can't learn fast enough; invite the PMO and portfolio decision makers to see real progress. Iteration planning: capacity and story size differ per team; don't commit beyond capacity; reduced capacity (holidays, absences) means less planned work; teams cannot predict with certainty; smaller stories and finished product teach the team its capability; plan a little, deliver, learn, replan (source note: the text points to 'Section 4.10' for estimation examples, but no such section exists - measurements are in APG 5.4). Execution practices (largely from XP) to sustain speed with quality: continuous integration (frequently integrate work and retest the whole); test at all levels (system-level end-to-end, unit, integration where needed, smoke tests, chosen regression tests; strong preference for automation); acceptance test-driven development (ATDD - the team agrees acceptance criteria, creates tests, then writes just enough code and automated tests; non-software teams test chunks of value); test-driven and behaviour-driven development (TDD, BDD - write automated tests before the product to design and mistake-proof it; hardware uses simulations); spikes (timeboxed research or experiments for estimation, acceptance criteria, user flow, critical technical or functional learning). Iterations and increments create a cadence of delivery and feedback - demo, then retrospective to inspect and adapt. Troubleshooting (Table 5-1, verified): unclear purpose or mission -> chartering for purpose (vision, mission, mission tests); unclear working agreements -> chartering for alignment (values, principles, working agreements); unclear team context -> chartering for context (boundaries, committed assets, prospective analysis); unclear requirements -> help craft a product vision, a roadmap via specification by example, user story mapping and impact mapping, team-product owner clarification, progressive decomposition into a backlog; poor user experience -> UX design practices in the team involving users early and often; inaccurate estimation -> split stories smaller, relative estimation by the whole team, agile modelling or spiking; unclear work assignments or progress -> teach self-management, kanban boards, daily standup walking the board; team struggles with obstacles -> servant leader clears them, a coach if options are unknown, escalate what can't be removed; delays from insufficiently refined backlog items -> workshop stories with the product owner, a definition of ready, smaller stories; defects -> technical practices such as pair work, collective product ownership, pervasive testing (test-driven and automated) and a robust definition of done; work is not complete -> team defines a definition of done with acceptance criteria plus project release criteria; technical debt (degraded code quality) -> refactoring, agile modelling, pervasive testing, automated code quality analysis, definition of done.

a-definable-vs-uncertain.title: Definable work vs high-uncertainty work
a-definable-vs-uncertain.notes: Project work ranges from definable to high-uncertainty. Definable work: clear procedures proven on similar projects; e.g., producing a car, appliance or home after design is complete; well-understood domain and processes; low execution uncertainty and risk. High-uncertainty (exploratory) work: new design, problem solving, not-done-before work requiring SMEs to collaborate to create a solution - e.g., software systems engineers, product designers, doctors, teachers, lawyers, problem-solving engineers. As definable work is automated, teams take on more high-uncertainty work. High-uncertainty projects have high rates of change, complexity and risk, which challenge predictive approaches that fix most requirements up front and control change through change requests; agile approaches were created to explore feasibility in short cycles and adapt quickly based on evaluation and feedback. (Section 2.1 continues on PDF 816.)

a-frameworks-scaled.title: Scaling frameworks: Scrum of Scrums, SAFe, LeSS, Enterprise Scrum, Disciplined Agile
a-frameworks-scaled.notes: Scrum of Scrums ('meta Scrum'): two or more Scrum teams of three to nine members coordinate; a representative from each meets, typically two to three times a week (potentially daily), reporting completed work, next work, current impediments and upcoming impediments that might block other teams; large programmes can add a Scrum of Scrum of Scrums (Fig A3-6). SAFe: a knowledge base of patterns for scaling across all levels of the enterprise; principles begin with take an economic view, apply systems thinking, assume variability and preserve options, build incrementally with fast integrated learning cycles, base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems (continues on PDF 921).

a-frameworks-team.title: Agile and lean frameworks: selection criteria, Scrum, XP, Kanban Method, Crystal, Scrumban, FDD, DSDM, Agile UP
a-frameworks-team.section: APG Annex A3.1-A3.9 (Figures A3-1 to A3-5, Tables A3-1 to A3-5)
a-frameworks-team.notes: No framework is mandatory; an approach built from scratch is fine if it follows the Manifesto's values and principles. Frameworks included are holistic, formalised for common use and popular (industry surveys). Fig A3-1 plots approaches by breadth of life cycle coverage and depth of guidance (team methods vs scaled approaches). Scrum: single-team framework of roles, events, artefacts and rules; sprints are consistent timeboxes of 1 month or less producing a potentially releasable increment; events: sprint, sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review, sprint retrospective; artefacts: product backlog, sprint backlog, increments; roles: product owner (maximises product value), development team (cross-functional, self-organising, has everything needed), scrum master (upholds the process, coaches, removes impediments). XP (Table A3-2, rendered): practices grouped by area - organisational (primary: sit together, whole team, informative workspace; secondary: real customer involvement, team continuity, sustainable pace), technical (pair programming, test-first programming, incremental design; secondary: shared code/collective ownership, documentation from code and tests, refactoring), planning (user stories, weekly cycle, quarterly cycle, slack; secondary: root cause analysis, shrinking teams, pay per use, negotiated scope contract, daily standups), integration (10-minute build, continuous integration, test-first; secondary: single code base, incremental deployment, daily deployment); core values communication, simplicity, feedback, courage, respect. Kanban Method: from lean manufacturing (Taiichi Ohno, Toyota, 1953); 'kanban' means visual sign or card; board as information radiator with columns for work states (simplest: to do, doing, done); 'start where you are', less prescriptive, no prescribed timeboxes; pull single items and limit WIP; suited to flexibility needs, continuous delivery, productivity and quality via WIP limits, efficiency, focus, variable workload and waste reduction; defining principles - start with current state, agree to pursue incremental evolutionary change, respect current process, roles and titles, encourage leadership at all levels; core properties - visualise workflow, limit WIP, manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops, improve collaboratively; completing work matters more than starting new work (Fig A3-2 board with doing/done sub-columns and WIP limits). Crystal (Fig A3-3, rendered): family scaled by number of people and criticality (defects cause loss of comfort, discretionary money, essential money or life); Crystal Clear (1-4 people), Yellow (6-20), Orange (20-40), Red (the next band, printed '5-100' on the axis - likely 50-100; lessons avoid quoting that figure); core values people and interaction, community, skills, talents, communications; common properties frequent delivery, reflective improvement, close/osmotic communication, personal safety, focus, easy access to expert users, technical environment with automated tests, configuration management and frequent integration. Scrumban: started as a transition from Scrum to Kanban, now a hybrid - Scrum framework plus kanban boards and WIP limits for improvement; daily meetings; a planning trigger when WIP falls below a limit; no predefined roles. FDD: built for a large software project; features are small business-valued capabilities; six roles (project manager, chief architect, development manager, chief programmer, class owner, domain expert); five iterative activities (develop overall model, build features list, plan by feature, design by feature, build by feature); supporting practices include domain object modelling, individual class ownership, feature teams, inspections, configuration management, regular builds, visibility of progress. DSDM (Fig A3-5, rendered): constraint-driven delivery - traditional approach fixes features and varies time and cost; DSDM fixes cost, time and quality and varies functionality through formal prioritisation; eight principles - focus on the business need, deliver on time, collaborate, never compromise quality, build incrementally from firm foundations, develop iteratively, communicate continuously and clearly, demonstrate control. Agile UP: lighter, faster offshoot of the Unified Process; disciplines model, implementation, test, deployment, configuration management, project management, environment; principles - the team knows what it's doing, simplicity, agility, focus on high-value activities, tool independence, tailoring to fit, situationally specific.

a-hybrid-tailoring.title: Hybrid life cycles (agile then predictive, combined, largely predictive with agile parts, largely agile with predictive parts, fit-for-purpose, transition strategy); mixing approaches; project factors that influence tailoring
a-hybrid-tailoring.notes: A hybrid approach combines predictive, iterative, incremental and/or agile elements; one approach is not required for the whole project. Agile development followed by a predictive rollout (Figure 3-6) - uncertain, complex development then a defined, repeatable rollout, perhaps by a different team (e.g., a new high-tech product then rollout and training to thousands of users). Case: a pharmaceutical company ran drug trials in an agile way but the FDA approval had to stay as a separate final phase because any change requires re-approval; integrating it iteratively failed, but quick-start guides and testing protocols shortened approval. Combined agile and predictive used simultaneously (Figure 3-7) - e.g., a team transitioning with short iterations, daily standups and retrospectives but still predictive upfront estimation, work assignment and progress tracking; neither fully agile nor predictive - hybrid. Largely predictive with agile components (Figure 3-8) - e.g., an engineering firm building a routine facility with a new roofing material runs small installation trials on the ground to learn the best method early. Largely agile with a predictive component (Figure 3-9) - when an element is non-negotiable or not executable with agile, e.g., integrating an external vendor component delivered once by a vendor that will not collaborate incrementally. Fit-for-purpose hybrids based on risk - e.g., a campus construction project completing some buildings earlier (incremental) while each building is predictive. Goal: produce business value in the best way for the environment; ask 'How can we be most successful?' - need feedback as value is produced? use increments; need to manage risk while exploring ideas? use iterations or agile; if intermediate value can't be delivered agile may not help - agile for the sake of agile is not the goal. Case: a government credit insurance system replacement - mostly agile with continual business input, but a premium-rate calculation defined in a 200-page OECD specification was coded by a separate team in a largely predictive way, coordinating only on inputs and outputs. Hybrid as a transition strategy: organisations can't switch overnight; add iterative techniques for learning and alignment, later incremental techniques for faster value and ROI; start with a less risky project of medium-to-low uncertainty before more complex ones. Mixing agile approaches: teams rarely use just one; frameworks are not customised to the team, so teams tailor; a common blend is Scrum (product backlog, product owner, scrum master, cross-functional development team, sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review, sprint retrospective) + a kanban board (visualise flow, expose impediments, manage WIP limits) + XP-inspired engineering practices (story cards, continuous integration, refactoring, automated testing, test-driven development) - a synergistic result. Table 3-2 (factor -> tailoring option): demand pattern steady or sporadic -> use a cadence (regular timebox) for demos, retrospectives and taking new work, or flow-based agile with a cadence for flexibility; rate of process improvement needed given team experience -> retrospect more often and select improvements; flow interrupted by delays or impediments -> make work visible with kanban boards and experiment with WIP limits; poor quality of increments -> test-driven development practices (mistake-proofing); more than one team needed -> learn agile program management or formal scaling frameworks, then craft a fitting approach; team inexperienced with agile -> train in the agile mindset and principles, then a workshop on the chosen approach (e.g., Scrum or Kanban).

a-lean-kanban-uncertainty.title: Lean and the Kanban Method; uncertainty, risk and the Stacey-inspired complexity model
a-lean-kanban-uncertainty.notes: Agile and the Kanban Method descend from lean thinking (a superset) and share a heritage: delivering value, respect for people, minimising waste, transparency, adapting to change, continuous improvement; teams may blend methods - the best outcome matters, not the origin. The Kanban Method is inspired by lean manufacturing and applied to knowledge work; emerged in the mid-2000s; less prescriptive and less disruptive than some agile approaches - the original 'start where you are' approach; teams can begin easily and progress to other approaches; debate continues whether it belongs to lean or agile. Uncertainty about requirements and about how to fulfil them with current knowledge and technology raises rates of change and complexity; as uncertainty increases so do the risk of rework and the need for a different approach; teams tackle high uncertainty with small increments of work they can verify and change, learning true customer requirements faster than from a static written specification. Figure 2-5 (inspired by the Stacey Complexity Model): axes - requirements uncertainty (agreement) and technical degree of uncertainty; low/low = simple, where linear approaches work well; moving outward = complicated, then complex, where adaptive approaches work well; high/high = chaos, fundamentally risky. Clear, stable requirements and clear technical challenges are easy to plan; rising uncertainty increases changes, wasted work and rework. Iterative and incremental approaches reduce waste and rework through feedback, using very short feedback loops, frequent process adaptation, reprioritisation, regularly updated plans and frequent delivery. Tip example: the Boston 'Big Dig' moved an elevated highway underground - high agreement on requirements and apparently low uncertainty until surprises emerged; with little opportunity for interim deliverables or prototypes, a predictive life cycle is likely; assess both requirements and means of delivery. Agile approaches suit new or novel tools, techniques, materials or domains, research and development, high change, unclear requirements or high risk, or goals hard to describe; small tested increments explore uncertainty cheaply in product specification (right product?), production capability (can it be built this way?) and process suitability (is this an effective way to work?). Limits: when both technology and requirements uncertainty are very high the project becomes chaotic and one variable must be contained to make it reliably possible.

a-life-cycle-types.title: Life cycle selection: predictive, iterative, incremental and agile characteristics; planning in every life cycle; iteration-based vs flow-based agile; suitability filters
a-life-cycle-types.notes: Four life cycles: predictive (bulk of planning up front, then executing in a single pass; sequential); iterative (feedback on unfinished work to improve and modify it); incremental (finished deliverables the customer may use immediately); agile (both iterative and incremental, refining work items and delivering frequently). Terminology: 'predictive' chosen over plan-driven, waterfall or serial to align with the PMBOK Guide. Table 3-1 (verified order): requirements - predictive fixed; iterative, incremental and agile dynamic. Activities - predictive performed once for the entire project; iterative repeated until correct; incremental performed once for a given increment; agile repeated until correct. Delivery - predictive single delivery; iterative single delivery; incremental frequent smaller deliveries; agile frequent small deliveries. Goal - predictive manage cost; iterative correctness of solution; incremental speed; agile customer value via frequent deliveries and feedback. All projects have these characteristics; inherent characteristics decide the best fit. Figure 3-1 presents the continuum as a square: frequency of delivery (low to high) vs degree of change (low to high) - predictive low/low, incremental high delivery, iterative high change, agile high/high. Predictive exploits known, proven things; iterative improves partially finished work via feedback; incremental gives usable finished deliverables; agile combines both, giving early feedback, customer visibility, confidence and control and possibly earlier ROI by delivering highest-value work first. Predictive characteristics: high certainty on firm requirements, stable team, low risk; serial execution with detailed plans; succeeds when change is restricted; constraints from detailed early plans manage risk and cost; M&C controls changes to scope, schedule, budget; departmentally efficient serial work usually delivers business value only at the end; unexpected changes, disagreements or difficult technology cause unanticipated costs. Sidebar 'planning is always there': every life cycle plans - the difference is how much and when; predictive plans as much as possible up front (plan drives the work, detailed requirements, delivery estimates, comprehensive procurement); iterative plans prototypes whose outputs modify early plans; incremental plans successive subsets; agile plans and replans as information comes from frequent deliveries. Iterative: successive prototypes or proofs of concept, each yielding stakeholder feedback and insight that is fed back by repeating activities; timeboxing iterations of a few weeks; useful when complexity is high, change is frequent or stakeholders differ on the desired final product; may take longer because optimised for learning rather than speed (Figure 3-3: analyse, design, prototype, refine cycles before build, test, deliver). Incremental: optimised for speed of delivery - customers accept a subset; plan initial deliverables and start the first as soon as possible (some agile projects deliver within days; others 1 to several weeks); deviations from the original vision are manageable because value comes sooner; e.g., builders finishing one floor completely (fixtures, paint) so the customer approves style before the rest - reducing rework and dissatisfaction; completeness is subjective - a prototype then a minimum viable product (MVP) to a subset of customers whose feedback shapes the final feature. Tips: when requirements seem to change daily, a prototype the business approves encourages feedback; use a proof of concept with evaluation criteria to explore a new business service. Agile: requirements are expected to change; incremental delivery uncovers hidden or misunderstood requirements. Iteration-based agile: equal-duration timeboxes delivering completed, working, tested features; the team swarms on the most important feature then the next, never doing all requirements then all analysis. Flow-based agile: features pulled from the backlog by capacity, workflow defined as task-board columns with work-in-progress (WIP) limits per column; each feature may take a different time; small WIP surfaces issues early; the team and stakeholders choose the schedule for planning, reviews and retrospectives. Agile life cycles fulfil the Manifesto principles - early, continuous delivery and a functional valuable increment as the primary measure of progress. Agile suitability filters: assessment models score project and organisational factors for fit or risk (synthesised in APG Appendix X3).

a-manifesto-mapping.title: Agile Manifesto values and principles mapped to the Agile Practice Guide (Annex A2)
a-manifesto-mapping.notes: Table A2-1 (rendered): individuals and interactions over processes and tools -> 4.2 servant leadership, 4.3 team composition, 5.1 chartering, 5.2.4 daily standups, 6.2 culture; working software over comprehensive documentation -> 5.2.2 backlog preparation, 5.2.3 refinement, 5.2.5 demonstrations/reviews, 5.2.7 execution practices; customer collaboration over contract negotiation -> 4.3, 5.4 measurements, 6.2, 6.3 procurement and contracts, 6.7 structure; responding to change over following a plan -> 5.2.1 retrospectives, 5.2.3, 5.2.5. Table A2-2 lists the twelve principles (customer satisfaction through early, continuous delivery; welcome changing requirements; deliver frequently, preferring shorter timescales; business and developers work together daily; build around motivated individuals and trust them; face-to-face conversation is most efficient; working software is the primary measure of progress; sustainable pace; technical excellence and good design; simplicity - maximising work not done; self-organising teams produce the best architectures, requirements and designs; regular reflection and adjustment) with section cross-references. The principle-to-section column alignment in the extracted text is not reliable; lessons use the principles themselves (already covered in APG 2.2) and cite Annex A2 generally rather than individual row mappings.

a-manifesto-mindset.title: Agile Manifesto values and twelve principles; agile as mindset, values, principles and practices; agile as an umbrella term; two strategies to become agile
a-manifesto-mindset.notes: The Manifesto for Agile Software Development (2001) values individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan - the items on the right have value, the items on the left are valued more. Twelve principles (paraphrased): (1) highest priority is customer satisfaction through early and continuous delivery of valuable software; (2) welcome changing requirements, even late, for the customer's competitive advantage; (3) deliver working software frequently, weeks rather than months, preferring the shorter timescale; (4) business people and developers work together daily; (5) build projects around motivated individuals - give environment and support and trust them; (6) face-to-face conversation is the most efficient and effective way to convey information to and within a team; (7) working software is the primary measure of progress; (8) sustainable development - sponsors, developers and users can maintain a constant pace indefinitely; (9) continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility; (10) simplicity - maximising the amount of work not done - is essential; (11) the best architectures, requirements and designs emerge from self-organising teams; (12) at regular intervals the team reflects on how to become more effective and adjusts. Principles now apply well beyond software. Figure 2-3 (inspired by Ahmed Sidky): agile is a mindset defined by 4 values, guided by 12 principles and manifested through many practices; practitioners select practices based on need; many techniques predate the Manifesto by years or decades. Figure 2-4: agile is a blanket term for approaches, techniques, frameworks, methods or practices fulfilling the values and principles (Scrum, XP, FDD, DSDM, AUP, Crystal, ScrumBan); agile and the Kanban Method are shown as subsets of lean, sharing lean concepts such as focus on value, small batch sizes and elimination of waste. The guide uses the term 'approach'. Two strategies: (1) adopt a formal agile approach designed and proven to work, and learn it well before tailoring - premature, haphazard tailoring limits benefits; (2) change project practices to fit the context and make progress on a core value or principle (timeboxes, iterative feature refinement, splitting a large project into releases) even if not part of formal organisational practice. The goal is not agile for its own sake but a continuous flow of value to customers and better business outcomes.

a-org-business-pmo-structure.title: Business practices, multiteam scaling, the agile PMO, organisational structure and evolving the organisation
a-org-business-pmo-structure.notes: Business practices: support functions may need to change - finance may capitalise products differently, procurement may restructure contracts for frequent delivery, HR may find individual incentives and appraisals of self-organising staff less suitable; transparency and collaboration are key. Scaling (6.5): Scrum and XP target a single small, usually colocated cross-functional team; frameworks for multiple teams include Scaled Agile Framework, Large Scale Scrum, Disciplined Agile, and approaches like Scrum of Scrums (Annex A3); start small and learn; the critical success factor is a healthy agile team - if a single team cannot succeed, do not scale up, fix organisational impediments instead. Agile PMO (6.6): exists to shepherd business value; value-driven (operates like a consulting business, tailoring services to each project's needs - an 'intrapreneur' approach); invitation-oriented (offers services to those interested rather than mandating, so practices become 'sticky'); multidisciplinary (beyond PM: organisational design, change management). Agile centre-of-excellence services: developing standards and templates (user stories, test cases, cumulative flow diagrams); training and mentoring; multiproject coordination and release/portfolio themes; organisational learning (velocity profiles, retrospective findings); managing stakeholders (product owner training, acceptance testing guidance, championing SMEs); recruiting and evaluating team leaders; specialised tasks (retrospective facilitators, troubleshooters, coaches). Organisational structure (6.7): geography (distributed teams face competing goals, cultural and language barriers - encourage dialogue); functionalised structures resist cross-organisation collaboration (spectrum projectised-matrix-functional); smaller deliverables drive more frequent handoffs and faster flow; allocate one person per department fully to the top-priority project; procurement-heavy organisations lose knowledge when vendors leave - use retrospectives while the vendor is engaged. Evolving the organisation (6.8): change incrementally; treat the change as an agile project with a prioritised backlog; each change an experiment; track on a kanban board (to do, in progress, done). Continues on PDF 893.

a-org-change-culture.title: Organisational considerations: change management, readiness for change, culture and safety, assessing culture
a-org-change-culture.notes: Every project exists in an organisational context; leaders may not be able to change it but must navigate it. Change management (see PMI's Managing Change in Organizations: models of change dynamics, a framework, and practices at project, program and portfolio level); project agility is more sustained as the organisation adjusts (Fig 6-1 shows agile considerations and change management concepts as overlapping bodies of knowledge). Two drivers: changes associated with accelerated delivery (the receiving organisation may not absorb outputs at the faster pace, delaying ROI - customer acceptance matters even more) and changes associated with agile approaches themselves (more handoffs, iterative rework viewed negatively). Change-friendly characteristics: executive willingness to change; willingness to change how employees are viewed, reviewed and assessed; centralisation or decentralisation of PPM functions; focus on short-term budgeting and metrics versus long-term goals; talent management maturity. Roadblocks: work decomposed into departmental silos instead of cross-functional teams; procurement based on short-term pricing rather than long-term competencies; leaders rewarded for local efficiencies rather than end-to-end flow; specialists without incentives to become T-shaped; decentralised portfolios spreading people over many projects. Responses: visible, active executive sponsorship; change management incl. communication and coaching; progressively pacing adoption project by project; incremental introduction of practices; leading by example. Culture is the organisation's DNA, ranging from highly predictive to lean startup (everything an experiment); predictive organisations can still encourage empirical measurement and small experiments. The most important cultural norm is a safe, honest, transparent environment for reflection and learning from failure. Assessing culture (Fig 6-2): record priorities as positions on sliding scales between pairs - speed vs stability, quantity vs quality, exploration vs execution, flexibility vs predictability, plus other factors - then pick techniques that fit; the specific model matters less than understanding the forces. Sidebar quote attributed to Drucker on culture and strategy; tip: culture and structure must progress together.

a-pmbok-ka-mapping.title: Applying agile across the PMBOK Guide Knowledge Areas (Annex A1)
a-pmbok-ka-mapping.notes: Table A1-1 repeats the 49-process Process Group/Knowledge Area mapping (consistent with PMBOK Table 1-4, already verified). Table A1-2, per Knowledge Area: Integration - team members act as local domain experts deciding how plans and components integrate; the PM's expectations do not change, but detailed product planning and delivery are delegated to the team; PM builds a collaborative decision-making environment; broad skill bases help. Scope - less time defining scope up front, more on establishing a process for ongoing discovery and refinement; prototypes and releases refine requirements; scope is defined and redefined throughout; the requirements constitute the backlog. Schedule - short cycles with review and adaptation; iterative and on-demand pull-based scheduling; large organisations may need roadmaps and scaling factors (team size, geography, regulatory, organisational and technical complexity) and hybrid techniques; the PM's role does not change but they must know adaptive tools. Cost - lightweight high-level estimation of labour costs, detailed estimates just in time for short horizons; with strict budgets, scope and schedule are adjusted to stay within cost. Quality - frequent quality and review steps throughout rather than at the end; retrospectives check quality process effectiveness, find root causes and trial improvements; small batches uncover inconsistencies early when change is cheaper. Resources - self-organising teams of generalising specialists; collaboration critical with high variability; physical and human resource planning less predictable, so fast-supply agreements and lean methods matter. Communications - more frequent, faster communication; streamlined access to information, frequent checkpoints, colocation, transparent artefacts and regular stakeholder reviews. Risk - frequent reviews of incremental work and cross-functional teams; risk considered when selecting iteration content and managed each iteration; requirements are a living document reprioritised by risk exposure. Procurement - sellers may extend the team; shared risk-reward models; a master services agreement for the overall engagement with adaptive work in an appendix or supplement so it can change without affecting the overall contract. Stakeholders - direct engagement rather than through management layers; co-creative exchange among client, user and developer; regular interaction mitigates risk and builds trust; 'aggressive transparency' (open meetings, public artefacts) surfaces misalignment and dependencies early.

a-servant-leadership.title: Agile mindset questions, servant leadership (purpose-people-process, characteristics, responsibilities) and the project manager's role in agile
a-servant-leadership.notes: Implementation strategy questions: how can the team act in an agile manner; what can it deliver quickly for early feedback; how can it be transparent; what work can be avoided to focus on high priorities; how can servant leadership help the team's goals? Servant leadership = leading through service to the team, understanding and addressing members' needs and development to enable the highest team performance; the servant leader facilitates the team's discovery and definition of agile and practises and radiates agile. Order of approach: purpose (define the 'why' with the team so they coalesce; optimise at project level, not person level), people (an environment where everyone can succeed and contributes across the work), process (don't seek the 'perfect' agile process - look for results; a cross-functional team delivering finished value often and reflecting on product and process is agile, whatever it calls its process). Characteristics: promoting self-awareness; listening; serving those on the team; helping people grow; coaching vs controlling; promoting safety, respect and trust; promoting others' energy and intelligence. Not unique to agile, but integrates well; facilitative leaders are more likely to become agile; growth mindset - belief that people can learn new skills. Responsibilities: manage relationships to build communication and coordination within the team and across the organisation, removing impediments and streamlining processes. Facilitate - shift from 'managing coordination' to 'facilitating collaboration'; help everyone do their best thinking; encourage participation, understanding and shared responsibility; expose bottlenecks within and between teams so teams resolve them; impartial bridge-builders and coaches rather than deciding for others. Remove organisational impediments - per the first Manifesto value, streamline processes (e.g., review documentation requirements with a department; challenge lengthy finance, CCB or audit processes; there's little point delivering every 2 weeks if release takes 6 or more weeks). Pave the way for others' contribution - team space with facilities, management agreement for one project at a time, stories with the product owner, regulatory process refinement with auditors, incremental budgeting with finance. Example responsibilities: educate stakeholders on why and how to be agile (value-based prioritisation, accountable empowered teams, quality from frequent reviews); support the team through mentoring, encouragement, training and career development ('we lead teams by standing behind them'), growing people even if they leave the team; help with technical PM activities such as quantitative risk analysis; celebrate successes and build bridges with external groups. Sidebar: interpersonal and emotional intelligence skills matter as much as technical skills - initiative, integrity, honesty, collaboration, humility, willingness to communicate - to adapt to changes. Role of the PM in agile: many frameworks don't address it and some think it unnecessary with self-organising teams, but pragmatic organisations find PMs add significant value with different responsibilities; 'the value of project managers is not in their position, but in their ability to make everyone else better'. PMs use servant leadership: the PMBOK definition stands, but in high-change projects there is more complexity than one person can manage; cross-functional teams coordinate their own work with the product owner; PMs shift from the centre to serving the team and management - coaching people who want help, fostering collaboration, aligning stakeholder needs, distributing responsibility to those with the knowledge.

a-suitability-filter.title: Agile suitability filter: culture, team and project attributes on a radar chart
a-suitability-filter.section: APG Appendix X3 (Figures X3-1 to X3-13)
a-suitability-filter.notes: Origins: DSDM (1994) project and organisational suitability questionnaires; Crystal's team size and criticality criteria (lighter controls for small, less critical projects; more rigour for large, mission- or life-critical ones); Boehm and Turner's model; APG synthesises these and adds the hybrid middle ground. Three categories: culture (buy-in to approach, trust in team, decision-making powers of team), team (team size, experience levels, access to the customer/business), project (likelihood of change, criticality of product or service, incremental delivery). Instructions: complete as a group (small project: sponsor, technical lead, customer; large: sponsoring group, execution team, impacted business groups, governance, customers) because any single person is biased; the conversation is the value; follow stakeholder consensus even if it differs from the result; score 1-10 with anchors at 1, 5 and 10 (intermediate values fine); if the group cannot agree, discuss openly before compromising. Scales (rendered): lower scores favour agile - buy-in, experience and access: yes = 1, partial = 5, no = 10; trust and decision-making: yes = 1, probably = 5, unlikely = 10; team size: 1-9 = 1, 10-20 = 2, 21-30 = 3, 31-45 = 4, 46-60 = 5, 61-80 = 6, 81-110 = 7, 111-150 = 8, 151-200 = 9, 201+ = 10; likelihood of change (share of requirements changing or discovered monthly): 50% = 1, 25% = 5, 5% = 10; criticality (loss from defects): comfort/time = 1, discretionary funds, essential funds = 5, single life, many lives = 10; incremental delivery: yes = 1, maybe/sometimes = 5, unlikely = 10. Interpretation: plot on the radar chart (Fig X3-11) - clustering at the centre indicates agile; the middle band indicates hybrid (or agile with extra risk reduction such as training, validation and documentation, or predictive with proof-of-concept work); the outer band indicates predictive; spikes on one or two axes suggest hybrid. Mismatches are inputs to risk management; the tool is a diagnostic, not an inclusion/exclusion gate. Case studies (rendered): online drug store - extremely volatile requirements, 2-day iterations and weekly releases, high buy-in and trust, small experienced team with business access, fairly high criticality (essential funds) - plot clustered centrally with one spike on criticality, very successful agile; military messaging system - 5 years running, no agile buy-in, mixed trust, decisions by committees, no end-to-end incremental demonstration, many lives at risk, locked requirements, 300+ people from one vendor but experienced roles, no direct customer access (contract analysts replied within about 10 days) - plot mostly in the predictive zone, with experience and trust lower; parts could have run as agile but the core was one large project.

a-tailoring-agile.title: Tailoring agile approaches: cautions, Shu-Ha-Ri, self-supporting practice pairs and tailoring guidelines
a-tailoring-agile.notes: Tailoring is advanced: gain experience and succeed with an approach as designed, in several environments, before tailoring it. Dropping a practice because it is unpopular (e.g., 'retrospectives were unpopular so we dropped them') signals a deeper team problem and removes the very practice that improves the process. Shu-Ha-Ri skill progression: Shu (obey and protect the rules), Ha (consciously change or digress), Ri (separate - find an individual path); start at Shu before tailoring (Ha) or inventing (Ri). Tailor collaboratively with those affected to gain buy-in and avoid resistance; coaches can help. How to use: first use the approach as designed; find the matching situation in Table X2-1; discuss with those impacted; trial the change for an iteration or two (or a few features in flow); review at a retrospective and continue, modify or drop; institutionalise successful tailoring for similar projects. Beware of taking things away: many practices are self-supporting pairs (colocation and frequent business conversation enable lightweight requirements; XP's rigorous testing enables courageous refactoring). Table X2-1 (rendered): very large teams - split into smaller projects, technology trial then implementation project, more frequent smaller releases, reduce to the critical core team, multiple smaller teams coordinated by (agile/lean) program management, or a scaled framework such as DA, SAFe or LeSS (each with implementation risk and process weight); dispersed teams - instant messaging, video, electronic boards; meet face to face early to build trust; round-robin check-ins and consensus checks for remote meetings; iteration-based approaches; across many time zones, fewer whole-team sessions and more frequent small (2-3 person) meetings; safety-critical products needing extra documentation and conformance - keep agile but add conformance review, documentation and certification layers, documentation may be part of done, hybrid approaches (e.g., aircraft flight systems, drug companies); stable requirements and execution - question whether full agile is needed; lengthen build/feedback cycles if they rarely refine requirements; if design changes a lot but roll-out is repeatable, use hybrid life cycles per phase; functional silos - ask people to form cross-functional teams themselves; change compensation that rewards functional areas first; transparency causes fear - lead by example with visible decision-making (status board or whiteboard); team members with little domain knowledge - self-direction may cause rework, so provide more assigning and directing until skills grow; build centres of competency; lack of executive buy-in - find common ground and improvement areas, use experiments and retrospectives, educate executives, explain agile via lean thinking (short cycles, small batches, frequent reviews, retrospectives); agile terms clash with culture - rename terms (e.g., 'planning workshop' instead of 'planning game') and define each term.

a-team-composition.title: Agile team composition: team size, dedication, cross-functional roles (team member, product owner, team facilitator), generalising specialists, structures, multitasking cost, workspaces, silos
a-team-composition.notes: Agile optimises the flow of value (rapid feature delivery) rather than how people are 'utilised'; benefits: more collaboration, valuable work finished faster, far less waste from multitasking and re-establishing context. Agile teams: most effective size about three to nine members; ideally colocated; 100% dedicated; self-managing (members decide who does the work within the next period's scope); thrive with servant leadership; cross-functional teams collectively own the work and have all skills to deliver completed increments frequently; limiting WIP helps collaboration; collaborate by pairing, swarming and mobbing to avoid 'mini-waterfalls' (all requirements, then all design, then all build in a period - assumptions may prove invalid late and effort is wasted). Table 4-1 (verified): dedicated people -> increased focus and productivity; small team, fewer than ten people. Cross-functional team members -> develop and deliver often; deliver finished value as an independent team; integrate all work activities to deliver finished work; feedback from inside the team and from others such as the product owner. Colocation or ability to manage location challenges -> better communication; improved team dynamics; knowledge sharing; reduced cost of learning; able to commit to working with each other. Mixed team of generalists and specialists -> specialists give dedicated expertise, generalists flexibility; members often become generalising specialists. Stable work environment -> depend on each other to deliver; agreed approach to the work; simplified team cost calculations (run rate); preservation and expansion of intellectual capital. Table 4-2 roles: cross-functional team member (all skills needed for working product - e.g., designers, developers, testers; deliver potentially releasable product on a regular cadence; finished work fastest, higher quality, no external dependencies); product owner (guides product direction; ranks work by business value; works with the team daily giving feedback and setting direction; work small enough for an index card; works with stakeholders and customers; usually a business background with deep subject matter expertise, may draw on architects or product managers; needs training to manage flow; creates the backlog for and with the team; strong product ownership is a critical success factor - otherwise unvalued features waste effort); team facilitator (servant leader - may be called project manager, scrum master, project team lead, team coach or team facilitator; all agile teams need servant leadership; skills of facilitation, coaching and impediment removal take time; external coaches bring experience but weak relationships, internal coaches the reverse). Generalising specialists / T-shaped people: a focus specialty plus breadth across skills and strong collaboration, vs I-shaped people with depth but little breadth; reduce hand-offs and single-person constraints; a single person's throughput is irrelevant and focusing on it can create bottlenecks; the objective is flow efficiency (throughput of the whole team) rather than resource efficiency; small batch sizes promote teamwork; the product owner keeps the team on the highest-value work. Structures: colocated; distributed (cross-functional teams in different locations); dispersed (each member in a different place) - workable despite communication costs. Case: a US financial institution's follow-the-sun program (work handed off daily across time zones) started as one dispersed team with joint webcam standups and early-starting US roles, then split into five colocated, distributed cross-functional teams of developers and testers with central analysts and program-level product reviews. Case: the guide's own writing team was self-organising and incremental but not 100% dedicated, and tracked dispersion as a risk. Dedicated members: part-time (25% or 50%) members multitask and task-switch, lowering throughput and predictability; task switching costs 20%-40% productivity, rising exponentially with the number of tasks - someone split across two projects is effectively 20%-40% on each, not 50%, and makes more mistakes; temporarily assigned specialists (e.g., database administrators, research analysts) need explicit expectations about allocation and duration - part-time assignments create risk. Workspaces: a space to work together, see team state and collaborate; balance 'caves and common' - open collaborative areas plus quiet private spaces; distributed teams decide virtual vs physical mix, use document sharing and video tools, meet in person periodically to build trust; techniques: fishbowl window (long-lived video link opened all workday between locations) and remote pairing (shared screens with voice and video, accounting for time zones). Overcoming silos: start with foundational trust and a safe environment where everyone has an equal voice, plus the agile mindset; siloed reporting lines and differing metrics impede cross-functional teams - managers should focus on flow efficiency and team-based metrics and dedicate individuals to the team; first aim for a cross-functional team 100% dedicated to one team, even if only developers and testers communicating daily.

c-7.1-plan-cost.title: 7.1 Plan Cost Management: the cost management plan
c-7.1-plan-cost.notes: Define how costs will be estimated, budgeted, managed, monitored and controlled; key benefit: guidance on cost management; once or at predefined points; occurs early and sets the framework for the other cost processes. Inputs: charter (preapproved financial resources; approval requirements); plan (schedule management plan, risk management plan - both affect estimation and management); EEFs (culture and structure, market conditions, currency exchange rates, published commercial cost-rate information and seller price lists, PMIS, regional productivity differences); OPAs (financial controls procedures - time reporting, expenditure reviews, accounting codes, contract provisions; historical information; financial databases; estimating and budgeting policies). Tools: expert judgment (similar projects, industry information, estimating and budgeting, EVM); alternatives analysis (strategic funding options - self-funding, equity, debt; ways to acquire resources - make, purchase, rent, lease); meetings. Output: cost management plan - units of measure (hours, days, weeks; metres, litres, tons, cubic yards; lump sum in currency); level of precision (rounding, e.g., US$995.59 to US$1,000); level of accuracy (acceptable range such as +/-10%, may include contingency); organisational procedures links (WBS framework; the control account is the WBS component used for project cost accounting, with a code linking to the organisation's accounting system); control thresholds (agreed % variation before action); rules of performance measurement (where in the WBS control accounts are measured; EVM techniques such as weighted milestones, fixed-formula, percent complete; tracking methods and EVM equations for EAC forecasts as a validity check on the bottom-up EAC); reporting formats; additional details (strategic funding choices, currency fluctuation procedure, cost recording procedure).

c-7.2-estimate-costs.title: 7.2 Estimate Costs: ROM vs definitive accuracy, estimating techniques, three-point (triangular and beta), reserves, cost of quality
c-7.2-estimate-costs.notes: Approximate the cost of resources needed for the work; key benefit: determines monetary resources required; performed periodically as needed. A cost estimate is a quantitative assessment of likely costs, a prediction based on information known at that time; consider alternatives and trade-offs (make vs buy, buy vs lease, sharing resources). Usually in currency, sometimes staff hours/days to remove currency effects. Reviewed and refined as detail grows; accuracy improves through the life cycle: a rough order of magnitude (ROM) estimate in initiation may be -25% to +75%; later definitive estimates may narrow to -5% to +10%. Estimate all resources charged: labour, materials, equipment, services, facilities, plus inflation allowance, cost of financing, contingency. Inputs: plan (cost management plan - methods, precision, accuracy; quality management plan - activities and resources for quality objectives; scope baseline - scope statement funding constraints by period, WBS relationships, WBS dictionary and statements of work); documents (lessons learned, project schedule - resource types, quantities and time; duration estimates matter when resources are charged per unit of time or costs vary seasonally; cost of financing, resource requirements, risk register); EEFs (market conditions and supply/demand, published commercial information and price lists, exchange rates and inflation); OPAs (estimating policies, templates, historical information). Tools: expert judgment; analogous (values or attributes of a similar previous project - scope, cost, budget, duration, size, weight); parametric (statistical relationship, e.g., cost per square foot; accuracy depends on the model); bottom-up (estimate individual work packages or activities in greatest detail and roll up; cost and accuracy influenced by size of the components); three-point - most likely cM, optimistic cO, pessimistic cP; triangular distribution cE = (cO + cM + cP) / 3; beta distribution cE = (cO + 4cM + cP) / 6 (both formulas stated in the source here); data analysis - alternatives analysis (e.g., cost, schedule, resource and quality impact of buy vs make), reserve analysis (contingency reserves / contingency allowances: budget within the cost baseline for identified risks - known-unknowns, e.g., anticipated but unquantified rework; any level from activity to project; % of estimate, fixed amount or quantitative analysis; used, reduced or eliminated as information improves; clearly identified; part of the cost baseline and funding requirements), cost of quality (investment in conformance vs cost of nonconformance; short-term savings vs later problems); PMIS (spreadsheets, simulation, statistical tools); decision making - voting to engage the team, improve accuracy and commitment. Outputs: cost estimates (probable costs plus contingency for identified risks and management reserve for unplanned work; direct labour, materials, equipment, services, facilities, IT, financing and interest, inflation, exchange rates, contingency; indirect costs at activity or higher levels if included); basis of estimates (how developed, assumptions, constraints, risks included, range e.g. US$10,000 +/-10%, confidence level); document updates (assumption log, lessons learned, risk register).

c-7.3-determine-budget.title: 7.3 Determine Budget: cost aggregation, management reserve, funding limit reconciliation, cost baseline vs project budget, S-curve
c-7.3-determine-budget.notes: Aggregate estimated costs of activities or work packages into an authorised cost baseline; key benefit: the baseline against which performance is monitored and controlled; once or at predefined points. Project budget = all funds authorised to execute the project. Cost baseline = approved time-phased project budget including contingency reserves but excluding management reserves. Inputs: plan (cost management plan; resource management plan - rates, travel costs and other foreseen costs; scope baseline); documents (basis of estimates - inclusion/exclusion of indirect costs; cost estimates - activity estimates aggregate to work packages; project schedule - dates used to place costs in calendar periods; risk register - aggregate response costs); business documents (business case - critical success factors incl. financial; benefits management plan - target benefits such as NPV, timeframe, metrics); agreements (costs of purchased products, services, results); EEFs (exchange rates for multi-year, multi-currency projects); OPAs (budgeting policies, historical information, budgeting tools, reporting methods). Tools: expert judgment (financial principles, funding requirements and sources); cost aggregation (activity estimates -> work packages -> control accounts -> whole project, following the WBS); data analysis - reserve analysis establishing management reserves (withheld for management control; unforeseen work within scope; unknown-unknowns; not in the cost baseline but part of the overall project budget and funding requirements; when used, the amount is added to the cost baseline through an approved change); historical information review (parametric or analogous models, simple like cost per square foot or complex with multiple adjustment factors; reliable when historical data is accurate, parameters are readily quantifiable and models are scalable); funding limit reconciliation (reconcile planned expenditure with funding limits; variance may require rescheduling work with imposed date constraints to level the spending rate); financing (acquiring funds, often external for long-term infrastructure, industrial and public projects; funders may impose requirements). Outputs: cost baseline (summation of approved budgets: activity estimates + activity contingency -> work package estimates + work package contingency -> control accounts -> cost baseline; + management reserve = project budget; time-phased so typically shown as an S-curve; called the performance measurement baseline when using EVM; management reserve moves into the baseline only via change control). Figure 7-9: cumulative cost baseline S-curve, expenditures, step-shaped funding requirements, BAC, management reserve on top giving the project budget. Project funding requirements: total and periodic (quarterly, annually) derived from the cost baseline (projected expenditures plus anticipated liabilities); funding is often incremental and uneven (steps); total funds = cost baseline + management reserve; may include sources. Document updates: cost estimates, project schedule, risk register. Data flow: agreements from 12.2; cost baseline and project funding requirements to 7.4 Control Costs.

c-7.4-control-costs.title: 7.4 Control Costs: purpose and earned value fundamentals (PV, EV, AC, BAC, CV, SV, CPI, SPI)
c-7.4-control-costs.notes: Monitor project status to update costs and manage changes to the cost baseline; key benefit: baseline maintained; performed throughout. Updating the budget requires actual costs; any increase to the authorised budget is approved only through Perform Integrated Change Control. Tracking spending without regard to the value of work accomplished has little value beyond tracking outflow; cost control analyses spending vs work accomplished; key is managing the approved cost baseline. Cost control: influence factors that change the baseline; act on change requests in time; manage actual changes; keep expenditure within authorised funding by period, WBS component, activity and in total; monitor cost performance to isolate variances; monitor work performance against funds spent; prevent unapproved changes being included in reported cost or resource usage; inform stakeholders of approved changes and costs; bring expected overruns within acceptable limits. Inputs: plan (cost management plan, cost baseline, performance measurement baseline); lessons learned register; project funding requirements (projected expenditures plus anticipated liabilities); work performance data (costs authorised, incurred, invoiced, paid); OPAs (cost control policies, tools, reporting methods). Tools: expert judgment (variance analysis, EVA, forecasting, financial analysis); earned value analysis - compares the PMB with actual schedule and cost performance; EVM integrates scope, cost and schedule baselines into the PMB and monitors three dimensions per work package and control account. Planned value (PV): authorised budget assigned to scheduled work (excludes management reserve); at a point in time it defines the physical work that should have been done; total PV = PMB; total planned value for the project = budget at completion (BAC). Earned value (EV): work performed expressed as the budget authorised for that work; cannot exceed the PV budget for a component; used for percent complete; needs progress measurement criteria per WBS component; monitored incrementally (status) and cumulatively (trends). Actual cost (AC): realised cost incurred for the work measured by EV in a period; must match the definition used for PV and EV (e.g., direct hours only, direct costs only, or all costs incl. indirect); no upper limit. Variance analysis (cause, impact, corrective actions): CV = EV - AC; SV = EV - PV; VAC = BAC - EAC. SV shows ahead/behind at a point in time; SV ends at zero when the project completes because all PV is earned; best used with CPM and risk management. CV = budget surplus or deficit at a point in time; at the end equals BAC minus actual amount spent; negative CV is often hard to recover. The acceptable % range of variance tends to decrease as more work is done. SPI = EV / PV: schedule efficiency; < 1.0 less work done than planned; > 1.0 more; measures all work, so the critical path must also be analysed to judge the finish date. CPI = EV / AC: cost efficiency of budgeted resources; the most critical EVA metric; < 1.0 cost overrun for work completed; > 1.0 underrun. Trend analysis: charts of PV, EV and AC per period and cumulative (Figure 7-12 S-curves show a project over budget and behind schedule). (Continued on PDF 301.) Data flow: WPD from 4.3; project funding requirements from 7.3; WPI and cost forecasts to 4.5; change requests to 4.6.

c-7.4-forecasting-tcpi.title: 7.4 Control Costs (continued): EAC forecasting methods, ETC, VAC, reserve analysis, TCPI, Table 7-1
c-7.4-forecasting-tcpi.notes: Figure 7-12: cumulative S-curves of PV, EV and AC against a data date, with BAC, EAC, ETC, management reserve and project budget marked - example over budget and behind schedule. Forecasting: when BAC is no longer viable, consider the forecasted EAC; forecasts are projections from current performance and other knowledge, regenerated from work performance data. EAC is typically actual cost for completed work plus an estimate to complete (ETC). Most common: the PM and team's manual bottom-up forecast - EAC = AC + bottom-up ETC (new estimate of the remaining work), compared with calculated EACs for risk scenarios using cumulative CPI and SPI. Three common calculated methods: (1) ETC at the budgeted rate - EAC = AC + (BAC - EV): accepts actual performance to date but assumes future work at plan; when performance is unfavourable, assume improvement only if supported by risk analysis; (2) ETC at the present CPI - EAC = BAC / CPI: past cost efficiency continues; (3) ETC considering both SPI and CPI - EAC = AC + [(BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI)]: useful when the schedule affects remaining effort; variants weight CPI and SPI (80/20, 50/50). Reserve analysis during control: monitor contingency and management reserves - still needed, used for risk responses, add savings from captured opportunities to contingency or take as margin/profit, remove unused contingency when risks don't occur, request more if new risk analysis requires. TCPI: the cost performance that must be achieved on the remaining work to meet a management goal = cost to finish outstanding work / remaining budget. TCPI based on BAC = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC); once an EAC is approved it may replace BAC: TCPI based on EAC = (BAC - EV) / (EAC - AC). Figure 7-13: if cumulative CPI falls below baseline, remaining work must immediately be performed at TCPI (BAC) to stay within the BAC; whether achievable is a judgment (risk, time remaining, technical performance); the alternative is the TCPI (EAC) line. Table 7-1 (verified): PV - authorised budget assigned to scheduled work; EV - work performed in terms of its authorised budget (EV = sum of PV of completed work); AC - realised cost of work performed; BAC - sum of all budgets for the work (the cost baseline); CV = EV - AC (positive under cost, neutral on, negative over); SV = EV - PV (positive ahead, neutral on, negative behind); VAC = BAC - EAC (positive under, negative over); CPI = EV / AC (>1 under cost, 1 on, <1 over); SPI = EV / PV (>1 ahead, 1 on, <1 behind); EAC = BAC / CPI if CPI expected to continue; EAC = AC + BAC - EV if future work at planned rate; EAC = AC + bottom-up ETC if initial plan no longer valid; EAC = AC + [(BAC - EV)/(CPI x SPI)] if both indices influence remaining work; ETC = EAC - AC assuming work proceeds on plan, or ETC = reestimate from the bottom up; TCPI = (BAC - EV)/(BAC - AC) efficiency to complete on plan; TCPI = (BAC - EV)/(EAC - AC) efficiency to complete the current EAC; TCPI >1 harder to complete, 1 same, <1 easier. Source note: the Table 7-1 'How Used' text for SPI repeats cost wording ('how much costs are over or under the budgeted amount for work planned') - lessons describe SPI in schedule terms and flag this. PMIS monitors PV, EV, AC, shows trends and forecasts ranges. Outputs: WPI (work and cost variances at work package and control account level; CV, CPI, EAC, VAC, TCPI for work performance reports); cost forecasts (calculated or bottom-up EAC documented and communicated); change requests; plan updates (cost management plan - thresholds, accuracy; cost baseline; performance measurement baseline - revised when variances are severe); document updates (assumption log - productivity assumptions, basis of estimates, cost estimates - actual efficiency, lessons learned, risk register - when variances cross or may cross the cost threshold).

c-cost-overview.title: Project Cost Management overview: four processes, life-cycle cost, measuring cost, earned schedule trend, tailoring, agile
c-cost-overview.section: 7 intro, key concepts, trends, tailoring, agile (Figure 7-1)
c-cost-overview.notes: Planning, estimating, budgeting, financing, funding, managing and controlling costs so the project completes within the approved budget. Processes: 7.1 Plan Cost Management (how costs will be estimated, budgeted, managed, monitored, controlled); 7.2 Estimate Costs (approximation of monetary resources needed); 7.3 Determine Budget (aggregate estimated costs of activities or work packages into an authorised cost baseline); 7.4 Control Costs (monitor status, update costs, manage changes to the cost baseline). On small projects estimating and budgeting may be one process. The ability to influence cost is greatest early in the project, so early scope definition is critical. Key concepts: primarily the cost of resources to complete activities, but also consider effects of project decisions on recurring costs of using, maintaining and supporting the product (life-cycle costing - e.g., fewer design reviews may cut project cost but raise operating cost). Stakeholders measure cost differently and at different times (when committed, ordered, delivered, or incurred/recorded). Predicting the product's financial performance (ROI, discounted cash flow, payback) is often outside the project, but may be included (e.g., capital facilities). Trend: earned schedule (ES) extends EVM - replaces SV = EV - PV with SV = ES - AT (actual time); if ES - AT is greater than 0 the project is ahead of schedule; SPI = ES / AT; also forecasts completion dates from ES, AT and estimated duration. (Source wording says 'if the amount of earned schedule is greater than 0'; the lesson will state the comparison as ES - AT > 0 and flag the wording.) Tailoring: knowledge management and financial databases, estimating and budgeting policies, use of EVM, agile approaches, governance. Agile: with high uncertainty or undefined scope, detailed cost calculations may not pay off; use lightweight estimation for a fast high-level labour cost forecast, detailed estimates just-in-time for short horizons; under strict budgets, scope and schedule are adjusted to stay within cost. ITTOs for 7.1-7.4 recorded in ittos.json from Figure 7-1.

e-eefs.title: Enterprise environmental factors (internal and external)
