e-eefs.notes: EEFs = conditions not under the project team's control that influence, constrain or direct the project; internal and/or external; inputs to many processes, especially most planning processes; may enhance or constrain options and affect outcomes positively or negatively. Internal: organisational culture, structure and governance (vision, mission, values, norms, leadership style, hierarchy, ethics, code of conduct); geographic distribution of facilities and resources (factory locations, virtual teams, shared systems, cloud); infrastructure (facilities, equipment, telecom, IT hardware, capacity); IT software (scheduling tools, configuration management systems, web interfaces, work authorisation systems); resource availability (contracting/purchasing constraints, approved providers, collaboration agreements); employee capability. External: marketplace conditions (competitors, market share, brand, trademarks); social and cultural influences (political climate, codes of conduct, ethics, perceptions); legal restrictions (security, data protection, business conduct, employment, procurement laws); commercial databases (benchmarks, standard cost-estimating data, industry risk studies, risk databases); academic research; government or industry standards (regulations on products, production, environment, quality, workmanship); financial considerations (exchange, interest and inflation rates, tariffs, location); physical environmental elements (working conditions, weather, constraints).

e-governance.title: Organisational and project governance frameworks
e-governance.notes: Governance = organisational or structural arrangements at all levels designed to determine and influence members' behaviour; multidimensional (people, roles, structures, policies) and requires direction and oversight through data and feedback. It is the framework within which authority is exercised: rules, policies, procedures, norms, relationships, systems and processes, influencing how objectives are set and achieved, risk is monitored and assessed, and performance optimised. PMI's governance practice guide describes four domains - alignment, risk, performance, communications - each with functions of oversight, control, integration and decision making. Project governance = the framework, functions and processes guiding project management activities to create a unique product, service or result meeting organisational, strategic and operational goals. No single framework fits all; tailor to culture, project types and needs.

e-management-elements.title: Management elements (general management principles)
e-management-elements.notes: Components comprising key functions or principles of general management, allocated according to the governance framework and structure type: division of work by specialised skills; authority to perform work; responsibility assigned by skill and experience; discipline of action; unity of command (one person gives orders to an individual); unity of direction (one plan and one head for activities with the same objective); organisational goals above individual goals; fair pay; optimal use of resources; clear communication channels; right materials to the right person at the right time; fair and equal treatment; clear security of positions; workplace safety; open contribution to planning and execution; optimal morale. In hierarchical structures, responsibility, accountability and authority at each level determine how these functions are performed.

e-opas.title: Organisational process assets: processes/policies/procedures and knowledge repositories
e-opas.notes: OPAs = plans, processes, policies, procedures and knowledge bases specific to and used by the performing organisation, including lessons learned, historical information, completed schedules, risk data and earned value data; inputs to many processes; the team may update and add to them. Two categories. (1) Processes, policies and procedures: generally not updated by project work; established by the PMO or another function and changed only through organisational policy, though some organisations let teams tailor templates, life cycles and checklists. Initiating/Planning examples: tailoring guidelines; policies (HR, health and safety, security, quality, procurement, environmental); life cycles and methods; templates (plans, registers, report formats, contracts, risk categories, probability and impact definitions and matrices, stakeholder register); preapproved supplier lists and contract types (fixed-price, cost-reimbursable, T&M). Executing/M&C examples: change control procedures; traceability matrices; financial controls (time reporting, expenditure reviews, accounting codes); issue and defect management; resource availability control; communication requirements (technology, media, record retention, security); work authorisation procedures; templates (risk register, issue log, change log); guidelines, proposal evaluation and performance measurement criteria; verification and validation procedures. Closing: closure guidelines (final audits, evaluations, deliverable acceptance, contract closure, resource reassignment, knowledge transfer). (2) Organisational knowledge repositories: updated throughout the project - configuration management repositories, financial data repositories, historical information and lessons learned, issue and defect data, metrics data, and project files from previous projects (baselines, calendars, network diagrams, risk registers and reports, stakeholder registers).

e-organizational-systems.title: Organisational systems and systems principles
e-organizational-systems.notes: Projects operate within constraints imposed by structure and governance; the PM must understand where responsibility, accountability and authority reside to use power, influence, competence, leadership and political capability. System factors: management elements, governance frameworks, organisational structure types. A system is a collection of components producing results not obtainable individually; a component is an identifiable element providing a function. Principles: systems are dynamic; systems can be optimised; components can be optimised; systems and their components cannot be optimised at the same time; systems are nonlinear in responsiveness. Management examines optimisation trade-offs between components and the system; the PM must take the results into account.

e-pmo.title: Project management office: types and functions
e-pmo.notes: A PMO is an organisational structure that standardises project governance processes and facilitates sharing of resources, methodologies, tools and techniques; responsibilities range from support to directly managing projects. Supportive PMO: consultative - templates, best practices, training, information, lessons learned; acts as a repository; low control. Controlling PMO: support plus required compliance (frameworks/methodologies, templates and tools, governance conformance); moderate control. Directive PMO: directly manages projects; PMs assigned by and report to the PMO; high control. A PMO may have organisation-wide responsibility, support strategic alignment, integrate strategic project data, and act as liaison between portfolios, programs, projects and measurement systems (e.g., balanced scorecard). It may make recommendations, lead knowledge transfer, terminate projects. Primary support functions: managing shared resources, developing methodology and standards, coaching/mentoring/training/oversight, monitoring compliance through project audits, managing policies, procedures and templates (OPAs), coordinating communication across projects.

e-project-influences.title: Project influences: EEFs, OPAs and organisational systems
e-project-influences.notes: Projects operate in environments whose influences may be favourable or unfavourable. Two major categories: enterprise environmental factors (EEFs), originating outside the project and often outside the enterprise, with impact at organisational, portfolio, program or project level; and organisational process assets (OPAs), internal to the organisation, from the organisation, a portfolio, program, other project or a combination. Figure 2-1: EEFs split internal/external; OPAs split into processes, policies and procedures and the corporate knowledge base. Organisational systems (Section 2.4) also shape power, influence, interests, competence and political capability.

e-structure-types.title: Organisational structure types and their influence on projects
e-structure-types.notes: No one-size-fits-all structure; it results from trade-offs. Table 2-1 compares by work-group arrangement, PM authority, PM role, resource availability, who manages the budget and PM administrative staff. Organic/simple: flexible, side-by-side; authority little or none; part-time coordinator role; owner or operator manages budget. Functional (centralised): arranged by job being done; authority little or none; part-time role; functional manager manages budget; admin staff part-time. Multi-divisional: by product, process, portfolio, program, region or customer type; authority little or none; functional manager budget. Weak matrix: job function; authority low; part-time role done as part of another job; resource availability low; functional manager budget. Balanced matrix: job function; authority low to moderate; part-time role embedded as a skill; resource availability low to moderate; budget mixed. Strong matrix: by job function with PM as a function; authority moderate to high; full-time designated role; resources moderate to high; PM manages budget; full-time admin staff. Project-oriented (composite, hybrid): by project; authority high to almost total; full-time; resources high to almost total; PM manages budget; full-time staff. Virtual: network structure; authority low to moderate; full- or part-time; budget mixed. Hybrid: mix of other types; everything mixed. PMO: mix; authority high to almost total; full-time; PM manages budget. Selection factors: alignment with objectives, specialisation, span of control/efficiency/effectiveness, clear escalation path, clear line and scope of authority, delegation, accountability and responsibility assignment, adaptability and simplicity of design, efficiency, cost, physical locations (colocated, regional, virtual), clear communication.

f-business-documents.title: Project business documents: business case and benefits management plan
f-business-documents.notes: Two business documents, interdependent and iteratively maintained across the life cycle. Business case = documented economic feasibility study establishing the validity of benefits of a selected component that lacks sufficient definition; basis for authorising further project management activities; lists objectives and reasons for initiation; used before initiation (may yield go/no-go) and to measure success at the end. The sponsor is generally accountable for the business case; the PM provides recommendations and oversight to keep business case, project management plan, charter and benefits plan success measures aligned with each other and with organisational goals. They may be held at program level. A needs assessment often precedes the business case (understanding goals, issues and opportunities and recommending proposals). Business case contents: business needs (what prompts action, situational statement of problem/opportunity and value, affected stakeholders, scope); analysis of the situation (strategies/goals, root causes, gap analysis of needed vs existing capabilities, known risks, critical success factors, decision criteria classed required/desired/optional, options such as do nothing ('business as usual', project not authorised), do the minimum, do more than the minimum); recommendation (option, analysis results, constraints/assumptions/risks/dependencies, success measures, implementation approach with milestones, dependencies, roles); evaluation (plan for measuring benefits, including ongoing operations). Benefits management plan = how and when benefits will be delivered and measured; a benefit is an outcome providing value to the sponsoring organisation and intended beneficiaries. Elements: target benefits (financial value expressed as NPV), strategic alignment, timeframe, benefits owner (accountable for monitoring and reporting realised benefits), metrics (direct and indirect), assumptions, risks. Uses business case and needs assessment data (e.g., cost-benefit analyses). Figure 1-8 timeline: needs assessment and business case are pre-project; charter at starting the project; project management plan through organising/preparing and carrying out the work; benefits management plan spans the life cycle.

f-business-value.title: Business value: tangible and intangible benefits
f-business-value.notes: PMI defines business value as the net quantifiable benefit derived from a business endeavour; it may be tangible, intangible or both. Business value in projects is the benefit a project's results provide to stakeholders. Tangible examples: monetary assets, stockholder equity, utility, fixtures, tools, market share. Intangible examples: goodwill, brand recognition, public benefit, trademarks, strategic alignment, reputation.

f-charter-and-plan-defs.title: Project charter and project management plan defined
f-charter-and-plan-defs.notes: Project charter: issued by the sponsor, formally authorises the existence of the project and gives the PM authority to apply organisational resources to project activities. Project management plan: describes how the project will be executed, monitored and controlled. Both detailed in Chapter 4.

f-data-information-reports.title: Work performance data, information and reports and how they flow
f-data-information-reports.notes: Work performance data (WPD) = raw observations and measurements from executing work (percent physically complete, quality and technical measures, activity start/finish dates, number of change requests and defects, actual costs and durations), usually recorded in the PMIS. Work performance information (WPI) = WPD collected from controlling processes, analysed in context and integrated across areas (deliverable status, change-request implementation status, forecast estimate to complete). Work performance reports (WPR) = physical or electronic representation of WPI in project documents intended to drive decisions or raise issues, actions or awareness (status reports, memos, dashboards, recommendations). Figure 1-7 flow: Executing processes produce WPD -> controlling processes turn it into WPI -> overall project control (Monitor and Control Project Work) produces WPR -> project communications to team and stakeholders; project change control (Perform Integrated Change Control) returns approved change requests and plan/document updates. Exam-critical sequence: data (Executing) -> information (Monitoring & Controlling processes) -> reports (4.5).

f-guide-purpose.title: Purpose of the PMBOK Guide: generally recognised good practice, tailoring, guide vs methodology
f-guide-purpose.notes: The project management body of knowledge (BOK) is everything known in the profession, published or not, and keeps evolving; the Guide covers only the subset that is 'generally recognized' (applies to most projects most of the time, with consensus on value) and 'good practice' (applying it improves the odds of success). Choosing the right mix of processes, ITTOs and life-cycle phases for a project is tailoring. The Guide is not a methodology (a system of practices, techniques, procedures and rules); organisations build methodologies on top of it. The Guide is based on The Standard for Project Management, an ANSI standard built on consensus, openness, due process and balance; both are descriptive, not prescriptive - nothing in them must be performed. Portfolio and program management have their own PMI standards and appear in the Guide only where they interact with projects.

f-importance-of-pm.title: Project management defined and why it matters
f-importance-of-pm.notes: Project management is the application of knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to project activities to meet project requirements, achieved by applying and integrating the processes identified for the project. Effective PM helps meet business objectives, satisfy stakeholders, be more predictable, raise chances of success, deliver the right products at the right time, resolve issues, respond to risks in time, optimise resources, identify/recover/terminate failing projects, manage and balance constraints (scope, quality, schedule, cost, resources) and manage change. Poor PM leads to missed deadlines, overruns, poor quality, rework, uncontrolled expansion, reputational loss, unhappy stakeholders and failed objectives. PM should be a strategic competency: tie results to business goals, compete, sustain the organisation and adjust plans to environmental change.

f-initiation-context.title: Project initiation context: the four categories of factors that create projects
f-initiation-context.notes: Leaders initiate projects in response to factors acting on the organisation, in four categories: meet regulatory, legal or social requirements; satisfy stakeholder requests or needs; implement or change business or technological strategies; create, improve or fix products, processes or services. These factors should link to strategic objectives and business value. Table 1-1 (visually verified) gives specific factors - new technology, competitive forces, material issues, political changes, market demand, economic changes, customer request, stakeholder demands, legal requirement, business process improvements, strategic opportunity or business need, social need, environmental considerations - and shows one factor can fall into more than one category (e.g., market demand maps to stakeholder needs, create/improve products and strategy; material issues map to regulatory and fix products).

f-key-components.title: Key components of the Guide and how they interrelate
f-key-components.notes: Key components: project life cycle, project phase, phase gate, project management processes, Process Groups and Knowledge Areas. Figure 1-5 places a generic life cycle (starting the project, organising and preparing, carrying out the work, ending the project) with phase gates on a timeline, and shows the five Process Groups and ten Knowledge Areas operating across it. Process Groups are not phases.

f-knowledge-areas.title: The ten Knowledge Areas
f-knowledge-areas.notes: A Knowledge Area is an area of PM defined by its knowledge requirements and described by its processes, practices, inputs, outputs, tools and techniques. Integration (identify, define, combine, unify and coordinate processes), Scope (all the work required and only the work required), Schedule (timely completion), Cost (planning, estimating, budgeting, financing, funding, managing, controlling costs within the approved budget), Quality (incorporating the quality policy for project and product quality requirements), Resource (identify, acquire, manage resources), Communications (planning through ultimate disposition of project information), Risk (planning, identification, analysis, response planning, implementation, monitoring), Procurement (acquiring products, services or results from outside the project team), Stakeholder (identify people affected, analyse expectations and engage them). Some projects need extra areas, e.g., financial or safety and health management in construction.

f-life-cycles.title: Project and development life cycles: predictive, iterative, incremental, adaptive, hybrid
f-life-cycles.notes: Project life cycle = the phases a project passes through from start to completion (sequential, iterative or overlapping); all projects map to the generic life cycle. Within it, the phases that develop the product form the development life cycle. Predictive (waterfall): scope, time and cost fixed early; scope changes carefully managed. Iterative: scope set early but time and cost estimates are revised as understanding grows; iterations repeat cycles. Incremental: successive iterations add functionality within a predetermined time frame; the deliverable is complete only after the final iteration. Adaptive (agile/change-driven): detailed scope defined and approved before each iteration. Hybrid: known/fixed parts predictive, evolving parts adaptive. The team chooses the best life cycle; flexibility comes from choosing processes per phase and adjusting phase attributes. Project life cycle is independent of the product life cycle (concept, delivery, growth, maturity, retirement).

f-operations-and-projects.title: Operations management and where operations meet projects
f-operations-and-projects.notes: Operations management (outside the Guide's scope) concerns ongoing production of goods or services, transforming inputs into outputs efficiently. Ongoing operations are outside a project's scope, but they intersect: developing, upgrading or expanding products; improving operations or product development; end of product life cycle; each closeout phase. At each point deliverables and knowledge transfer between project and operations, by moving project resources/knowledge to operations or operational resources to the project.

f-opm.title: Organisational project management (OPM) and strategy alignment
f-opm.notes: Portfolio management aligns with strategy by selecting, prioritising and resourcing work; program management harmonises components and interdependencies to realise benefits; project management enables organisational goals. OPM is a framework integrating portfolio, program and project management with organisational enablers to achieve strategic objectives; its purpose is to make sure the organisation undertakes the right projects and allocates critical resources appropriately, and that all levels understand the strategic vision. Figure 1-4: strategy drives portfolio value decisions; programs and projects deliver results; operations realise business value; feedback via business impact analysis and value performance analysis into portfolio review and adjustment.

f-phases-and-gates.title: Project phases and phase gates
f-phases-and-gates.notes: A phase is a collection of logically related activities culminating in one or more deliverables. Attributes: name, number, duration, resource requirements, entrance criteria, exit criteria. Typical names include concept development, feasibility, requirements, design, prototype, build, test, transition, commissioning, milestone review, lessons learned. Phases are set by management needs, nature of the project, organisation/industry/technology, project elements and decision points (funding, go/no-go). Multiple phases improve insight and allow corrective or preventive action in later phases. A phase gate at the end of a phase compares performance to the business case, charter, project management plan and benefits management plan, leading to a decision: continue, continue with modification, end the project, remain in the phase, or repeat the phase or parts. Other names: phase review, stage gate, kill point, phase entrance/exit.

f-pm-processes.title: Project management processes, ITTOs and how often processes run
f-pm-processes.notes: Each process turns one or more inputs into one or more outputs using tools and techniques; an output is a deliverable or an outcome (end result of a process). Processes are linked by their outputs: an output becomes an input to another process or a project/phase deliverable. Three frequency categories: once or at predefined points (Develop Project Charter, Close Project or Phase); periodically as needed (Acquire Resources as resources are needed; Conduct Procurements before the item is needed); continuously (Define Activities under rolling wave or adaptive approaches; most monitoring and controlling processes).

f-portfolio-management.title: Portfolio management aims
f-portfolio-management.notes: Portfolio management is the centralised management of one or more portfolios to achieve strategic objectives; components need not be interdependent. Aims: guide investment decisions, select the optimal mix of programs and projects, make decisions transparent, prioritise team and physical resources, raise likelihood of the desired ROI, and centralise management of the aggregate risk profile. It confirms alignment with strategy and prioritises components by contribution. Example: an infrastructure firm with power and water portfolios; designing, building then operating a power plant can be grouped as one program inside the portfolio.

f-portfolio-program-project.title: Portfolios, programs, projects and operations compared
f-portfolio-program-project.notes: A project can be stand-alone, within a program or within a portfolio. Program = related projects, subsidiary programs and program activities managed in a coordinated way to obtain benefits not available individually; programs are not large projects. A very large project is a megaproject (guideline: US$1 billion or more, affects 1 million or more people, runs for years). Portfolio = projects, programs, subsidiary portfolios and operations managed as a group to achieve strategic objectives. They share stakeholders and resources, which can cause conflict and needs coordination. Program and project management do things the 'right way'; portfolio management does the 'right' programs and projects. Table 1-2 compares definition, scope (projects: defined objectives, progressively elaborated; programs: encompass component scopes; portfolios: organisational scope changing with strategy), change (projects control it; programs adapt to optimise benefits; portfolios monitor the wider environment), planning, management, monitoring and success measures (projects: product and project quality, timeliness, budget compliance, customer satisfaction; programs: delivery of intended benefits; portfolios: aggregate investment performance and benefit realisation).

f-process-groups.title: The five Project Management Process Groups
f-process-groups.notes: A Process Group is a logical grouping of processes to achieve specific objectives; independent of phases. Initiating: define a new project or phase by obtaining authorisation. Planning: establish scope, refine objectives and define the course of action. Executing: complete the work in the project management plan to satisfy requirements. Monitoring and Controlling: track, review and regulate progress and performance, identify needed plan changes and initiate them. Closing: formally complete or close the project, phase or contract. Outputs of one process can feed processes in other groups.

Total 49. Machine-readable copy: docs/pmp-curriculum/process-map.json.

f-program-management.title: Program management and program-level interdependencies
f-program-management.notes: Program management applies knowledge, skills and principles to achieve program objectives and gain benefits and control not available by managing components individually; a program component is a project or program within it. Project management focuses on interdependencies within a project; program management on interdependencies between projects and the program level: aligning with strategy, allocating program scope, managing component interdependencies, shared risks and constraints, resolving issues between components and program, managing change in a shared governance framework, allocating budgets across projects and assuring benefits realisation. Example: a communications satellite system with projects for satellite and ground station design/build, launch and system integration.

f-project-definition.title: What a project is: temporary, unique, deliverables and objectives; when a project ends
f-project-definition.notes: A project is a temporary endeavour to create a unique product, service or result. Objective = an outcome toward which work is directed (a position, purpose, result, product or service). Deliverable = any unique and verifiable product, result or capability to perform a service required to complete a process, phase or project; may be tangible or intangible. Deliverables can be a product (component, enhancement, correction or new end item), a service or capability, a result (e.g., research findings, a document) or a combination. Repetitive elements do not remove uniqueness (two similar office buildings still differ in location, design, people). Projects occur at every organisational level, with one person or many units. Temporary = definite beginning and end, not necessarily short. A project ends when objectives are achieved, they will not or cannot be met, funding is exhausted, the need no longer exists, human or physical resources are no longer available, or it is terminated for legal cause or convenience. Deliverables may outlive the project (e.g., a monument).

f-projects-drive-change.title: Projects drive change: current state, transition state, future state
f-projects-drive-change.notes: From a business view a project moves an organisation from a current state to a desired future state to achieve a specific objective; some projects pass through a transition state of several steps. Figure 1-1 shows business value rising over time as project activities move the organisation from current to future state.

f-success-measures.title: Project success measures and financial measures
f-success-measures.notes: Traditionally time, cost, scope and quality defined success; now achievement of project objectives also counts. Stakeholders may disagree on success, so document measurable objectives and agree answers to: what does success look like, how will it be measured, what factors may affect it. Further criteria: completing the benefits management plan; meeting financial measures in the business case - net present value (NPV), return on investment (ROI), internal rate of return (IRR), payback period (PBP), benefit-cost ratio (BCR); nonfinancial business case objectives; reaching the future state; contract terms; strategy and goals; stakeholder satisfaction; customer/end-user adoption; integration of deliverables into operations; agreed quality; governance criteria; other agreed measures (e.g., throughput). Constant business alignment raises the chance of success. A project can succeed on scope/schedule/budget yet fail from a business viewpoint if business needs or the market change before completion. (Formulas for NPV, IRR etc. are not given in the Guide; lessons will flag any formula as supplementary.)

f-tailoring.title: Tailoring project management to the project
f-tailoring.notes: Methodologies may be developed in-house, bought from vendors, obtained from professional associations or acquired from government agencies; the Guide is not one. Tailoring = selecting the appropriate processes, inputs, tools, techniques, outputs and life-cycle phases; the PM tailors with the team, sponsor and/or organisational management, and some organisations mandate a methodology. Needed because every project is unique and not every element is needed on every project. Tailoring should address the competing constraints of scope, schedule, cost, resources, quality and risk, whose importance differs per project, considering environment, culture, stakeholder needs, required governance levels and whether the customer is internal or external. Even a tailorable methodology may need further tailoring per project.

f-vocabulary-ethics.title: Common vocabulary and the PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct
f-vocabulary-ethics.notes: A shared vocabulary is a mark of a profession; the PMI Lexicon supplies it and the Guide's glossary includes the Lexicon plus more terms. The Code of Ethics rests on four values chosen by the global community: responsibility, respect, fairness and honesty. It has aspirational standards (conduct practitioners strive for; hard to measure but expected of professionals, not optional) and mandatory standards (firm requirements; breaches by PMI members, certification holders or volunteers go to PMI's Ethics Review Committee).

g-apg-glossary.title: Agile Practice Guide glossary: agile terms and definitions
g-apg-glossary.notes: Acronyms: ATDD, BDD, BRD, DA, DoD, DoR, DSDM, Evo, LeSS, LSD, PDCA, PMO, ROI, RUP, SAFe, SBE, XP. Key definitions for lessons and items: A3 (problem-solving on a single A3 sheet); ATDD (collaboratively creating acceptance criteria and tests before delivery); agile (a mindset of values and principles per the Manifesto); agile coach; agile life cycle (both iterative and incremental); agile mindset (four values and twelve principles); anti-pattern (known flawed pattern of work); backlog refinement (progressive elaboration of requirements, collaboratively reviewing, updating and writing them); g-glossary-a-c.title: Glossary definitions A-C (Acceptance Criteria to Criteria): key precise wordings and glossary-only facts
g-glossary-a-c.notes: Definitions are consistent with the body; items noted for teaching precision: accuracy (within a quality management system, an assessment of correctness); acquisition (obtaining human and material resources; implies a cost, not necessarily financial); activity (a distinct, scheduled portion of work); activity duration (calendar time between start and finish); actual duration (actual start to the data date if in progress, or to actual finish); adaptive life cycle (a project life cycle that is iterative or incremental); agreements (any document or communication defining initial intentions - contract, MOU, letters of agreement, verbal agreements, email); assumption (a factor considered true, real or certain without proof or demonstration); attribute sampling (noting presence or absence of a characteristic in each unit); authority (the right to apply resources, expend funds, make decisions or give approvals); backward pass (calculating late start and late finish dates working backward from the project end date); baseline (approved version of a work product changed only through formal change control, used for comparison); benefits management plan (processes for creating, maximising and sustaining benefits of a project or program); bid documents (all documents used to solicit information, quotations or proposals); budget (approved estimate for the project, any WBS component or activity); buffer (see reserve); cause and effect diagram (a decomposition technique tracing an undesirable effect back to its root cause); change (modification to any formally controlled deliverable, plan component or document); change control system (procedures describing how modifications to deliverables and documentation are managed); change log (comprehensive list of submitted changes and their status); change management plan (establishes the CCB, documents its authority, describes how the change control system is implemented); checklist analysis; checksheets (tally sheet usable as a checklist when gathering data); claim (request, demand or assertion of rights by a seller against a buyer or vice versa under a contract, e.g., for a disputed change); claims administration; code of accounts (numbering system uniquely identifying each WBS component); colocation (team physically close to improve communication, relationships and productivity); communication requirements analysis (via interviews, workshops, lessons learned); configuration management plan and system; conformance (results within limits defining acceptable variation); constraint (limiting factor affecting execution of a project, program, portfolio or process); contingency (an event that could affect execution and may be accounted for with a reserve); contingency reserve (time or money in the schedule or cost baseline for known risks with active response strategies); contract (mutually binding agreement obligating the seller to provide and the buyer to pay); contract change control system; control (compare actual with planned, analyse variances, assess trends, evaluate alternatives, recommend corrective action); control account (management control point integrating scope, budget, actual cost and schedule and comparing to EV); control chart (process data over time against control limits with a centreline to detect trends); control limits - glossary-only detail: the area of three standard deviations either side of the centreline or mean of a normal distribution, reflecting expected variation (see also specification limits); cost baseline (excludes management reserves); cost-benefit analysis (benefits against costs); CPAF/CPFF/CPIF and cost-reimbursable contract definitions consistent with Section 12; crashing; criteria. The CCB definition here says 'approving, delaying, or rejecting' where the body says 'deferring' - same meaning.

g-glossary-c-s.title: Glossary definitions C-S (Critical Path to Start-to-Finish): precise wordings and glossary-only facts
g-glossary-c-s.notes: Consistent with the body; items valuable for precision or found only in the glossary: data (discrete, unorganised, unprocessed measurements or raw observations) vs information (organised or structured data processed for a purpose to make it meaningful) vs knowledge (mixture of experience, values and beliefs, context, intuition and insight used to make sense of new experiences); data date (point in time when project status is recorded); decision tree analysis (diagramming and calculation technique for evaluating a chain of options under uncertainty); defect (imperfection or deficiency where a component does not meet requirements or specifications and must be repaired or replaced) and rework (action to bring a defective component into compliance); development approach (method to create and evolve the product - predictive, iterative, incremental, agile, hybrid); discrete effort (an activity that can be planned and measured and yields a specific output - glossary note: one of three EVM activity types used to measure work performance; level of effort (LOE) is another - an activity that does not produce definitive end products and is measured by the passage of time; the third type, apportioned effort, is not defined in this glossary - lessons will flag this); duration (total work periods to complete an activity, in hours, days or weeks) vs effort (labour units required) - contrast; early/late start and finish dates defined relative to network logic, data date or project completion date and constraints; earned value management (methodology combining scope, schedule and resource measurements to assess performance and progress); EEFs here say 'not under the immediate control of the team'; estimate; execute (directing, managing, performing and accomplishing work, providing deliverables and work performance information); fallback plan (alternative actions if the primary plan must be abandoned); fee (profit component of seller compensation); fixed-price contract (fee for a defined scope regardless of cost or effort); float = slack (total float and free float); forward pass; functional organisation (staff grouped by specialisation, PM has limited authority); grade (category for items with the same functional use but different quality requirements); ground rules; imposed date (fixed date, e.g., 'start no earlier than', 'finish no later than'); incentive fee; independent estimates (third party analyses information to predict cost, schedule etc.); input (any item required by a process before it proceeds, possibly a predecessor's output) and output (product, result or service generated by a process, possibly an input to a successor); invitation for bid (generally equivalent to RFP, narrower in some areas); issue (a current condition that may impact objectives) vs risk (uncertain future event or condition); lag and lead; lessons learned, register and repository; logical relationship (dependency between two activities or an activity and a milestone); management reserve (budget or schedule held outside the performance measurement baseline for management control, for unforeseen in-scope work); management skills (plan, organise, direct and control people); master schedule and milestone schedule; matrix organisation (PM shares responsibility with functional managers for priorities and directing work); methodology; milestone; monitor (collect data, produce measures, report and disseminate information) - control defined separately; Monte Carlo simulation (model iterated many times with random inputs from distributions and probabilistic branches); network logic, network path, node; opportunity (risk with a positive effect); OBS (hierarchical representation of the project organisation relating activities to performing units); organisational learning; percent complete; performance measurement baseline (integrated scope, schedule and cost baselines); performance reviews; phase gate (decision to continue, continue with modification or end a project or program); planned value; planning package (below the control account with known content but no detailed activities); plurality; policy, practice, procedure, process definitions; procurement audits (review of contracts and contracting processes for completeness, accuracy, effectiveness); procurement documents (bid and proposal documents incl. IFB, invitation for negotiations, RFI, RFQ, RFP and seller responses) vs procurement documentation (all documents used in signing, executing and closing an agreement, possibly predating the project); product (quantifiable artefact, end item or component); progressive elaboration (iteratively increasing plan detail as information and estimates improve); project funding requirements; project initiation (launching a process that can result in authorisation); project management system (aggregation of processes, tools, techniques, methodologies, resources and procedures); project management team vs project team; project team directory; quality audits, checklists, metrics, policy, report, requirement; quality management system (organisational framework of policies, processes, procedures, resources; the project quality plan should be compatible with it); RACI; regression analysis; regulations (requirements imposed by a governmental body) vs standard (established by authority, custom or general consent as a model); requirement here 'to satisfy a business need'; reserve (provision to mitigate cost and/or schedule risk, often qualified as management or contingency reserve); residual risk (risk remaining after responses are implemented); resource histogram; resource leveling (may affect the critical path) vs resource smoothing (uses free and total float without affecting the critical path); responsibility (an assignment that can be delegated, creating a duty to perform); result (outcomes and documents); risk appetite (degree of uncertainty an organisation or individual will accept in anticipation of reward); risk threshold (level of exposure above which risks are addressed and below which they may be accepted); risk exposure (aggregate measure of the potential impact of all risks at a point in time); risk category, risk owner (monitors risks and selects and implements a response), risk review (meeting examining response effectiveness), risk response definitions (acceptance, avoidance, enhancement, escalation - shifting ownership to a higher organisational level, exploiting, mitigation, sharing, transference); role; schedule model and scheduling tool; scope (sum of products, services and results); secondary risk; self-organising teams; seller proposals; service level agreement (contract between a service provider - internal or external - and the end user defining expected service level); specification and specification limits (area either side of the mean meeting customer requirements; may be wider or narrower than the control limits); sponsor (person or group providing resources and support and accountable for enabling success) and sponsoring organisation; stakeholder analysis; standard; start date; SF relationship.

g-glossary-s-w.title: Glossary definitions S-W (Start-to-Start to Work Performance Reports)
g-glossary-s-w.notes: SS; statement of work (narrative description of products, services or results to be delivered); statistical sampling; successor activity; summary activity; SWOT analysis; tacit knowledge (personal, hard to articulate - beliefs, experience, insights); tailoring (determining the appropriate combination of processes, inputs, tools, techniques, outputs and life cycle phases); team charter (team values, agreements, operating guidelines and expectations of acceptable behaviour); team management plan (component of the resource management plan describing when and how members are acquired and how long they are needed - glossary-only term); technique vs tool (technique = defined systematic procedure employed by a human resource, possibly using tools; TCPI; tolerance (quantified acceptable variation for a quality requirement); tornado diagram (special bar chart in sensitivity analysis comparing variables' relative importance); total float; trend analysis (mathematical models forecasting outcomes from historical results); variance and variation (actual condition differing from the expected baseline condition); variance analysis; VAC; verified deliverables; virtual teams; voice of the customer (translating customer requirements into technical requirements for each phase of product development); WBS, WBS component (any level), WBS dictionary, work package (lowest level, cost and duration estimated and managed); work performance data, information (data from controlling processes analysed against plan components, documents and other WPI) and reports.

g-glossary-scope-acronyms.title: Glossary: inclusion/exclusion rules and common acronyms
g-glossary-scope-acronyms.notes: Includes terms unique or nearly unique to project management (project scope statement, work package, WBS, CPM) and terms used differently or more narrowly than in everyday usage (early start date); excludes application-area-specific terms, terms used as in everyday language (calendar day, delay), compound terms clear from their parts, obvious variants, and terms used once and not critical. Acronyms: AC, BAC, CCB, COQ, CPAF, CPFF, CPI, CPIF, CPM, CV, EAC, EF, ES, ETC, EV, EVM, FF (finish-to-finish), FFP, FPEPA, FPIF, FS, IFB (invitation for bid - appears in the acronym list though not discussed in the body), LF, LOE (level of effort), LS, OBS, PDM, PMBOK, PV, QFD, RACI, RAM, RBS (in the acronym list RBS = risk breakdown structure; the body also uses 'resource breakdown structure' without an acronym - lessons spell both out), RFI, RFP, RFQ, SF, SOW, SPI, SS, SV, SWOT, T&M, WBS, VAC.

h-13.1-identify-stakeholders.title: 13.1 Identify Stakeholders: stakeholder analysis and stakes, mapping models (grids, cube, salience, directions of influence), stakeholder register
h-13.1-identify-stakeholders.notes: Identify stakeholders regularly and analyse and document their interests, involvement, interdependencies, influence and potential impact on success; key benefit: the right focus for engaging each stakeholder or group; performed periodically as needed. Often first done before or alongside chartering; repeat at the start of each phase and with significant change, consulting plan components and documents each time. Inputs: charter (key stakeholder list, responsibilities); business documents (first iteration - business case objectives and initial stakeholder list; benefits management plan - beneficiaries); plan (not available initially; later the communications management plan and stakeholder engagement plan); documents (unlikely initially; later change log - new stakeholders or changed relationships, issue log, requirements documentation); agreements (parties are stakeholders and may reference others); EEFs (culture, political climate, governance; standards, regulations, codes of conduct; trends; geographic distribution); OPAs (stakeholder register templates, registers from previous projects, lessons learned about stakeholder preferences). Tools: expert judgment (politics and power structures, culture and environment, industry, team members' expertise); data gathering - questionnaires and surveys (one-on-one reviews, focus groups, mass collection), brainstorming and brain writing (participants consider the question individually before the group session; face-to-face or virtual); data analysis - stakeholder analysis (list with positions, roles, stakes, expectations, attitudes/levels of support, interest in information; stakes include interest (affected by decisions or outcomes), rights - legal (e.g., occupational health and safety) or moral (protecting historical sites, environmental sustainability), ownership (legal title to an asset), knowledge (specialist knowledge or knowledge of power structures), contribution (funds, resources, advocacy, buffering the project from organisational politics)); document analysis; data representation - stakeholder mapping/representation: power/interest, power/influence or impact/influence grids (group by authority, concern about outcomes, ability to influence outcomes or cause changes; suit small projects or simple relationships); stakeholder cube (three-dimensional refinement of the grids, aids communication strategies); salience model (power, urgency - need for immediate attention due to time constraints or high stakes, legitimacy - appropriateness of involvement; an adaptation substitutes proximity for legitimacy; suits large complex communities and helps determine relative importance); directions of influence (upward - senior management, sponsor, steering committee; downward - the team and temporary specialists; outward - suppliers, government departments, public, end users, regulators; sideward - peers such as other PMs or middle managers competing or collaborating over resources); prioritisation (for many stakeholders, frequently changing membership or complex relationships); meetings (facilitation workshops, guided small-group discussions, virtual groups with social media). Outputs: stakeholder register - identification information (name, position, location, contact details, project role), assessment information (major requirements, expectations, potential influence, phase of greatest influence or impact), stakeholder classification (internal/external; impact/influence/power/interest; upward/downward/outward/sideward; or another model); change requests (none in the first iteration; later new stakeholders or information may require changes); plan updates (none at the very beginning; later requirements, communications, risk and stakeholder engagement plans); document updates (assumption log - power, interest and engagement information is largely assumption-based, plus constraints on interacting with stakeholders; issue log; risk register). Data flow: charter from 4.1; agreements from 12.2; change requests to 4.6.

h-13.2-plan-engagement.title: 13.2 Plan Stakeholder Engagement: update triggers, prioritisation, engagement assessment matrix (unaware to leading), stakeholder engagement plan
h-13.2-plan-engagement.notes: Develop approaches to involve stakeholders based on needs, expectations, interests and potential impact; key benefit: an actionable plan for effective interaction; performed periodically as needed. First version after initial identification; developed early and updated as the community changes. Update triggers: start of a new phase; changes in organisation structure or industry; stakeholders joining or leaving or their importance changing; outputs of change, risk or issue management requiring a strategy review - possibly changing stakeholders' relative importance. Inputs: charter (purpose, objectives, success criteria); plan (resource management plan - roles; communications management plan - strategies are both inputs to and recipients of stakeholder processes; risk management plan - thresholds and attitudes help choose the strategy mix); documents (assumption log; change log - stakeholders request, decide on or are affected by changes; issue log; project schedule - activities owned or executed by stakeholders; risk register - owners or affected parties; stakeholder register); agreements (coordinate with procurement/contracting to manage contractors and suppliers); EEFs (culture, political climate, governance, personnel policies, stakeholder risk appetites, channels, trends, geography); OPAs (social media, ethics, security policies; issue, risk, change and data management policies; communication requirements; information guidelines; lessons learned on stakeholder preferences; software tools for engagement). Tools: expert judgment (politics and power inside and outside, culture, analytical techniques, communication strategies, knowledge of stakeholders from previous projects); benchmarking (compare stakeholder analysis with world-class organisations or projects); data analysis - assumption and constraint analysis (tailor strategies), root cause analysis (underlying reasons for a stakeholder's level of support, to pick a strategy that improves engagement); decision making - prioritisation/ranking (requirements and stakeholders; those with most interest and highest influence often at the top); data representation - mind mapping (stakeholder information and relationships), stakeholder engagement assessment matrix (compares current with desired engagement; levels: unaware - unaware of the project and impacts; resistant - aware but resistant to change, unsupportive; neutral - aware, neither supportive nor unsupportive; supportive - aware and supportive; leading - aware and actively engaged in ensuring success; C = current, D = desired; the gap directs the communication needed and closing it is essential to monitoring engagement; Figure 13-6 verified example: stakeholder 1 C = unaware, D = supportive; stakeholder 2 C = neutral, D = supportive; stakeholder 3 C and D both supportive - no gap); meetings. Output: stakeholder engagement plan (plan component identifying strategies and actions to promote productive involvement in decision making and execution; formal or informal, detailed or broad; specific strategies for individuals or groups). Data flow: charter from 4.1; agreements from 12.2.

h-13.3-manage-engagement.title: 13.3 Manage Stakeholder Engagement: activities, inputs, communication and interpersonal skills (part 1)
h-13.3-manage-engagement.notes: Communicate and work with stakeholders to meet needs and expectations, address issues and foster appropriate involvement; key benefit: increase support and minimise resistance; performed throughout. Activities: engage stakeholders at appropriate stages to obtain, confirm or maintain commitment; manage expectations through negotiation and communication; address risks or concerns related to stakeholder management and anticipate future issues; clarify and resolve identified issues. Helps stakeholders understand goals, objectives, benefits, risks and how their contribution enhances success. Inputs: plan (communications management plan - methods, formats, technologies; risk management plan - categories, appetites, reporting formats; stakeholder engagement plan - guidance on managing expectations; change management plan - submitting, evaluating, implementing changes); documents (change log - communicated to stakeholders, issue log - concerns and action items, lessons learned, stakeholder register); EEFs (culture, political climate, governance, personnel policies, stakeholder risk thresholds, channels, trends, geography); OPAs (social media, ethics, security; issue, risk, change, data management; communication requirements; information guidelines; historical information). Tools: expert judgment (politics and power, culture, analytical techniques, communication strategies, stakeholder characteristics from previous projects, requirements, vendor and change management); communication skills - apply methods from the communications plan and use feedback to understand stakeholder reactions (formal and informal conversations, issue identification and discussion, meetings, progress reporting, surveys); interpersonal skills - conflict management (resolve conflicts in a timely manner), cultural awareness, negotiation (achieve support or agreement and resolve conflicts), observation/conversation (stay in touch with work and attitudes), political awareness (power relationships within and around the project). (Continued on PDF 565.) Data flow: change requests to 4.6.

h-13.3-manage-outputs.title: 13.3 Manage Stakeholder Engagement (continued): ground rules, meeting types, outputs
h-13.3-manage-outputs.notes: Ground rules, defined in the team charter, set expected behaviour of team members and other stakeholders regarding stakeholder engagement. Meetings: decision making, issue resolution, lessons learned and retrospectives, project kick-off, sprint planning, status updates. Outputs: change requests (changes to project or product scope may emerge; processed via 4.6); plan updates (communications management plan - new or changed stakeholder requirements; stakeholder engagement plan - new or changed strategies); document updates (change log, issue log, lessons learned, stakeholder register - new information provided to stakeholders about resolved issues, approved changes and status).

h-13.4-monitor-engagement.title: 13.4 Monitor Stakeholder Engagement: analysis, decision making, engagement matrix tracking, communication and interpersonal skills, outputs
h-13.4-monitor-engagement.notes: Monitor stakeholder relationships and tailor engagement strategies by modifying strategies and plans; key benefit: maintains or increases the efficiency and effectiveness of engagement as the project and environment change; performed throughout. Inputs: plan (resource management plan - team management methods; communications management plan; stakeholder engagement plan); documents (issue log, lessons learned, project communications distributed, risk register - incl. stakeholder-related risks, stakeholder register - identification, assessment, classification); work performance data (which stakeholders are supportive, level and type of engagement); EEFs (culture, political climate, governance, personnel policies, stakeholder risk thresholds, channels, trends, geography); OPAs (social media, ethics, security; issue, risk, change, data management; communication requirements; information guidelines; historical information). Tools: data analysis - alternatives analysis (options to respond to variances in desired engagement), root cause analysis (why engagement isn't having the planned effect), stakeholder analysis (positions of groups and individuals at any time); decision making - multicriteria decision analysis (prioritised, weighted criteria for successful engagement), voting (choose the best response to an engagement variance); data representation - stakeholder engagement assessment matrix (tracks changes in each stakeholder's engagement level); communication skills - feedback (ensure information is received and understood), presentations; interpersonal skills - active listening, cultural awareness, leadership (communicate the vision and inspire support), networking (access to information on engagement levels), political awareness; meetings (status meetings, standups, retrospectives, others agreed in the engagement plan; face-to-face is ideal but expensive - technology bridges the gap). Outputs: work performance information (status of engagement - current support vs desired levels in the engagement assessment matrix, stakeholder cube or other tool); change requests (corrective and preventive actions to improve engagement); plan updates (resource management plan - team responsibilities for engagement; communications management plan; stakeholder engagement plan); document updates (issue log - indicates attitudes, lessons learned, risk register - responses to stakeholder risks, stakeholder register). Data flow: WPD from 4.3; WPI to 4.5; change requests to 4.6.

h-stakeholder-intro.title: Project Stakeholder Management: purpose and four processes
h-stakeholder-intro.notes: Identify the people, groups or organisations that could impact or be impacted by the project, analyse expectations and impact, and develop strategies to engage stakeholders in decisions and execution. Processes: 13.1 Identify Stakeholders (identify stakeholders regularly and analyse and document their interests, involvement, interdependencies, influence and potential impact on success); 13.2 Plan Stakeholder Engagement (develop approaches to involve stakeholders based on needs, expectations, interests and potential impact); 13.3 Manage Stakeholder Engagement (communicate and work with stakeholders to meet needs and expectations, address issues and foster appropriate engagement); 13.4 Monitor Stakeholder Engagement (monitor relationships and tailor engagement strategies by modifying strategies and plans). (Overview continues on PDF 541.)

h-stakeholder-overview.title: Stakeholder Management key concepts, trends (broader definitions, co-creation), tailoring and agile considerations
h-stakeholder-overview.notes: Every project has stakeholders who impact or are impacted, positively or negatively, with limited to significant influence. Research and high-profile failures show the value of structured identification, prioritisation and engagement of all stakeholders - correct identification and engagement can decide success or failure. Start as soon as possible after the charter is approved, the PM is assigned and the team forms. Stakeholder satisfaction should be identified and managed as a project objective. Key to engagement: continuous communication with all stakeholders, including team members, to understand needs, address issues, manage conflicting interests and foster appropriate engagement. The process is iterative: review and update identification, prioritisation and engagement routinely, and at least when the project moves through phases, when stakeholders leave or join the community, or when there are significant changes in the organisation or wider community. Trends: broader definitions (beyond employees, suppliers, shareholders: regulators, lobby groups, environmentalists, financial organisations, the media, and those who simply believe they are stakeholders); identifying all stakeholders; involving all team members in engagement; reviewing the stakeholder community regularly, often alongside risk reviews; co-creation - consulting the most affected stakeholders and including them in the team as partners; capturing the value of engagement - positive (benefits of active support, especially from powerful stakeholders) and negative (true cost of poor engagement - recalls, reputational loss). Tailoring: stakeholder diversity, complexity of relationships (more networks means more complex flows of information and misinformation), communication technology. Agile: high change requires active engagement; adaptive teams engage stakeholders directly rather than through layers of management; client, user and developer co-create, increasing involvement and satisfaction; regular interaction mitigates risk, builds trust and enables earlier, cheaper adjustment; aggressive transparency - inviting stakeholders to meetings and reviews and posting artefacts publicly to surface misalignment, dependencies or issues quickly. ITTOs for 13.1-13.4 recorded in ittos.json from Figure 13-1.

i-4.1-develop-charter.title: 4.1 Develop Project Charter: purpose, who charters, inputs, tools, outputs
i-4.1-develop-charter.notes: Key benefits: direct link between the project and strategic objectives, formal record, shows organisational commitment. Performed once or at predefined points. The charter establishes a partnership between performing and requesting organisations; for external projects a formal contract is preferred but a charter can still set internal agreements. Approval of the charter formally initiates the project. Assign the PM as early as feasible - preferably while the charter is developed and always before planning starts. Charter may be developed by the sponsor or the PM with the initiating entity; it gives the PM authority to plan, execute and control. Projects are initiated by an entity external to the project (sponsor, program, PMO, portfolio governing body) at a level able to procure funding and commit resources. A charter is not a contract (no consideration or money exchanged). Inputs: business documents (business case - most commonly used, created for market demand, organisational need, customer request, technological advance, legal requirement, ecological impacts or social need; benefits management plan) - the PM does not update business documents (not project documents) but may recommend; agreements (contracts, MOUs, SLAs, letters of agreement or intent, verbal agreements, email); EEFs (standards, legal/regulatory, marketplace, culture and political climate, governance framework, stakeholder expectations and risk thresholds); OPAs (policies and procedures, governance framework, monitoring and reporting methods, charter template, historical information). Tools: expert judgment (strategy, benefits management, technical knowledge, duration and budget estimation, risk identification); data gathering (brainstorming, focus groups, interviews); interpersonal and team skills (conflict management, facilitation, meeting management); meetings with key stakeholders. Outputs: project charter - purpose; measurable objectives and success criteria; high-level requirements; high-level description, boundaries and key deliverables; overall project risk; summary milestone schedule; preapproved financial resources; key stakeholder list; approval requirements (what is success, who decides, who signs off); exit criteria; assigned PM with responsibility and authority level; name and authority of the sponsor. Assumption log - records all assumptions and constraints across the life cycle; high-level ones come from the business case, lower-level ones arise later. Data flow (Figure 4-3): charter feeds 4.2, 4.7, 5.1-5.3, 6.1, 7.1, 8.1, 9.1, 10.1, 11.1, 12.1, 13.1, 13.2; assumption log goes to project documents.

i-4.2-develop-pmp.title: 4.2 Develop Project Management Plan: baselining, change control, kick-off meeting
i-4.2-develop-pmp.notes: Key benefit: a comprehensive document defining the basis of all project work and how it will be performed. Performed once or at predefined points. The plan defines how the project is executed, monitored and controlled, and closed; may be summary or detailed; should be robust to a changing environment. It must be baselined - at least scope, time (schedule) and cost references - so performance can be measured. Before baselining it may be updated freely without a formal process; after baselining it may change only through Perform Integrated Change Control, giving progressive elaboration by controlled, approved updates through closure. Projects in a program/portfolio keep their plan consistent with it (e.g., a program rule that changes above a cost threshold go to the CCB must appear in the project plan). Inputs: project charter (starting point); outputs from other processes (subsidiary plans and baselines from planning processes); EEFs (standards, legal, vertical-market or focus-area bodies of knowledge, structure/culture/management practices/sustainability, governance, infrastructure); OPAs (policies, plan template with tailoring guidelines and closure/acceptance criteria, change control procedures, monitoring/reporting, risk control, communication requirements, information from similar projects, lessons learned). Tools: expert judgment (tailoring processes, extra plan components, tools, technical and management details, resources and skill levels, level of configuration management, which documents fall under formal change control, prioritising work); data gathering (brainstorming, checklists, focus groups, interviews); interpersonal skills (conflict management, facilitation, meeting management); meetings. Kick-off meeting: usually at the end of planning and start of executing; purpose - communicate objectives, gain team commitment, explain each stakeholder's roles and responsibilities. Small projects: one team plans and executes, so kick-off happens shortly after initiation within Planning. Large projects: a PM team plans and the rest of the team joins at development start, so kick-off is within Executing. Multiphase projects typically kick off each phase. Output: project management plan.

i-4.3-direct-manage.title: 4.3 Direct and Manage Project Work: executing the plan, approved changes, deliverables and WPD
i-4.3-direct-manage.notes: Lead and perform the planned work and implement approved changes; key benefit: overall management of work and deliverables, improving the probability of success; performed throughout. Allocates resources, manages efficient use, carries out plan changes from analysis of performance data; strongly affected by application area; PM and team direct activities and manage technical and organisational interfaces; review impact of changes and implement approved corrective action, preventive action and defect repair; collect WPD and pass to controlling processes; WPD also feeds lessons learned. Inputs: project management plan (any component); project documents (change log - status of all change requests; lessons learned register; milestone list; project communications; project schedule; RTM; risk register; risk report); approved change requests (from 4.6, approved by PM or CCB; may be corrective, preventive or defect repair; scheduled and implemented by the team); EEFs (structure/culture/practices, infrastructure, stakeholder risk thresholds such as allowable overrun %); OPAs (policies, issue and defect procedures and databases, performance measurement database, change and risk control procedures, previous project information). Tools: expert judgment (technical, cost and budget, legal and procurement, legislation, governance); PMIS (scheduling software, work authorisation systems, configuration management systems, information collection and distribution, interfaces to knowledge repositories, automated KPI reporting); meetings (kick-off, technical, sprint/iteration planning, Scrum daily standups, steering group, problem solving, progress update, retrospectives). Outputs: deliverables (apply change control once the first version is complete; configuration management controls versions); work performance data (raw observations - work completed, KPIs, technical performance measures, actual dates, story points completed, deliverable status, change request and defect counts, actual costs and durations); issue log (created first here; type, raised by and when, description, priority, assignee, target date, status, final solution; updated by M&C); change requests; plan updates (via change request); document updates (activity list, assumption log, lessons learned register, requirements documentation, risk register, stakeholder register); OPA updates. Data flow: deliverables go to 8.3 Control Quality (then validated in 5.5); WPD goes to all M&C control processes (5.5, 5.6, 6.6, 7.4, 8.3, 9.6, 10.3, 11.7, 12.3, 13.4); change requests to 4.6; lessons to 4.4.

i-4.4-manage-knowledge.title: 4.4 Manage Project Knowledge: tacit vs explicit knowledge, knowledge and information management, lessons learned register
i-4.4-manage-knowledge.notes: Use existing knowledge and create new knowledge to achieve objectives and contribute to organisational learning; key benefits: prior knowledge is leveraged and project knowledge is available to operations and future projects; performed throughout. Explicit knowledge can be codified in words, pictures, numbers; tacit knowledge is personal and hard to express (beliefs, insights, experience, know-how). Knowledge management has two purposes - reuse existing and create new knowledge - underpinned by knowledge sharing and knowledge integration. Misconceptions: that it is just documenting knowledge, or just collecting lessons learned at the end. Codified explicit knowledge lacks context and is open to interpretation; tacit knowledge carries context but is shared through conversation and interaction. The most important part is creating an atmosphere of trust so people are motivated to share; tools fail without motivation. Practice mixes knowledge management (people interacting) and information management (codifying explicit knowledge). Inputs: plan (all components); documents (lessons learned register, project team assignments, RBS, source selection criteria, stakeholder register - to see what knowledge exists and is missing); deliverables; EEFs (trusting, no-blame culture and value placed on learning; geographic distribution; knowledge experts; legal/confidentiality); OPAs (policies on confidentiality, security, retention, copyright, classified information, metadata, authorised technology and social media; personnel administration and competency frameworks; communication requirements - formal communication suits sharing information, informal communication is better for creating new knowledge and integrating across diverse groups; formal learning reviews before, during and after). Tools: expert judgment; knowledge management (networking incl. online forums, communities of practice and special interest groups, meetings incl. virtual, work shadowing and reverse shadowing, discussion forums, seminars and conferences, workshops and learning reviews, storytelling, creativity and ideas management, knowledge fairs and cafes, interactive training; face-to-face builds trust best, virtual maintains it; choice depends on innovation, complexity and team diversity); information management (codifying lessons, lessons learned register, library services, information gathering, PMIS with document management; enhance with a 'contact me' function); interpersonal skills (active listening, facilitation, leadership, networking, political awareness). Outputs: lessons learned register (category, description, impact, recommendations, proposed actions; challenges, problems, realised risks and opportunities; created early in this process and then updated by many processes; can include video, pictures, audio; at end of project or phase transferred to the lessons learned repository, an OPA); plan updates; OPA updates (new knowledge codified or embedded in deliverables and improved processes).

i-4.5-monitor-control-work.title: 4.5 Monitor and Control Project Work: integrated monitoring, data analysis techniques, work performance reports
i-4.5-monitor-control-work.notes: Track, review and report overall progress against plan performance objectives; key benefits: stakeholders understand current state, actions taken and forecasts of cost and schedule; performed throughout. Monitoring = collecting, measuring and assessing measurements and trends to improve processes; control = determining corrective or preventive actions or replanning and following up. Concerns: compare actual to plan; assess periodically and recommend corrective/preventive action; check individual risk status; keep an accurate information base on products and documentation; support status reporting, progress measurement and forecasting; forecasts for current cost and schedule; monitor implementation of approved changes; report to program management; keep aligned with business needs. Inputs: plan (any component); documents (assumption log, basis of estimates, cost forecasts, issue log, lessons learned register, milestone list, quality reports, risk register, risk report, schedule forecasts); work performance information (WPD compared with plan components, documents and variables, using metrics defined at the start - e.g., money spent is meaningful only against budget, work performed, resources used and funding schedule; compare with variance thresholds to decide on preventive or corrective action); agreements (oversee contractor work); EEFs (PMIS, infrastructure, stakeholder expectations and risk thresholds, standards); OPAs (policies, financial controls, monitoring and reporting methods, issue and defect procedures, knowledge base). Tools: expert judgment (EVA, data interpretation, estimating, trend analysis, technical, risk, contract management); data analysis - alternatives analysis (choose corrective or combined actions), cost-benefit analysis (cheapest effective corrective action), earned value analysis (integrated scope, schedule, cost view), root cause analysis (main reasons for a deviation), trend analysis (forecast future performance from past results, warn early of slippage, supports preventive action), variance analysis (planned vs actual; here from an integrated perspective across cost, time, technical and resource variances); decision making (voting - unanimity, majority, plurality); meetings (face-to-face, virtual, formal, informal; user groups, review meetings). Outputs: work performance reports (status and progress reports, EV graphs, trend lines and forecasts, reserve burndown charts, defect histograms, contract performance, risk summaries; dashboards, heat reports, stop-light charts; circulated via the communications plan); change requests (expand, adjust or reduce project scope, product scope, quality requirements, schedule or cost baselines; corrective, preventive, defect repair); plan updates; document updates (cost forecasts, issue log, lessons learned register, risk register, schedule forecasts). Data flow: receives WPI from all control processes (5.5, 5.6, 6.6, 7.4, 8.3, 9.6, 10.3, 11.7, 12.3, 13.4); sends WPR to 4.6, 9.5 Manage Team, 10.2 Manage Communications, 11.7 Monitor Risks.

i-4.6-integrated-change-control.title: 4.6 Perform Integrated Change Control: CCB, configuration vs change control, decisions and the change log
i-4.6-integrated-change-control.notes: Review all change requests; approve and manage changes to deliverables, project documents and the plan; communicate decisions. Key benefit: changes considered in an integrated way addressing overall project risk (which often comes from changes made without regard to overall objectives). Performed start to finish; ultimate responsibility of the PM. Changes may affect project and product scope, any plan component or document; any stakeholder may request at any time; level of control depends on application area, complexity, contract and context. Before baselines exist, formal change control is not required; once baselined, change requests go through 4.6. The configuration management plan defines which artefacts are under configuration control; any change to a configuration element needs a change request. Verbal changes must be recorded in writing in the change/configuration management system. Requests may need schedule and cost impact estimates. Any change that may affect a baseline always requires the formal integrated process. Every documented change request is approved, deferred or rejected by a responsible individual (usually sponsor or PM, named in the plan or procedures). A CCB is a formally chartered group responsible for reviewing, evaluating, approving, deferring or rejecting changes and recording and communicating decisions. Customer or sponsor approval may be needed after CCB approval unless they sit on the CCB. Changes that don't affect baselines (only performance against them) are usually decided by the PM; baseline-affecting changes include cost, schedule, resource and risk impacts and go to the CCB; only approved changes enter a revised baseline.
