Inputs: plan (change management plan - directs change control and documents CCB roles; configuration management plan - configurable items; scope, schedule and cost baselines to assess impact); documents (basis of estimates, RTM, risk report); work performance reports (resource availability, schedule and cost data, EV reports, burnup/burndown); change requests; EEFs (legal, standards, governance, contracting constraints); OPAs (change control procedures, change authorisation procedures, configuration management knowledge base). Tools: expert judgment (technical, legislation, legal and procurement, configuration management, risk); change control tools - configuration control focuses on the specification of deliverables and processes; change control on identifying, documenting, approving or rejecting changes. Configuration activities: identify configuration item; record and report configuration item status; perform configuration verification and audit. Change activities: identify, document, decide on, track changes. Data analysis (alternatives analysis; cost-benefit analysis - is the change worth its cost); decision making (voting - unanimity, majority, plurality; autocratic - one person decides for the group; multicriteria decision analysis - decision matrix against predefined criteria); meetings (change control meetings with the CCB: assess impacts on time, cost, resources, risks, discuss alternatives, communicate decisions; roles documented in the change management plan). Outputs: approved change requests (implemented via 4.3; deferred or rejected ones communicated to the requester); plan updates (baselines changed only from the last baseline forward - past performance is never changed); document updates (change log records disposition of all change requests). Data flow (Figure 4-13, visually verified): receives work performance reports and change requests from 4.5, and change requests from 4.3, 5.5, 5.6, 6.6, 7.4, 8.2, 8.3, 9.3, 9.4, 9.5, 9.6, 10.3, 11.5, 11.6, 11.7, 12.1, 12.2, 12.3, 13.1, 13.3, 13.4; sends approved change requests to exactly three processes - 4.3 Direct and Manage Project Work (to implement), 8.3 Control Quality (to verify implementation) and 12.3 Control Procurements (contract changes); plan updates and change log updates go to the plan and project documents.

i-4.7-close-project.title: 4.7 Close Project or Phase: administrative closure, contract closure, transition, final report
i-4.7-close-project.notes: Finalise all activities for the project, phase or contract; key benefits: information archived, planned work completed, team resources released; performed once or at predefined points. The PM reviews the plan to confirm all work is done and objectives met. Administrative closure activities: satisfy exit criteria (documents and deliverables up to date, issues resolved, delivery and formal acceptance confirmed by the customer, all costs charged, accounts closed, personnel reassigned, excess material handled, facilities and equipment reallocated, final reports produced); contractual completion (confirm formal acceptance of seller work, finalise open claims, update records, archive); collect records, audit success or failure, manage knowledge sharing and transfer, identify lessons learned, archive; transfer products to the next phase or operations; send suggestions for improving organisational policies to the right unit; measure stakeholder satisfaction. Also establishes procedures to investigate and document reasons if the project is terminated early. Inputs: charter (success criteria, approval requirements, who signs off); plan (all components); documents (assumption log, basis of estimates, change log, issue log - check none open, lessons learned register - finalised, milestone list, project communications, quality control measurements, quality reports, requirements documentation, risk register, risk report - check no open risks); accepted deliverables (from 5.5; may include partial deliverables for phased or cancelled projects); business documents (business case - did expected outcomes occur; benefits management plan - were benefits achieved as planned); agreements (formal procurement closure requirements in contract terms and the procurement management plan); procurement documentation (collected, indexed and filed: schedule, scope, quality and cost performance, change documentation, payment records, inspection results, as-built drawings, manuals - used for lessons learned and evaluating contractors); OPAs (closure guidelines incl. audits, evaluations, product validations, acceptance criteria, contract closure, resource reassignment, team appraisals, knowledge transfer; configuration management knowledge base). Tools: expert judgment (management control, audit, legal and procurement, legislation); data analysis - document analysis (lessons and knowledge sharing), regression analysis (interrelationships between project variables that contributed to outcomes, to improve future projects), trend analysis (validate organisational models), variance analysis (improve organisational metrics by comparing plan to result); meetings (confirm acceptance, validate exit criteria, formalise contract completion, evaluate satisfaction, gather lessons, transfer knowledge, celebrate; close-out reporting, customer wrap-up, lessons learned, celebration meetings). Outputs: project document updates (all finalised; final lessons learned register covering benefits management, business case accuracy, life cycles, risk and issue management, stakeholder engagement); final product, service or result transition (handover to the group that will operate, maintain and support it - or intermediate result for phase closure); final report (summary description; scope objectives, criteria and evidence of completion; quality objectives, criteria, verification and milestone dates, variance reasons; cost objectives, acceptable range, actuals, variance reasons; validation summary; schedule objectives and whether benefits were achieved, with estimates for future realisation; how business needs were met; risks and issues and how handled); OPA updates (project documents, operational and support documents, project or phase closure documents - formal completion and transfer, reviewing prior phase documentation and customer acceptance from Validate Scope; for terminated projects, why terminated and how finished and unfinished deliverables are transferred; lessons learned repository). Data flow (Figure 4-15, verified): inputs from 4.1 (charter), plan, documents, 5.5 (accepted deliverables), 12.1 (procurement documentation), 12.2 (agreements), business documents and OPAs; outputs to the customer (final product transition), project documents (lessons learned register) and the enterprise (final report, OPA updates).

i-change-request-types.title: Change requests and their types; issue log
i-change-request-types.notes: Issue = an unexpected problem, gap, inconsistency or conflict requiring action; tracked in the issue log. Change request = a formal proposal to modify any document, deliverable or baseline; any stakeholder may request a change; may come from inside or outside the project; optional or legally/contractually mandated; processed through Perform Integrated Change Control. Types: corrective action (intentional activity that realigns project work performance with the plan - fixes a deviation that has happened), preventive action (intentional activity ensuring future performance aligns with the plan - avoids a predicted deviation), defect repair (intentional activity to modify a nonconforming product or component), updates (changes to formally controlled documents or plans to reflect modified or additional content).

i-common-tt.title: Recurring tools and techniques: expert judgment, brainstorming, focus groups, interviews, facilitation, meeting management, checklists
i-common-tt.notes: Expert judgment = judgment based on expertise in an application area, Knowledge Area, discipline or industry from any group or person with specialised education, knowledge, skill, experience or training. Brainstorming = a facilitated group technique to generate a list of ideas quickly, in two parts: idea generation and analysis. Focus groups bring stakeholders and SMEs together for a conversational discussion (more conversational than one-to-one interviews). Interviews obtain information by talking directly with stakeholders. Conflict management brings stakeholders into alignment. Facilitation = ability to guide a group event to a successful decision with effective participation, mutual understanding, all contributions considered, full buy-in according to the agreed decision process, and follow-up of actions. Meeting management = preparing the agenda, inviting a representative of each key stakeholder group, sending minutes and actions. Checklists (from organisational experience or industry) guide plan development or verify completeness. These recur across many processes; the Guide cross-references their home sections (e.g., 5.2.2.2, 9.5.2.1, 10.2.2.6, 11.2.2.2).

i-integration-overview.title: Project Integration Management: purpose, the seven processes and their ITTOs
i-integration-overview.notes: Integration = identify, define, combine, unify and coordinate processes and activities across Process Groups; characteristics of unification, consolidation, communication and interrelationship, from start to completion. Choices about resource allocation, balancing competing demands, alternative approaches, tailoring, managing interdependencies among Knowledge Areas. Processes: 4.1 Develop Project Charter (document formally authorising the project and giving the PM authority to apply resources); 4.2 Develop Project Management Plan (define, prepare, coordinate all components and consolidate into an integrated plan); 4.3 Direct and Manage Project Work (lead and perform the planned work and implement approved changes); 4.4 Manage Project Knowledge (use existing and create new knowledge to achieve objectives and contribute to organisational learning); 4.5 Monitor and Control Project Work (track, review, report overall progress against plan objectives); 4.6 Perform Integrated Change Control (review all change requests, approve and manage changes to deliverables, OPAs, documents and the plan, communicate decisions); 4.7 Close Project or Phase (finalise all activities for project, phase or contract). Presented discretely but overlap in practice. Full ITTO lists recorded in docs/pmp-curriculum/ittos.json from Figure 4-1.

i-key-concepts.title: Key concepts, trends and tailoring for Integration Management; agile considerations
i-key-concepts.section: 4 key concepts, trends, tailoring, agile considerations
i-key-concepts.notes: Integration is specific to the PM: other areas may be handled by specialists, but accountability for integration cannot be delegated or transferred; the PM combines results from all areas and is ultimately responsible for the whole project. Projects are integrative (a contingency cost estimate integrates cost, schedule and risk processes) and links between Process Groups are iterative (planning hands executing a plan early and updates it as changes occur). Integration ensures alignment of deliverable dates, life cycle and benefits plan; provides the plan; creates and uses knowledge; manages performance and changes; makes integrated decisions on key changes; measures progress and acts; collects data, analyses it and communicates information; completes the work and formally closes phases, contracts and the project; manages phase transitions. Complexity and varied expectations demand more sophisticated integration. Trends: automated tools and PMIS; visual management tools; project knowledge management for a mobile workforce; expanding PM responsibilities (business case, benefits management, broader stakeholder engagement); hybrid methodologies (agile, business analysis for requirements, complexity tools, organisational change management). Tailoring: project life cycle, development life cycle (predictive/adaptive, incremental/iterative, hybrid), management approaches, knowledge management, change, governance (control boards, committees, reporting), lessons learned, benefits reporting timing. Agile: team members act as local domain experts and decide how plans and components integrate; PM's expectations unchanged but detailed product planning and delivery control is delegated to the team; PM builds collaborative decision-making and the ability to respond to change; generalising specialists help.

i-pmp-components.title: Project management plan components vs project documents (Table 4-1)
i-pmp-components.notes: The plan describes how the project will be executed, monitored and controlled, and closed; integrates subsidiary plans and baselines; components chosen by project need. Subsidiary plans: scope (how scope is defined, developed, monitored, controlled, validated), requirements (how requirements are analysed, documented, managed), schedule (criteria and activities for developing, monitoring, controlling the schedule), cost (how costs are planned, structured, controlled), quality (how quality policies, methodologies and standards are implemented), resource (how resources are categorised, allocated, managed, released), communications (how, when, by whom information is administered and disseminated), risk (how risk activities are structured and performed), procurement (how goods and services are acquired from outside), stakeholder engagement (how stakeholders are engaged per needs, interests, impact). Baselines: scope (approved scope statement, WBS and WBS dictionary), schedule (approved schedule model), cost (approved time-phased budget). Additional components often made in this process: change management plan (how change requests are formally authorised and incorporated), configuration management plan (how information about which items is recorded and updated so the product remains consistent/operative), performance measurement baseline (integrated scope-schedule-cost plan), project life cycle description, development approach (predictive, iterative, agile, hybrid), management reviews (points for progress review and corrective/preventive decisions). Table 4-1 lists 18 plan components and 33 project documents (activity attributes and list, assumption log, basis of estimates, change log, cost estimates and forecasts, duration estimates, issue log, lessons learned register, milestone list, physical resource assignments, project calendars, project communications, project schedule, network diagram, scope statement, team assignments, quality control measurements, quality metrics, quality report, requirements documentation, RTM, RBS, resource calendars, resource requirements, risk register, risk report, schedule data, schedule forecasts, stakeholder register, team charter, test and evaluation documents). Project documents are not part of the plan. Exam trap: the scope statement is a project document on its own but part of the scope baseline.

k-11.1-plan-contents-pim.title: 11.1 risk management plan (continued): probability and impact matrix and scoring, reporting formats, tracking
k-11.1-plan-contents-pim.notes: Probability and impact matrix: prioritisation rules may be set by the organisation in advance (OPAs) or tailored to the project; threats and opportunities share a common matrix using negative impact definitions for threats and positive ones for opportunities; descriptive terms (very high to very low) or numbers; numeric probability x impact gives a probability-impact score that ranks risks within each priority level. Figure 11-5 example: probability scale Very High 0.90, High 0.70, Medium 0.50, Low 0.30, Very Low 0.10; impact scale Very Low 0.05, Low 0.10, Moderate 0.20, High 0.40, Very High 0.80; each cell = product (e.g., 0.90 x 0.80 = 0.72; 0.50 x 0.40 = 0.20; 0.10 x 0.05 = 0.005 shown as 0.01); the threat half mirrors the opportunity half. Shading as rendered marks three priority zones: darkest (high) cells 0.72, 0.36, 0.56, 0.28, 0.40, 0.24; mid-grey (medium) cells such as 0.18, 0.09, 0.14, 0.10, 0.20, 0.12, 0.08; unshaded (low) the remainder - zone boundaries are an example, not a rule. Reporting formats: how outcomes are documented, analysed and communicated, incl. content and format of the risk register and risk report. Tracking: how risk activities are recorded and risk processes audited.

k-11.1-plan-risk.title: 11.1 Plan Risk Management: risk management plan, RBS, risk appetite and thresholds, probability and impact definitions
k-11.1-plan-risk.notes: Define how to conduct risk management; key benefit: the degree, type and visibility of risk management are proportionate to risks and to the project's importance; once or at predefined points. Begin when the project is conceived and complete early; revisit at major phase changes, significant scope change or if effectiveness reviews require. Inputs: charter (high-level description, boundaries, requirements, risks); plan (all approved subsidiary plans - keep the risk plan consistent with them); stakeholder register (roles and attitudes to risk - helps set roles and thresholds); EEFs (overall risk thresholds set by the organisation or key stakeholders); OPAs (organisational risk policy; risk categories possibly as an RBS; common definitions; risk statement formats; templates for the risk management plan, risk register and risk report; roles and responsibilities; authority levels for decisions; lessons learned). Tools: expert judgment (organisation's approach incl. enterprise risk management, tailoring, likely risk types); data analysis - stakeholder analysis to determine risk appetite; meetings (may be part of the kick-off or a specific planning meeting; PM, selected team members, key stakeholders, risk process owners, possibly customers, sellers, regulators; a skilled facilitator keeps focus, builds agreement, overcomes bias and resolves disagreement). Output: risk management plan - risk strategy (general approach); methodology (approaches, tools, data sources); roles and responsibilities (lead, support, risk team members per activity); funding (funds for risk activities; protocols for applying contingency and management reserves); timing (when and how often, activities added to the schedule); risk categories - often a risk breakdown structure (RBS: hierarchical representation of potential sources of risk; Figure 11-4 extract - level 0 all sources; level 1 technical, management, commercial, external; level 2 e.g., scope definition, requirements definition, estimates/assumptions/constraints, technical processes, technology, technical interfaces; project, program/portfolio, operations management, organisation, resourcing, communication; contractual terms, internal procurement, suppliers and vendors, subcontracts, client stability, partnerships and joint ventures; legislation, exchange rates, site/facilities, environmental/weather, competition, regulatory) or a custom categorisation such as a list or objective-based structure; stakeholder risk appetite expressed as measurable thresholds around each objective (determine acceptable overall exposure and inform probability and impact definitions); definitions of risk probability and impacts (project-specific, reflecting appetite and thresholds; typically five levels for a detailed approach, three for a simple one; Table 11-1 verified example: Very High >70%, >6 months, >$5M, very significant impact on overall functionality; High 51-70%, 3-6 months, $1M-$5M, significant impact on overall functionality; Medium 31-50%, 1-3 months, $501K-$1M, some impact in key functional areas; Low 11-30%, 1-4 weeks, $100K-$500K, minor impact on overall functionality; Very Low 1-10%, 1 week, <$100K, minor impact on secondary functions; Nil <1%, no change; impacts read as negative for threats and positive for opportunities). (Plan contents continue on PDF 445.) Data flow: charter from 4.1; risk management plan to the project management plan.

k-11.2-identify-risks.title: 11.2 Identify Risks: participants, risk statements, techniques (checklists, assumption and constraint analysis, SWOT, prompt lists - PESTLE, TECOP, VUCA), risk register and risk report
k-11.2-identify-risks.notes: Identify individual risks and sources of overall project risk and document characteristics; key benefit: documentation of existing risks and sources so the team can respond; performed throughout and iteratively (frequency and participation set in the risk management plan). Participants: PM, team, risk specialist, customers, external SMEs, end users, other PMs, operations managers, stakeholders, organisational risk experts - but all stakeholders should be encouraged to identify risks; involving the team builds ownership. Use a consistent risk statement format for clear, unambiguous risks. Risk owners may be nominated here and confirmed in Qualitative analysis; preliminary responses may be recorded and confirmed in Plan Risk Responses. Inputs: plan (requirements, schedule, cost, quality, resource and risk management plans; scope, schedule, cost baselines - WBS as a framework for identification); documents (assumption log, cost and duration estimates and resource requirements - ideally as ranges indicating risk, issue log, lessons learned, requirements documentation, stakeholder register - who can identify risks and act as owners); agreements (milestones, contract type, acceptance criteria, awards and penalties); procurement documentation (procurement may raise or lower risk; seller performance reports, approved changes, inspections); EEFs (published material, commercial risk databases and checklists, academic studies, benchmarking, industry studies); OPAs (project files with actual data, process controls, risk statement formats, checklists from similar projects). Tools: expert judgment (account for experts' bias); data gathering - brainstorming (comprehensive list, often with multidisciplinary outside experts, free-form or structured, RBS categories as a framework, ensure ideas are clearly described), checklists (based on history; quick, but never exhaustive - must not replace proper identification; explore items not on the list; review and prune regularly), interviews (trust and confidentiality); data analysis - root cause analysis (threats from a problem statement such as 'delayed', opportunities from a benefit statement such as 'early delivery'), assumption and constraint analysis (threats from inaccurate, unstable, inconsistent or incomplete assumptions; opportunities from removing or relaxing constraints), SWOT analysis (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats; broadens identification with internally generated risks; opportunities from strengths, threats from weaknesses; strengths may offset threats, weaknesses may hinder opportunities), document analysis (uncertainty, ambiguity or inconsistency in documents indicate risk); facilitation; prompt lists (predetermined list of risk categories to stimulate ideas: lowest RBS level for individual risks; PESTLE - political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental; TECOP - technical, environmental, commercial, operational, political; VUCA - volatility, uncertainty, complexity, ambiguity - for sources of overall risk); meetings (risk workshop, usually with brainstorming, skilled facilitator, right participants - sponsor, SMEs, sellers, customer representatives on larger projects). Outputs: risk register (results of later risk processes are recorded here too): list of identified risks with unique IDs and structured statements distinguishing cause, risk and effect; potential risk owners; list of potential responses; optional data - short title, category, status, causes, effects, risk triggers (events or conditions indicating a risk is about to occur), WBS reference, timing (when identified, when it might occur, when it may cease to matter, action deadline). Risk report (developed progressively; later processes add results): sources of overall risk with the most important drivers of exposure; summary of individual risks - numbers of threats and opportunities, distribution across categories, metrics and trends. Document updates: assumption log, issue log, lessons learned. Data flow (Figure 11-7): procurement documentation from 12.1, agreements from 12.2.

k-11.3-qualitative.title: 11.3 Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis: bias, data quality, probability and impact, other parameters, categorisation, P-I matrix, bubble charts, risk owners
k-11.3-qualitative.notes: Prioritise individual risks for further analysis or action by assessing probability, impact and other characteristics; key benefit: focus on high-priority risks; performed throughout (in agile often before each iteration). Assessments are subjective, so identify and manage participants' risk attitudes and correct for bias (a key facilitator role); evaluate the quality of available risk information. Establishes relative priorities for Plan Risk Responses, assigns a risk owner to each risk (responsible for planning and ensuring implementation of the response) and lays the foundation for Quantitative analysis if required. Inputs: risk management plan (roles, budgets, schedule activities, categories/RBS, probability and impact definitions, P-I matrix, thresholds - if missing, develop here and get sponsor approval); documents (assumption log, risk register, stakeholder register - potential owners); EEFs (industry studies, published material); OPAs (information from similar projects). Tools: expert judgment (often via facilitated workshops or interviews; consider bias); interviews (structured or semi-structured, trust and confidentiality); data analysis - risk data quality assessment (accuracy and reliability of risk data; e.g., questionnaire on completeness, objectivity, relevancy, timeliness with a weighted average score; gather better data if unacceptable), risk probability and impact assessment (likelihood; effect on schedule, cost, quality, performance - negative for threats, positive for opportunities; explore differing perceptions; record justifying assumptions; use the plan's definitions; low-probability, low-impact risks go on a watch list), assessment of other parameters - urgency (time within which a response must be implemented; short = high urgency), proximity (time before the risk could affect objectives; short = high proximity), dormancy (time after occurrence before impact is discovered; short = low dormancy), manageability, controllability, detectability (ease of detecting occurrence), connectivity (links to other risks), strategic impact, propinquity (degree a risk is perceived to matter by stakeholders); facilitation; risk categorisation (by source/RBS, area affected/WBS, phase, budget, roles, common root causes - focuses responses on the most exposed areas and enables generic responses for groups); data representation - probability and impact matrix (grid dividing risks into priority groups; separate matrices per objective, or combine assessments, or take the highest priority across objectives), hierarchical charts for more than two parameters, e.g., bubble chart (Figure 11-10: detectability on x, proximity on y, bubble size = impact value; large bubbles in the high-proximity/low-detectability area are unacceptable, small bubbles in the opposite area acceptable); meetings (risk workshop to review risks, assess probability, impact and other parameters, categorise, prioritise, allocate risk owners, confirm scales, record new risks). Outputs (documents only): assumption log, issue log, risk register (probability and impact assessments, priority level or score, risk owner, urgency, category, watch list), risk report (most important risks, prioritised list of all risks, summary conclusion).

k-11.4-quantitative-intro.title: 11.4 Perform Quantitative Risk Analysis: when it is used, inputs
k-11.4-quantitative-intro.notes: Numerically analyse the combined effect of identified individual risks and other uncertainty on overall objectives; key benefit: quantifies overall project risk exposure and supports response planning; not required on every project but performed throughout where used. Needs high-quality risk data and a sound scope, schedule and cost baseline, usually specialised software and modelling expertise, and extra time and cost; use is specified in the risk management plan; most appropriate for large or complex, strategically important, contractually required or stakeholder-required cases. It is the only reliable method to assess overall project risk by evaluating the aggregated effect of all individual risks and other uncertainty. Uses risks assessed in Qualitative analysis as significant; outputs feed Plan Risk Responses; may be repeated after response planning to test response effectiveness. Inputs: plan (risk management plan - whether required, resources, frequency; scope, schedule and cost baselines as starting points); documents (assumption log - assumptions and constraints may be modelled; basis of estimates - purpose, classification, accuracy, methodology, source reflected in modelled variability; cost estimates; cost forecasts - ETC, EAC, BAC, TCPI compared with results to find confidence levels; duration estimates; milestone list - schedule targets; resource requirements; risk register; risk report; schedule forecasts); EEFs (industry studies, published material); OPAs (similar completed projects). Expert judgment: translating risk information into numeric model inputs, choosing representations of uncertainty, modelling techniques and tools, interpreting outputs. (Tools continue on PDF 469.)

k-11.4-quantitative-tools.title: 11.4 Perform Quantitative Risk Analysis (continued): probability distributions, Monte Carlo, criticality, sensitivity/tornado, decision trees and EMV, influence diagrams, outputs
k-11.4-quantitative-tools.notes: Interviews generate model inputs (trust, confidentiality); facilitated risk workshops build understanding, consensus, focus and handle conflict and bias. Representations of uncertainty: uncertain durations, costs or resource requirements are modelled as probability distributions - most commonly triangular, normal, lognormal, beta, uniform or discrete; choose carefully. Individual risks may be covered by distributions or modelled as probabilistic branches (optional activities whose chance of occurring in a run equals the risk's probability; best for risks independent of planned activities); related risks (common cause, logical dependency) are modelled with correlation; other uncertainty may be modelled as branches describing alternative paths. Data analysis: simulation - typically Monte Carlo: cost risk uses cost estimates; schedule risk uses the network diagram and duration estimates; integrated cost-schedule analysis uses both; software iterates the model thousands of times with randomly chosen input values; outputs the range of outcomes (end date, cost at completion) as a histogram or a cumulative probability S-curve. Figure 11-13 example: target $2.2M has a 23% chance of being met; expected value $2.35M; 85% chance of costing $2.45M or less. Criticality analysis (schedule): criticality index = how often an element appears on the critical path across runs, as a percentage; focus responses on elements with highest effect. Sensitivity analysis: which risks or uncertainty sources have the most potential impact; correlates variation in outcomes with variation in model elements; tornado diagram shows correlation coefficients ordered by descending strength (Figure 11-14 example items such as manufacturing reactors, a control system failing an installation test, a piling contractor delivering early). Decision tree analysis: choose among alternatives; branches for decisions and chance events with costs and risks; end points are outcomes; evaluate by expected monetary value (EMV) of each branch and select the optimal path. Figure 11-15 (verified arithmetic): build new plant (invest $120M) - strong demand 60% revenue $200M net $80M, weak demand 40% revenue $90M net -$30M; EMV = 0.60 x 80 + 0.40 x (-30) = 48 - 12 = $36M. Upgrade plant (invest $50M) - strong 60% revenue $120M net $70M, weak 40% revenue $60M net $10M; EMV = 0.60 x 70 + 0.40 x 10 = 42 + 4 = $46M. Decision EMV = $46M (upgrade), also the lower-risk choice avoiding a possible $30M loss. Source note: the figure labels these as 'EMV (before costs)' although investment costs are already netted in the branch values - lessons will present the netted calculation and flag the label. Influence diagrams: entities, outcomes and influences with relationships; uncertain elements as ranges or distributions; evaluated by simulation (e.g., Monte Carlo); outputs like S-curves and tornado diagrams. Outputs (risk report updates): assessment of overall project risk exposure - chances of success (probability of meeting key objectives) and degree of inherent variability remaining (range of outcomes); detailed probabilistic analysis (S-curves, tornado diagrams, criticality analysis with narrative; contingency reserve needed for a specified confidence level; risks with greatest effect on the critical path; major drivers of overall risk); prioritised list of individual risks (from sensitivity analysis); trends in results over time; recommended risk responses (inputs to Plan Risk Responses).

k-11.5-plan-responses.title: 11.5 Plan Risk Responses: response criteria, threat and opportunity strategies, contingent responses, overall-risk strategies, secondary and residual risks
k-11.5-plan-responses.notes: Develop options, select strategies and agree actions for overall exposure and individual risks; key benefit: appropriate ways to address risk; allocates resources and inserts activities into documents and the plan; performed throughout. Responses should be appropriate to the risk's significance, cost-effective, realistic, agreed by all parties, and owned by a responsible person; the nominated risk owner develops plans for every sufficiently important risk; the PM also responds to the level of overall risk. Select the strategy or mix most likely to work; structured decision techniques, or for large/complex projects mathematical optimisation or real options analysis. Develop specific actions incl. primary and backup strategies. Contingency plan (fallback plan) for when the selected strategy is not fully effective or an accepted risk occurs. Secondary risks = risks arising directly from implementing a response. Contingency reserve (time or cost) may be allocated with conditions that trigger its use. Inputs: plan (resource management plan - coordinate response resources; risk management plan - roles and thresholds; cost baseline - contingency fund); documents (lessons learned, project schedule, project team assignments, resource calendars, risk register - priority guides strategy: high-priority risks need proactive responses, low-priority ones may only go on the watch list or get contingency; owners, preliminary responses, root causes, triggers and warning signs, near-term risks; risk report - overall exposure and prioritised risks; stakeholder register - potential response owners). Source note: Figure 11-16 and the text list project team assignments as an input, while the data flow Figure 11-17 lists resource breakdown structure in its place - a source inconsistency; lessons follow the ITTO figure and text. EEFs (stakeholder risk appetite and thresholds); OPAs (templates, historical databases, lessons learned). Tools: expert judgment (threat, opportunity, contingent and overall strategies; specialist technical input); interviews with risk owners; facilitation. Strategies for threats (five): escalate (threat outside project scope or response beyond the PM's authority; managed at program, portfolio or other organisational level; PM notifies the right party, who must accept ownership; escalated to the level matching the affected objectives; not monitored further by the team though may be recorded for information); avoid (eliminate the threat or protect the project from its impact; for high-priority, high-probability, large-impact threats; change the plan or the endangered objective to reduce probability to zero or isolate objectives; e.g., remove the cause, extend the schedule, change strategy, reduce scope; clarify requirements, obtain information, improve communication, acquire expertise); transfer (shift ownership and impact to a third party, usually paying a risk premium; insurance, performance bonds, warranties, guarantees, agreements); mitigate (reduce probability and/or impact; early action more effective; less complex processes, more tests, a more stable seller, prototypes; if probability can't be reduced, target severity drivers - e.g., redundancy); accept (acknowledge without proactive action; for low-priority threats or where nothing else is possible or cost-effective; active acceptance - most commonly a contingency reserve of time, money or resources; passive - periodic review only). Strategies for opportunities (five): escalate (as for threats); exploit (ensure it definitely happens, raising probability to 100% - e.g., assign the most talented resources, new technology); share (transfer ownership to a third party who shares the benefit, often with a premium - partnerships, teams, special-purpose companies, joint ventures; choose the owner best able to capture it); enhance (increase probability and/or impact; act early; focus on causes or on factors driving the size of the benefit - e.g., more resources to finish early); accept (active - contingency to take advantage; passive - periodic review). Contingent response strategies: plans executed only under predefined conditions when there will be enough warning; triggers (e.g., missing intermediate milestones, gaining higher priority with a seller) defined and tracked; called contingency or fallback plans. Strategies for overall project risk: avoid (significantly negative and outside thresholds - e.g., remove high-risk scope; cancellation is the most extreme avoidance, only if the threat is and will remain unacceptable); exploit (significantly positive - add high-benefit scope, or modify thresholds with stakeholder agreement); transfer/share (third party manages: transfer for negative with premium, share for positive - collaborative buyer-seller structures, joint ventures, special-purpose companies, subcontracting key elements); mitigate/enhance (replan, change scope and boundaries, priority, resource allocation, delivery times); accept (continue even outside thresholds; active - overall contingency reserve; passive - periodic review). Data analysis: alternatives analysis; cost-benefit analysis - cost effectiveness = (change in impact level) / (implementation cost), higher ratio = more effective. Decision making: multicriteria decision analysis with criteria such as response cost, likely effectiveness, resource availability, timing (urgency, proximity, dormancy), impact level, effect on related risks, secondary risks; strategies may change later if ineffective. Outputs: change requests; plan updates (schedule, cost, quality, resource, procurement management plans - e.g., make-or-buy or contract type changes; scope, schedule, cost baselines); document updates (assumption log, cost forecasts, lessons learned, project schedule - response activities, project team assignments - qualified people, budget, time and technical resources per action, risk register - agreed strategies, specific actions, trigger conditions/symptoms/warning signs, budget and schedule activities, contingency plans and triggers, fallback plans for when a primary response proves inadequate after the risk occurs, residual risks expected to remain after responses or deliberately accepted, secondary risks; risk report). Data flow: change requests to 4.6.

k-11.6-implement-responses.title: 11.6 Implement Risk Responses: ensuring agreed responses are actually executed
k-11.6-implement-responses.notes: Implement agreed risk response plans; key benefit: responses executed as planned to address overall exposure, minimise threats and maximise opportunities; performed throughout. Common problem: teams identify, analyse and plan responses, document them, then take no action; only if risk owners put in the required effort is risk managed proactively. Inputs: risk management plan (roles for allocating response owners, level of detail, thresholds = acceptable target the responses must achieve); documents (lessons learned, risk register - agreed responses and owners, risk report - overall exposure, agreed strategy, major risks and responses); OPAs (lessons learned repository on response effectiveness). Tools: expert judgment (validate or modify responses, implement efficiently); influencing (owners outside the team or with competing demands may need encouragement to act); PMIS (integrate response activities with schedule, resource and cost software). Outputs: change requests (to cost and schedule baselines or other components); document updates (issue log, lessons learned, project team assignments, risk register - changes to agreed responses, risk report). Data flow: change requests to 4.6.

k-11.7-monitor-risks.title: 11.7 Monitor Risks: what monitoring determines, inputs (part 1)
k-11.7-monitor-risks.notes: Monitor implementation of agreed responses, track identified risks, identify and analyse new risks, evaluate risk process effectiveness; key benefit: decisions based on current information about overall exposure and individual risks; performed throughout. Uses execution performance information to determine whether: responses are effective; overall risk has changed; status of individual risks has changed; new risks have arisen; the risk approach is still appropriate; assumptions are still valid; risk policies and procedures are followed; cost or schedule contingency reserves need modification; project strategy is still valid. Inputs: risk management plan (how and when to review, policies, roles, reporting formats); documents (issue log - updated issues may require risk register updates, lessons learned, risk register - risks, owners, responses, actions, control actions to assess response effectiveness, symptoms and warning signs, residual and secondary risks, watch list; risk report). (Continued on PDF 493.) Data flow: WPD from 4.3; WPR from 4.5; WPI to 4.5; change requests to 4.6.

k-11.7-monitor-risks-tools.title: 11.7 Monitor Risks (continued): technical performance analysis, reserve analysis, risk audits, risk reviews, outputs
k-11.7-monitor-risks-tools.notes: Inputs continued: work performance data (responses implemented, risks occurred, active and closed); work performance reports (variance analysis, earned value and forecasting data - relevant for performance-related risks). Tools: data analysis - technical performance analysis (compare technical accomplishments with the schedule of technical achievement using objective, quantifiable measures such as weight, transaction times, number of delivered defects, storage capacity; deviation can indicate threats or opportunities), reserve analysis (compare remaining contingency reserves with remaining risk to judge adequacy; may be shown as a burndown chart); audits - risk audits assess the effectiveness of the risk management process; the PM ensures they happen at the frequency in the risk management plan; may be part of routine reviews, a risk review meeting or separate meetings; format and objectives defined beforehand; meetings - risk reviews (scheduled regularly; examine and document response effectiveness for overall and individual risks; may identify new risks incl. secondary risks, reassess risks, close outdated risks, record issues from occurred risks, capture lessons; part of status meetings or dedicated). Outputs: work performance information (occurred risks compared with expectations - shows effectiveness of response planning and implementation); change requests (incl. recommended corrective and preventive actions for overall or individual risk); plan updates (any component); document updates (assumption log, issue log, lessons learned, risk register - new, outdated, realised risks and updated responses; risk report - status of major risks, overall level, top risks, responses and owners, conclusions, recommendations, risk audit conclusions); OPA updates (templates for the risk management plan, risk register and risk report; risk breakdown structure).

k-risk-overview.title: Project Risk Management overview: seven processes, individual vs overall risk, threats and opportunities, risk appetite and thresholds, trends (non-event risks, resilience, integrated risk), tailoring, agile
k-risk-overview.section: 11 intro, key concepts, trends, tailoring, agile (Figure 11-1)
k-risk-overview.notes: Risk management planning, identification, analysis, response planning, response implementation and monitoring; objectives: increase probability and/or impact of positive risks and decrease those of negative risks to optimise success. Processes: 11.1 Plan Risk Management (how to conduct risk management); 11.2 Identify Risks (individual risks and sources of overall project risk, documenting characteristics); 11.3 Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis (prioritise individual risks by probability, impact and other characteristics); 11.4 Perform Quantitative Risk Analysis (numerically analyse the combined effect of identified individual risks and other uncertainty on overall objectives); 11.5 Plan Risk Responses (develop options, select strategies, agree actions for overall exposure and individual risks); 11.6 Implement Risk Responses (implement agreed plans); 11.7 Monitor Risks (monitor implementation, track identified risks, identify and analyse new risks, evaluate process effectiveness). Key concepts: all projects are risky (unique, complex, constrained, changing expectations); take risk in a controlled, intentional way to create value, balancing risk and reward; risk management addresses risks not handled by other processes and is directly related to success. Two levels: individual project risk = an uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on one or more objectives; overall project risk = the effect of uncertainty on the project as a whole, from all sources including individual risks, representing stakeholders' exposure to positive and negative variation in outcome. Exploit or enhance opportunities; avoid or mitigate threats; unmanaged threats cause delay, overruns, shortfalls, reputational loss; captured opportunities reduce time and cost or improve performance. Overall risk management keeps exposure within an acceptable range by reducing negative drivers, promoting positive ones and maximising the probability of meeting objectives. Risk processes are iterative: risk shapes strategy in planning and is monitored throughout as risks emerge. Acceptable exposure is defined by measurable risk thresholds reflecting the risk appetite of the organisation and stakeholders; thresholds express acceptable variation around an objective, are communicated to the team and reflected in impact level definitions. Trends: non-event risks - variability risk (uncertainty about key characteristics of a planned event, activity or decision: productivity above or below target, more or fewer test errors, unseasonal weather; addressed with Monte Carlo analysis and actions to narrow the spread) and ambiguity risk (uncertainty about what might happen: requirements, technical solution, regulatory developments, systemic complexity; addressed by defining knowledge gaps and filling them with expert input or benchmarking, incremental development, prototyping, simulation); event-based examples - a key seller going out of business, the customer changing a requirement after design, a subcontractor proposing enhancements. Project resilience against emergent 'unknowable-unknowns' (recognisable only after they occur): budget and schedule contingency for emergent risks in addition to a specific risk budget for known risks; flexible processes with strong change management; empowered team with clear objectives trusted within agreed limits; frequent review of early warning signs; clear stakeholder input on where scope or strategy can adjust. Integrated risk management: risks owned at the right level (project, program, portfolio, enterprise); some delegated down, some escalated; coordinated enterprise-wide approach builds risk efficiency. Tailoring (recorded in the risk management plan): project size, complexity (innovation, new technology, commercial arrangements, interfaces, external dependencies), importance, development approach (waterfall vs agile - risk addressed at the start of and during each iteration). Agile: high variability means more uncertainty; frequent reviews of incremental products and cross-functional teams accelerate knowledge sharing; risk considered when selecting iteration content and identified, analysed and managed each iteration; requirements are a living document; work reprioritised as risk understanding improves. ITTOs for 11.1-11.7 recorded in ittos.json from Figure 11-1 (two process labels for 11.3 and 11.4 are displaced in the extracted text; blocks mapped by content and to be cross-checked against Figures 11-8 and 11-11).

m-10.1-plan-communications.title: 10.1 Plan Communications Management: requirements analysis, technology factors, communication models, push/pull/interactive methods, plan contents
m-10.1-plan-communications.notes: Develop an approach and plan for communications based on each stakeholder's information needs, organisational assets and project needs; key benefit: a documented approach to engage stakeholders effectively and efficiently with relevant, timely information; performed periodically as needed. Developed early (during stakeholder identification and project management plan development), reviewed regularly and modified when the stakeholder community changes or at each new phase; also decide storage, retrieval and ultimate disposition of information. Inputs: charter (key stakeholder list, possibly roles); plan (resource management plan - team communication requirements; stakeholder engagement plan - strategies often fulfilled via communications); documents (requirements documentation - may include stakeholder communications; stakeholder register); EEFs (culture, political climate, governance; personnel policies; stakeholder risk thresholds; established channels, tools and systems; global/regional/local trends and habits; geographic distribution); OPAs (policies on social media, ethics, security; issue, risk, change and data management; communication requirements; guidelines for development, exchange, storage, retrieval; historical information; stakeholder and communications data from previous projects). Tools: expert judgment (politics and power structures, culture, change management, industry, communications technologies, legal and security policies, stakeholders); communication requirements analysis (information needs = type and format of information combined with its value; sources: stakeholder register and engagement plan, number of potential communication channels or paths - one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many - organisation charts, project organisation and stakeholder relationships, development approach, disciplines and departments, logistics of how many people at which locations, internal and external information needs, legal requirements. Source note: this edition does not state the channels formula n(n-1)/2; if taught, label it as a supplementary calculation); communication technology (conversations, meetings, written documents, databases, social media, websites; factors: urgency of the need for information, availability and reliability of technology, ease of use and training, project environment - face-to-face or virtual, time zones, languages, culture - and sensitivity/confidentiality incl. social media policies); communication models - basic sender/receiver (ensures delivery, not understanding: encode, transmit message via a channel subject to noise, decode), interactive (adds acknowledge - receipt only, not agreement or comprehension - and feedback/response; noise includes distraction, differing perceptions, lack of knowledge or interest; sender ensures the message is clear, complete and correctly interpreted; receiver ensures it is received entirely, interpreted correctly and acknowledged or answered), cross-cultural model (Figure 10-4: sender's and receiver's current emotional state, culture - generational, national, professional discipline, gender - personality and biases influence encoding and decoding; noise in the medium; useful for person-to-person or small-group communication, not for emails, broadcasts or social media); communication methods - interactive (real-time multidirectional: meetings, phone, instant messaging, some social media, videoconferencing), push (sent to specific recipients - ensures distribution but not receipt or understanding: letters, memos, reports, emails, faxes, voicemail, blogs, press releases), pull (large or complex information or large audiences who access it at their discretion: web portals, intranets, e-learning, lessons learned databases, knowledge repositories); forms of communication: interpersonal (face-to-face individuals), small group (about three to six people), public (one speaker to a group), mass (minimal connection with large, sometimes anonymous audiences), networks and social computing (many-to-many); artefacts include notice boards, newsletters, letters, press releases, annual reports, emails and intranets, web portals, phone, presentations, team briefings, focus groups, meetings, consultation groups or staff forums, social media; interpersonal skills - communication styles assessment (preferred method, format and content; often for unsupportive stakeholders, after a stakeholder engagement assessment), political awareness (formal and informal power relationships and willingness to work within them; who wields power and influence), cultural awareness (adapt strategy to differences between individuals, groups and organisations); data representation - stakeholder engagement assessment matrix (gaps between current and desired engagement inform extra communications); meetings. Outputs: communications management plan (how communications are planned, structured, implemented and monitored): stakeholder communication requirements; information to communicate - language, format, content, detail; escalation processes; reason for distribution; timeframe and frequency and acknowledgment; person responsible for communicating; person authorising release of confidential information; recipients and their needs; methods or technologies; resources (time, budget); method for updating the plan; glossary of terminology; flow charts of information flow, authorisation workflows, report lists, meeting plans; constraints from legislation, technology, policies; may include guidelines and templates for meetings, e-meetings, email, project website and software. Plan updates: stakeholder engagement plan. Document updates: project schedule, stakeholder register. Data flow: charter from 4.1.

m-10.2-manage-communications.title: 10.2 Manage Communications: effective communication techniques and inputs (part 1)
m-10.2-manage-communications.notes: Ensure timely and appropriate collection, creation, distribution, storage, retrieval, management, monitoring and ultimate disposition of project information; key benefit: efficient and effective information flow between team and stakeholders; performed throughout. Covers choice of technologies, methods and techniques and allows flexibility for changing needs; goes beyond distribution to ensure information is appropriately generated, formatted and received, and gives stakeholders the chance to request more information, clarification and discussion. Techniques and considerations: sender-receiver models with feedback loops; choice of media (written vs oral, informal memo vs formal report, push vs pull, technology); writing style (active vs passive voice, sentence structure, word choice); meeting management (agenda, essential participants and attendance, dealing with conflicts and poor follow-up or wrong attendees); presentations (body language, visual aids); facilitation (consensus, difficult group dynamics, interest and enthusiasm); active listening (acknowledging, clarifying and confirming, understanding, removing barriers). Inputs: plan (resource management plan, communications management plan, stakeholder engagement plan); documents (change log - communicate approved, deferred and rejected changes; issue log; lessons learned; quality report - forwarded to those who can act; risk report - to risk owners and impacted stakeholders; stakeholder register); work performance reports (circulated through this process per the communications plan: status and progress reports, EV graphs, trends and forecasts, reserve burndown, defect histograms, contract performance, risk summaries; dashboards, heat reports, stop-light charts); EEFs (as in 10.1); OPAs (social media, ethics and security policies; issue, risk, change and data management; communication requirements; information guidelines; historical information). Tools (part 1): communication technology (factors: colocation, confidentiality, resources available, how culture shapes meetings and discussions); communication methods (keep flexible as the stakeholder community and its needs change). (Continued on PDF 421.) Data flow: work performance reports from 4.5.

m-10.2-manage-communications-tools.title: 10.2 Manage Communications (continued): communication skills, PMIS, project reporting, meeting management, networking, outputs
m-10.2-manage-communications-tools.notes: Communication skills: communication competence (tailored skills - clarity of purpose in key messages, effective relationships and information sharing, leadership behaviours); feedback (information about reactions to communications, deliverables or situations; supports interactive communication - e.g., coaching, mentoring, negotiating); nonverbal (body language, gestures, tone, facial expression; mirroring and eye contact; be aware of what you say and don't say); presentations (formal delivery of information: progress reports and updates, background for decisions, general information to raise the profile of the project and team, specific information to increase understanding and support; succeed when content and delivery consider the audience's expectations and needs and the project's needs). PMIS: electronic project management tools (PM software, meeting and virtual office support, web interfaces, portals and dashboards, collaborative work management), electronic communications management (email, fax, voicemail; audio, video, web conferencing; websites and web publishing), social media management (websites, blogs, applications to engage stakeholders and form online communities). Project reporting: collecting and distributing project information at the right level, format and detail for each stakeholder group, regularly or by exception; work performance reports come from 4.5, while this process develops ad hoc reports, presentations, blogs and other communications. Interpersonal skills: active listening (acknowledge, clarify and confirm, understand, remove barriers to comprehension); conflict management; cultural awareness; meeting management (prepare and distribute an agenda with objectives, start and finish on time, invite the right participants and ensure attendance, stay on topic, manage expectations, issues and conflicts, record actions and owners); networking (interacting to exchange information and develop contacts - access to informal organisations to solve problems, influence and increase support); political awareness (engage stakeholders appropriately to keep their support). Meetings support the communication strategy and plan. Outputs: project communications (performance reports, deliverable status, schedule progress, costs incurred, presentations, other required information); plan updates (communications management plan, stakeholder engagement plan); document updates (issue log, lessons learned, project schedule, risk register, stakeholder register); OPA updates (project records - correspondence, memos, minutes; planned and ad hoc reports and presentations).

m-10.3-monitor-communications.title: 10.3 Monitor Communications: right message, audience, channel, time; iteration with planning and managing
m-10.3-monitor-communications.notes: Ensure the information needs of the project and stakeholders are met; key benefit: optimal information flow as defined in the communications management plan and stakeholder engagement plan; performed throughout. Determines whether planned artefacts and activities increased or maintained stakeholder support; evaluate impact so the right message with the right content (same meaning for sender and receiver) reaches the right audience through the right channel at the right time. Methods: customer satisfaction surveys, lessons learned, team observation, issue log data, changes in the stakeholder engagement assessment matrix. May trigger iterations of Plan Communications Management and/or Manage Communications - illustrating the continuous nature of these processes; issues, KPIs, risks or conflicts may trigger immediate revision. Inputs: plan (resource management plan - actual project organisation, roles, org charts; communications management plan; stakeholder engagement plan); documents (issue log - history of stakeholder engagement issues and resolutions; lessons learned; project communications - what was distributed); work performance data (types and quantities of communications actually distributed); EEFs (culture, political climate, governance; channels, tools, systems; trends; geographic distribution); OPAs (social media, ethics and security policies; communication requirements; information guidelines; historical and lessons learned; stakeholder and communications data from previous projects). Tools: expert judgment (communications with the public, community and media and between virtual groups internationally; communications and PM systems); PMIS (standard tools to capture, store and distribute information per the plan; monitored for validity and effectiveness); data representation - stakeholder engagement assessment matrix (changes between desired and current engagement show communication effectiveness); interpersonal skills - observation/conversation (identify team issues, interpersonal conflicts, individual performance issues); meetings (decisions, stakeholder requests, discussions with suppliers and vendors). Outputs: work performance information (implemented vs planned communications; feedback such as survey results); change requests (revise stakeholder communication requirements - distribution, content, format, method; new procedures to remove bottlenecks); plan updates (communications management plan, stakeholder engagement plan); document updates (issue log, lessons learned, stakeholder register). Data flow: WPD from 4.3; WPI to 4.5; change requests to 4.6.

m-communications-intro.title: Project Communications Management: purpose, two parts, three processes
m-communications-intro.notes: Ensure information needs of the project and stakeholders are met by developing artefacts and implementing activities for effective information exchange. Two parts: developing a communication strategy that is effective for stakeholders, and carrying out activities to implement it. Processes: 10.1 Plan Communications Management (develop an approach and plan based on each stakeholder's or group's information needs, organisational assets and project needs); 10.2 Manage Communications (timely and appropriate collection, creation, distribution, storage, retrieval, management, monitoring and ultimate disposition of project information); 10.3 Monitor Communications (ensure information needs of the project and stakeholders are met). (Overview continues on PDF 397.)

m-communications-overview.title: Communications key concepts: forms and dimensions of communication, 5Cs of written communication, communication skills, trends, tailoring, agile
m-communications-overview.notes: Communication = exchange of information, intended or involuntary (ideas, instructions, emotions), via written (physical or electronic), spoken (face-to-face or remote), formal or informal, gestures (tone, facial expression), media (pictures, actions) and choice of words. Communications = means of sending/receiving via activities (meetings, presentations) or artefacts (emails, social media, reports, documentation). PMs spend most of their time communicating with internal and external stakeholders; communication bridges diverse backgrounds, expertise and interests. Dimensions: internal vs external; formal (reports, formal meetings, agendas, minutes, briefings, presentations) vs informal (emails, social media, websites, ad hoc discussions); hierarchical focus - upward (senior management), downward (team and contributors), horizontal (peers); official (annual reports, reports to regulators) vs unofficial (building profile and relationships flexibly); written and oral, verbal (words and inflection) and nonverbal (body language, actions). Two parts of success: a communication strategy based on project and stakeholder needs, from which the communications management plan is developed; and the project communications themselves (collection, creation, dissemination, storage, retrieval, management, tracking, disposition); strategy and plan also underpin monitoring. Misunderstandings can be reduced but not eliminated by the 5Cs of written communication (for traditional, non-social-media messages): correct grammar and spelling; concise expression without excess words; clear purpose directed to the reader's needs; coherent logical flow (introductions, summaries as markers); controlling the flow of words and ideas (graphics, summaries). Supporting skills: listening actively; awareness of cultural and personal differences; identifying, setting and managing stakeholder expectations; enhancing team skills in persuading, motivating, coaching, negotiating and resolving conflict. Fundamental attributes: clarity of purpose; understanding the receiver's needs and preferences; monitoring and measuring effectiveness. Trends: include stakeholders in project reviews (regular review of the stakeholder community's membership and attitudes); include stakeholders in project meetings, incl. agile-style short daily standups with team and key stakeholders; social computing (infrastructure, social media, personal devices; social networking builds relationships and trust); multifaceted approaches respecting cultural, practical and personal preferences for language, media, content and delivery, effective across generations and cultures. Tailoring: stakeholders internal/external; physical location and time zones; communications technology; language(s); knowledge management repository. Agile: ambiguity and change require more frequent, faster communication - streamlined information access, frequent team checkpoints, colocation, transparent posting of artefacts, regular stakeholder reviews. p-12.1-outputs-table.title: 12.1 Plan Procurement Management (continued): document updates, OPA updates, Table 12-1 comparison of procurement documentation
p-12.1-outputs-table.notes: Document updates: lessons learned (regulations and compliance, data gathering and analysis, source selection); milestone list (when sellers deliver); requirements documentation (technical and contractual/legal requirements); RTM; risk register (each approved seller brings unique risks depending on its organisation, contract duration, external environment, delivery method, contract type and agreed price); stakeholder register (regulators, contracting and legal personnel). OPA updates: information on qualified sellers. Simple projects may combine outputs; complex, contractor-heavy projects need several document types. Table 12-1 (representative, not prescriptive - organisation, environment and law dictate documents): procurement management plan - coordination and integration with other project work (resources, schedule, budget), timetable of key activities, procurement metrics, stakeholder responsibilities, assumptions and constraints, legal jurisdiction and payment currency, independent estimates, risk management issues, prequalified sellers; procurement strategy - delivery methods, type of agreements, procurement phases; statement of work - description of the procurement item, specifications, quality requirements and performance metrics, collateral services, acceptance methods and criteria, performance data and reports required, quality, period and place of performance, currency and payment schedule, warranty; bid documents - RFI, RFQ, RFP.

p-12.1-plan-procurement.title: 12.1 Plan Procurement Management: typical procurement steps, contract types, make-or-buy, source selection methods, procurement strategy, bid documents, SOW/TOR, source selection criteria, independent estimates
p-12.1-plan-procurement.notes: Document procurement decisions, specify the approach and identify potential sellers; key benefit: determines whether to acquire from outside and, if so, what, how and when (from other parts of the organisation or external sources); once or at predefined points. Define procurement roles early and staff the team with procurement expertise; participants may include purchasing and legal; document responsibilities in the plan. Typical steps: prepare the procurement SOW or terms of reference (TOR); prepare a high-level cost estimate for the budget; advertise; short-list qualified sellers; prepare and issue bid documents; sellers prepare and submit proposals; technical evaluation incl. quality; cost evaluation; final combined quality and cost evaluation to select the winner; finalise negotiations and sign. Schedule requirements influence the strategy, and procurement decisions affect the schedule (integrated with Develop Schedule, Estimate Activity Resources and make-or-buy). Inputs: charter (objectives, description, summary milestones, preapproved financial resources); business documents (business case alignment; benefits management plan drives procurement dates and contract language); plan (scope management plan - managing contractor scope; quality management plan - standards and codes for RFPs, prequalification, selection; resource management plan - what is purchased or leased; scope baseline - known scope elements form the SOW/TOR); documents (milestone list - when sellers must deliver; project team assignments - procurement skills and availability; requirements documentation - technical requirements and those with contractual/legal implications: health, safety, security, performance, environmental, insurance, intellectual property, equal employment, licences, permits; RTM; resource requirements; risk register - some risks are transferred via agreements; stakeholder register - incl. regulators, contracting and legal personnel); EEFs (marketplace conditions and available products; sellers' past performance and reputation; typical terms and conditions; unique local requirements such as local labour or sellers; legal advice; contract management systems incl. contract change control; multi-tier prequalified supplier systems; financial accounting and payment systems); OPAs (preapproved seller lists; formal procurement policies; contract types). Contract types - two broad families plus a hybrid: fixed-price (use when requirements are well defined and no significant scope change is expected): firm fixed price (FFP - most common, favoured by buyers; price set at the outset, changes only with scope changes); fixed price incentive fee (FPIF - financial incentives tied to cost, schedule or technical performance metrics; a price ceiling is set and all costs above it are the seller's responsibility); fixed price with economic price adjustments (FPEPA - for multi-year performance or payments in another currency; predefined adjustments for changed conditions such as inflation or commodity cost changes). Cost-reimbursable (use when scope is expected to change significantly; seller reimbursed for legitimate actual costs plus a fee as profit): cost plus fixed fee (CPFF - fixed fee calculated as a percentage of initial estimated costs; changes only with scope changes); cost plus incentive fee (CPIF - predetermined incentive fee for meeting performance objectives; cost overruns or underruns versus target shared by a prenegotiated formula, e.g., 80/20); cost plus award fee (CPAF - most of the fee earned against broad subjective criteria judged solely by the buyer, generally not appealable). Time and material (T&M, also 'time and means') - hybrid of cost-reimbursable and fixed-price; staff augmentation, experts, outside support when a precise SOW can't be quickly written. Types are often combined in practice. Tools: expert judgment (procurement, contract types and documents, regulations); market research (industry and seller capabilities; conferences, online reviews; refine objectives to leverage maturing technologies while balancing seller-base risk); make-or-buy analysis (factors: current resource allocation and skills, need for specialised or independent expertise, desire not to expand permanent employment, risks; may use payback period, ROI, IRR, discounted cash flow, NPV, benefit/cost analysis); source selection analysis (review prioritisation of competing demands first; publish the evaluation method in procurement documents; methods: least cost - standard/routine work with well-defined outcomes; qualifications only - small-value procurements, choose from a short list by credibility, qualifications, experience, references; quality-based/highest technical proposal score - rank technical proposals, negotiate with the top one if its financial proposal is acceptable; quality and cost-based - cost included, quality weighted higher when risk/uncertainty is greater; sole source - one seller asked for proposals, acceptable only when justified, an exception; fixed budget - budget disclosed in the RFP, best technical proposal within it; only when the SOW is precise, no changes anticipated and the budget cannot be exceeded); meetings (information exchange with potential bidders for a mutually beneficial approach; strategy for managing and monitoring the procurement). Outputs: procurement management plan (international/national/local competitive bidding; align external financing with the plan and schedule; coordination with scheduling processes; timetable; procurement metrics; roles and authority vs procurement department; constraints and assumptions; legal jurisdiction and payment currency; whether independent estimates are used as evaluation criteria; risk issues such as performance bonds or insurance; prequalified sellers); procurement strategy (after make-or-buy: delivery method - professional services: buyer/services provider with or without subcontracting, joint venture, provider as representative; industrial/commercial construction: turnkey, design build (DB), design bid build (DBB), design build operate (DBO), build own operate transfer (BOOT); contract payment types separate from delivery methods: lump sum, FFP, CPAF, CPIF, T&M, target cost; fixed-price for predictable well-defined work, cost plus for evolving work, incentives and awards to align objectives; procurement phases - sequencing and objectives, performance indicators and milestones, phase transition criteria, monitoring and evaluation plan, knowledge transfer); bid documents (bid/tender/quotation when selection is price-based; proposal when technical capability or approach matters most; request for information (RFI - more information about the goods/services needed, typically followed by RFQ or RFP); request for quotation (RFQ - how vendors would meet requirements and/or how much it will cost); request for proposal (RFP - when there is a problem whose solution is not easy to determine; most formal, strict rules on content, timeline and responses); documents describe the desired response form, the SOW and contractual provisions; detail consistent with value and risk; detailed enough for consistent responses yet flexible for seller suggestions); procurement statement of work (developed from the scope baseline; only the portion of scope in that contract; enough detail for sellers to judge capability - specifications, quantity, quality levels, performance data, period of performance, work location; clear, complete, concise; includes collateral services such as performance reporting or post-project support; revised until incorporated into a signed agreement); terms of reference (TOR, for services: tasks and coordination requirements, applicable standards, data to submit for approval, data and services the buyer will provide, schedule for initial submission and review/approval time); source selection criteria (capability and capacity; product and life-cycle cost; delivery dates; technical expertise and approach; relevant experience; adequacy of approach and work plan; key staff qualifications, availability and competence; financial stability; management experience; knowledge transfer and training; for international projects 'local content'; expressed as scores, colour codes or descriptions in a weighting system to select a seller or rank proposals for a negotiating sequence); make-or-buy decisions; independent cost estimates (own or outside professional estimate as a benchmark; significant differences may mean a deficient or ambiguous SOW or that sellers misunderstood or failed to respond fully); change requests. (Outputs continue on PDF 517.)

p-12.2-conduct-procurements.title: 12.2 Conduct Procurements: seller proposals, advertising, bidder conferences, proposal evaluation, negotiation, selected sellers, agreement components
p-12.2-conduct-procurements.notes: Obtain seller responses, select a seller and award a contract; key benefit: a qualified seller is selected and the legal agreement for delivery implemented; end results are established agreements including formal contracts; performed periodically as needed.
