Inputs: plan (scope management plan incl. seller scope; requirements management plan incl. how sellers manage their requirements; communications management plan - buyer-seller communication; risk management plan; procurement management plan; configuration management plan - how sellers provide configuration management consistent with the buyer; cost baseline - procurement budget and costs of managing the process and sellers); documents (lessons learned, project schedule - procurement activities and contractor due dates, requirements documentation, risk register, stakeholder register); procurement documentation (written record used to reach the agreement: bid documents - RFI, RFP, RFQ; procurement SOW - goals, requirements, outcomes for a quantifiable response; independent cost estimates - reasonableness check; source selection criteria with weights; the buyer may contract more than one seller to mitigate single-seller risk); seller proposals (basis for the evaluation body; good practice: price proposal separate from technical proposal; evaluated against source selection criteria to choose the seller best satisfying requirements); EEFs (procurement laws and local-seller requirements, external economy, marketplace, past seller experience, prior agreements, contract management systems); OPAs (prequalified preferred sellers, selection policies, agreement templates and guidelines, invoicing and payment policies). Tools: expert judgment (proposal evaluation, technical subject matter, finance, engineering, design, development, supply chain, regulatory environment, laws and compliance, negotiation); advertising (expand seller lists through general or trade publications; most government jurisdictions require public advertising or online posting); bidder conferences (also contractor, vendor or pre-bid conferences; buyer meets prospective sellers before proposals to ensure a clear, common understanding and no preferential treatment); data analysis - proposal evaluation (complete, fully responsive to bid documents, SOW, criteria); interpersonal skills - negotiation (clarify structure, rights, obligations and terms before signing; final language reflects all agreements; ends with a signed contract; led by a procurement team member with signing authority; PM and team may attend to assist). Outputs: selected sellers (in a competitive range from evaluation; complex, high-value, high-risk procurements generally need senior management approval before award); agreements (contract = mutually binding agreement obligating the seller to provide specified products/services/results and the buyer to compensate, a legal relationship subject to remedy in the courts; components may include: SOW or major deliverables; schedule, milestones or required schedule date; performance reporting; pricing and payment terms; inspection, quality and acceptance criteria; warranty and future support; incentives and penalties; insurance and performance bonds; subcontractor approvals; general terms and conditions; change request handling; termination clause and alternative dispute resolution); change requests; plan updates (requirements, quality, communications, risk, procurement management plans; scope, schedule, cost baselines - e.g., seller delivery changes or fluctuating material and labour prices); document updates (lessons learned, requirements documentation, RTM, resource calendars - seller availability, risk register, stakeholder register); OPA updates (prospective and prequalified seller lists; experience with sellers). Data flow (Figure 12-5, verified): inputs from plan, documents, procurement documentation, enterprise and sellers (seller proposals); outputs - selected sellers to 12.3; change requests to 4.6; agreements to 4.1, 4.5, 4.7, 6.5, 7.3, 9.6, 12.3, 13.1 and 13.2. Source note: Figure 12-5 does not list 5.2 Collect Requirements or 11.2 Identify Risks, although their own data flow diagrams (Figures 5-5 and 11-7) show agreements received from 12.2 - lessons note the inconsistency.

p-12.3-control-procurements.title: 12.3 Control Procurements: contract administration, payments linked to work, claims administration, inspections, audits, closed procurements
p-12.3-control-procurements.notes: Manage procurement relationships, monitor contract performance, make changes and corrections, close out contracts; key benefit: both seller's and buyer's performance meet requirements under the legal agreement; performed throughout as needed. Both buyer and seller administer the contract to meet obligations and protect rights; be aware of legal implications of actions; on multi-provider projects manage communication among providers; many organisations treat contract administration as a separate organisational function (procurement administrator may sit on the team but report elsewhere). Integrates project management processes with contractual relationships at multiple levels. Administrative activities: collect data and keep detailed physical and financial performance records with measurable procurement performance indicators; refine procurement plans and schedules; gather, analyse and report procurement data; monitor the procurement environment; pay invoices. Quality of controls - independence and credibility of procurement audits - is critical; the code of ethics, legal counsel and anti-corruption initiatives help. Financial component: monitor payments so terms are met and compensation is linked to progress; payments should closely match work accomplished; contracts tying payment to outputs and deliverables rather than inputs such as labour hours have better controls. Agreements can be amended any time before closure by mutual consent per the change control terms, typically in writing. Inputs: plan (requirements management plan, risk management plan - seller-created risk activities, procurement management plan, change management plan - seller-created changes, schedule baseline); documents (assumption log, lessons learned, milestone list, quality reports - seller non-compliance, requirements documentation, RTM, risk register, stakeholder register - contracted members, sellers, contracting officers); agreements (verify terms are met); procurement documentation (SOW, payment information, contractor performance information, plans, drawings, correspondence); approved change requests (modifications to terms, SOW, pricing, descriptions; all procurement changes documented in writing and approved before implementation through this process; seller changes may affect other sellers); work performance data (seller technical performance, activity status, costs incurred or committed, invoices paid); EEFs (contract change control system, marketplace, financial management and accounts payable system, the buyer's code of ethics); OPAs (procurement policies). Tools: expert judgment (functional areas, laws and compliance, claims administration); claims administration (contested changes and potential constructive changes - where buyer and seller cannot agree on compensation or that a change occurred - are claims; unresolved claims become disputes and then appeals; documented, processed, monitored and managed per contract terms; if unresolved by the parties, alternative dispute resolution (ADR) per contract procedures; negotiated settlement is preferred); data analysis - performance reviews (quality, resource, schedule and cost performance against the agreement), earned value analysis (SV, CV, SPI, CPI for degree of variance), trend analysis (forecast EAC to see if performance is improving or deteriorating); inspection (structured review of contractor work, from deliverable reviews to physical site walkthroughs by buyer and contractor); audits (structured review of the procurement process; audit rights and obligations described in the contract; observations to both PMs). Outputs: closed procurements (buyer, usually via its authorised procurement administrator, gives the seller formal written notice of completion; closure requirements are in the contract terms and procurement plan; typically all deliverables on time and meeting requirements, no outstanding claims or invoices, all final payments made, deliverables approved by the PM team); work performance information (deliverables received, technical performance achieved, costs incurred and accepted vs the SOW budget); procurement documentation updates (contract and schedules, requested unapproved changes, approved changes, seller technical documentation, deliverables, seller performance reports and warranties, invoices and payment records, inspection results); change requests (incl. requested but unresolved changes - buyer direction or seller action the other party considers a constructive change; uniquely identified and documented in correspondence because they may lead to claims); plan updates (risk management plan, procurement management plan, schedule baseline - incl. cascading seller delays affecting other sellers, cost baseline); document updates (lessons learned incl. claims to avoid recurrence, resource requirements, RTM - satisfied requirements, risk register, stakeholder register - changing contractors); OPA updates (payment schedules and requests per contract terms; seller performance evaluation documentation - ability to continue, eligibility for future work, ratings; prequalified seller list updates - sellers may be removed for poor performance; lessons learned repository - actual vs projected results of the procurement; procurement file - complete indexed contract documentation incl. the closed contract for the final project files). Data flow (Figure 12-7, verified): approved change requests from 4.6; WPD from 4.3; procurement documentation from 12.1; agreements from 12.2; outputs - closed procurements and documentation updates to the procurement documentation store; WPI to 4.5; change requests to 4.6.

p-procurement-overview.title: Project Procurement Management overview: three processes, legal nature of contracts, buyer-seller roles, centralised vs decentralised purchasing, trends, tailoring, agile
p-procurement-overview.section: 12 intro, key concepts, trends, tailoring, agile (Figure 12-1)
p-procurement-overview.notes: Processes to purchase or acquire products, services or results from outside the project team, including developing and administering agreements - contracts, purchase orders, memoranda of agreement (MOAs), internal service level agreements (SLAs). Authorised procurers may be team members, management or the purchasing department. Processes: 12.1 Plan Procurement Management (document procurement decisions, specify the approach, identify potential sellers); 12.2 Conduct Procurements (obtain seller responses, select a seller, award a contract); 12.3 Control Procurements (manage procurement relationships, monitor contract performance, make changes and corrections, close out contracts). Written from the buyer's viewpoint. Key concepts: significant legal obligations and penalties; the PM need not be a procurement-law expert but must know enough to decide intelligently, and is typically not authorised to sign legal agreements binding the organisation. Agreements describe a buyer-seller relationship, from labour hours at a rate to multiyear international construction contracts; the approach should match complexity and comply with laws. A contract should clearly state expected deliverables and results incl. knowledge transfer; anything not in the contract cannot be legally enforced; culture and local law affect enforceability internationally. A purchasing contract has terms and conditions; the PM team ensures procurements meet project needs while the procurement office ensures policy compliance. Agreement forms: contract, SLA, understanding, MOA, purchase order. Contracts get more extensive approval, often by legal, to ensure the products/services are adequately described and legal; legal terms often sit in standardised appendices. Complex projects may manage multiple contracts simultaneously or in sequence, each with its own life cycle. Seller names: contractor, vendor, service provider, supplier; buyer names: owner, subcontractor, acquiring organisation, service requestor, purchaser; the seller is first a bidder, then the selected source, then the contracted supplier. The winning seller may manage its work as a project: the buyer becomes its key customer/stakeholder; contract terms and the procurement statement of work (also called technical SOW) become key inputs and may constrain options (e.g., buyer approval of staffing); the seller may itself buy from lower tiers. The seller may be internal but external to the project and may join an integrated team after award. Decentralised purchasing: in small organisations without a procurement department the PM may negotiate and sign; centralised purchasing: a separate department purchases, negotiates and signs. International contracts state the legal jurisdiction. Trends: advances in tools (online procurement portals; building information model - BIM - in construction saves time and money and reduces claims; increasingly mandated); more advanced risk management (contracts allocate specific risks to the parties best able to manage them; buyer accepts risks contractors can't control - corporate policy and regulatory changes; contracts may require risk management); changing contracting processes (growth of multibillion-dollar megaprojects with international contractors; contractor works with the client on procurement for quantity discounts; internationally recognised standard contract forms to reduce claims); logistics and supply chain management (long-lead items drive schedule - 2 to 3 months in IT, 1 to 2 years or more in complex construction; may be procured early from top-level design; primary and backup sources; local-content purchase requirements); technology and stakeholder relations (site webcams for public projects improve communication and reduce disputes); trial engagements (paid initial work with several candidate sellers before committing). Tailoring: complexity of procurement (one or many), physical location, governance and regulatory environment (laws and auditing), availability of contractors. Agile: specific sellers may extend the team in a collaborative, shared-risk-and-reward model; large projects may combine adaptive and stable parts under a master services agreement (MSA) with adaptive work in an appendix or supplement so it can change without affecting the overall contract. ITTOs for 12.1-12.3 recorded in ittos.json from Figure 12-1.

q-8.1-plan-quality.title: 8.1 Plan Quality Management: COQ categories, cost-benefit, data representation, test and inspection planning, quality plan and metrics
q-8.1-plan-quality.notes: Identify quality requirements and/or standards for the project and deliverables and document how compliance will be demonstrated; key benefit: guidance on how quality will be managed and verified; once or at predefined points. Performed in parallel with other planning (quality changes may need cost/schedule adjustment and risk analysis). Inputs: charter (high-level description, product characteristics, approval requirements, measurable objectives, success criteria); plan (requirements management plan; risk management plan; stakeholder engagement plan; scope baseline - WBS and deliverables decide applicable standards and which deliverables/processes get quality review; acceptance criteria can significantly raise or lower quality costs; meeting all acceptance criteria implies stakeholder needs are met); documents (assumption log, requirements documentation incl. quality requirements, RTM - ensures each requirement is tested, overview of tests, risk register, stakeholder register - emphasis on customer and sponsor); EEFs (agency regulations, application-area rules and standards, geographic distribution, structure, marketplace, working/operating conditions, cultural perceptions); OPAs (organisational quality management system, quality templates such as check sheets and traceability matrices, historical databases and lessons learned). Tools: expert judgment (QA, QC, measurements, improvements, systems); data gathering - benchmarking (compare practices or standards with comparable projects, internal or external, same or other application areas), brainstorming, interviews (in an environment of trust and confidentiality); data analysis - cost-benefit analysis (is each quality activity cost-effective; benefits of meeting quality requirements: less rework, higher productivity, lower costs, more stakeholder satisfaction, higher profitability) and cost of quality: prevention costs (training, documenting processes, equipment, time to do it right), appraisal costs (testing, destructive testing loss, inspections) - together the cost of conformance, money spent during the project to avoid failures; internal failure costs (rework, scrap) and external failure costs (liabilities, warranty work, lost business) - cost of nonconformance, money spent during and after the project because of failures (Figure 8-5); optimal COQ balances prevention and appraisal against failure - beyond a point more prevention/appraisal is not cost-effective; decision making - multicriteria decision analysis/prioritisation matrix (weighted criteria scored across alternatives; here to prioritise quality metrics); data representation - flowcharts/process maps (sequence, decision points, loops, parallel paths; SIPOC = suppliers, inputs, process, outputs, customers with requirements and feedback loops - Figure 8-6; estimate COQ via branching logic and relative frequencies to compute expected monetary value of conformance and nonconformance work; identify where defects occur and where to add checks), logical data model (business-language view of data to find data integrity issues), matrix diagrams (strength of relationships between factors, causes, objectives; L, T, Y, X, C and roof-shaped; identify key quality metrics), mind mapping; test and inspection planning (how to test/inspect to meet needs and performance/reliability goals; industry dependent - alpha and beta tests in software, strength tests in construction, inspection in manufacturing, field and nondestructive tests in engineering); meetings. Outputs: quality management plan (how policies, procedures and guidelines will be implemented to meet quality objectives; reviewed early for value focus, lower cost, fewer rework overruns; contains quality standards, objectives, roles and responsibilities, deliverables and processes subject to review, QC and QM activities, tools, procedures for nonconformance, corrective action and continuous improvement); quality metrics (a specific project or product attribute and how Control Quality will verify compliance - e.g., % tasks on time, CPI, failure rate, defects per day, downtime per month, errors per line of code, customer satisfaction scores, % requirements covered by tests); plan updates (risk management plan, scope baseline incl. WBS dictionary quality requirements); document updates (lessons learned, RTM, risk register, stakeholder register). Data flow: charter from 4.1; outputs to plan and documents.

q-8.2-manage-quality.title: 8.2 Manage Quality: quality assurance, data representation tools, audits, Design for X, problem solving, improvement methods
q-8.2-manage-quality.notes: Translate the quality management plan into executable quality activities incorporating organisational quality policies; key benefits: higher probability of meeting quality objectives; identify ineffective processes and causes of poor quality; uses Control Quality data to report overall quality status; performed throughout. Sometimes called quality assurance, but broader: in projects QA focuses on the processes used - using them effectively and following standards to assure stakeholders the product will meet needs; Manage Quality includes all QA activities plus product design aspects and process improvements; it falls under conformance work in COQ. Purposes: design an optimal, mature product via design guidelines; build confidence that future output will meet requirements (quality audits, failure analysis); confirm quality processes are used and meet objectives; improve process efficiency and effectiveness. The organisation's QA department may do failure analysis, design of experiments and quality improvement. Manage Quality is everybody's work - PM, team, sponsor, performing organisation management, even the customer; in agile all team members do it throughout; in traditional projects specific members are often responsible. Inputs: quality management plan (acceptable quality level, how to ensure it, handling nonconforming products and corrective action); documents (lessons learned, quality control measurements - evaluate processes and deliverables against standards and validate measurement correctness, quality metrics - basis for test scenarios and improvement, risk report - sources of overall risk affecting quality objectives); OPAs (quality management system, templates incl. check sheets, traceability matrices, test plans, previous audit results, lessons learned). Tools: data gathering - checklists (structured, usually component-specific tool to verify steps were performed or requirements satisfied; should include scope baseline acceptance criteria); data analysis - alternatives analysis, document analysis (quality, test, performance reports and variance analyses point to processes out of control), process analysis (improvement opportunities, problems, constraints, non-value-added activities), root cause analysis (underlying reason for a variance, defect or risk; one root cause may drive several; removing all root causes stops recurrence); decision making - multicriteria decision analysis (implementation scenarios, suppliers; product decisions on life-cycle cost, schedule, satisfaction, defect-resolution risk); data representation - affinity diagrams (group potential causes of defects), cause-and-effect diagrams (fishbone, why-why, Ishikawa: break the problem statement into branches to find root cause; Figure 8-9 example 'product quality not matching requirements' with branches management, environment, material, equipment, process, people), flowcharts (steps leading to a defect), histograms (numerical data: defects per deliverable, ranking of causes, noncompliance counts), matrix diagrams, scatter diagrams (relationship between two variables, e.g., a process element and a defect); audits (structured, independent process to determine compliance with organisational and project policies, processes and procedures; usually by a team external to the project - internal audit, PMO or external auditor; objectives: identify good/best practices, nonconformity, gaps and shortcomings; share good practices; proactively help improve processes and productivity; add to the lessons learned repository; correcting deficiencies should reduce COQ and raise acceptance; scheduled or random, internal or external; can confirm implementation of approved changes); Design for X (DfX: technical guidelines applied during design to optimise a specific aspect - reliability, deployment, assembly, manufacturing, cost, service, usability, safety, quality; may cut cost, improve quality and performance, customer satisfaction); problem solving (define the problem, identify root cause, generate solutions, choose the best, implement, verify effectiveness - from Control Quality findings or audits); quality improvement methods (from QC findings, audits or problem solving; PDCA and Six Sigma most common). Outputs: quality reports (graphical, numerical or qualitative; escalated quality issues, improvement recommendations, corrective action recommendations - rework, defect/bug repair, 100% inspection - and summary of Control Quality findings); test and evaluation documents (from industry needs and templates; inputs to Control Quality; may include checklists and detailed RTMs); change requests; plan updates (quality management plan, scope, schedule, cost baselines); document updates (issue log, lessons learned, risk register). Data flow: change requests to 4.6.

q-8.3-control-quality.title: 8.3 Control Quality: check sheets, statistical sampling, inspection, testing, control charts, verified deliverables
q-8.3-control-quality.notes: Monitor and record results of quality activities to assess performance and ensure outputs are complete, correct and meet customer expectations; key benefit: verifying deliverables and work meet key stakeholders' requirements for final acceptance; determines whether outputs do what they were intended to do and comply with standards, requirements, regulations and specifications; performed throughout. Measures completeness, compliance and fitness for use before user acceptance and final delivery, demonstrating with reliable data that acceptance criteria are met. Effort varies by industry (stricter in pharmaceutical, health, transportation, nuclear); in agile all members perform it throughout; in waterfall at specific times toward the end of a project or phase by specified members. Inputs: quality management plan; documents (lessons learned, quality metrics, test and evaluation documents); approved change requests (defect repairs, revised work methods, revised schedules - implementation must be verified, confirmed complete, retested and certified; partial completion causes inconsistencies and delays); deliverables (from 4.3, inspected against acceptance criteria in the scope statement); work performance data (observations, quality metrics, technical performance measures, schedule and cost performance); EEFs (PMIS and quality management software, agency regulations, application-area standards); OPAs (quality standards and policies, templates such as check sheets and checklists, issue and defect reporting procedures). Tools: data gathering - checklists; check sheets (tally sheets organising facts to collect data on a potential quality problem; useful for attribute data during inspections, e.g., frequency of defect types - Figure 8-12: small scratch, large scratch, bent, missing component, wrong colour, labelling error by date); statistical sampling (inspect part of a population, e.g., 10 of 75 drawings at random; frequency and size set in Plan Quality Management); questionnaires and surveys (customer satisfaction after deployment; defects found this way count as external failure costs); data analysis - performance reviews (quality metrics vs actual results), root cause analysis (source of defects); inspection (examination of a work product for conformance to documented standards; any level from a single activity to the final product; also called reviews, peer reviews, audits, walkthroughs; also verifies defect repairs); testing/product evaluations (organised investigation giving objective information about quality per requirements; aims to find errors, defects, bugs; type and extent set in the quality plan; throughout and at the end - early testing lowers the cost of fixing; software: unit, integration, black-box, white-box, interface, regression, alpha; construction: cement strength, concrete workability, nondestructive tests, soil tests; hardware: environmental stress screening, burn-in, system testing); data representation - cause-and-effect diagrams, control charts (whether a process is stable/predictable; upper and lower specification limits come from requirements - maximum and minimum allowed; upper and lower control limits are different, calculated statistically to show the natural capability of a stable process; used to decide where corrective action is taken; used for manufactured lots but also cost and schedule variances, volume, frequency of scope changes), histograms (defects by source or component), scatter diagrams (planned vs actual performance); meetings - approved change requests review (verify implemented as approved, partial changes completed, tested, certified) and retrospectives/lessons learned (what succeeded, what to improve, what to carry into this and future projects, what to add to OPAs). Outputs: quality control measurements (documented results in the format set in the quality plan); verified deliverables (correctness determined; input to Validate Scope for formal acceptance; changed deliverables are re-inspected and re-verified); work performance information (requirements fulfilment, causes of rejection, rework needed, corrective action recommendations, verified deliverables list, quality metric status, need for process adjustments); change requests; plan updates (quality management plan); document updates (issue log - a nonconforming deliverable is often logged as an issue, lessons learned, risk register, test and evaluation documents). Data flow: deliverables and WPD from 4.3; approved change requests from 4.6; WPI to 4.5; change requests to 4.6; verified deliverables to 5.5.

q-quality-overview.title: Project Quality Management overview: three processes, interrelations, quality vs grade, prevention vs inspection, COQ, five levels, trends
q-quality-overview.section: 8 intro, key concepts, trends, tailoring, agile (Figures 8-1, 8-2)
q-quality-overview.notes: Incorporate the organisation's quality policy for planning, managing and controlling project and product quality requirements to meet stakeholders' objectives; also supports continuous process improvement. Processes: 8.1 Plan Quality Management (identify quality requirements/standards and document how compliance will be demonstrated); 8.2 Manage Quality (translate the quality management plan into executable quality activities incorporating organisational quality policies); 8.3 Control Quality (monitor and record results of quality activities to assess performance and ensure outputs are complete, correct and meet customer expectations). Plan = the quality the work needs to have; Manage = managing the quality processes throughout; quality requirements become test and evaluation instruments in Manage Quality, applied in Control Quality to verify requirements; Control = compare results with requirements so the result is acceptable. Two outputs used by other areas: verified deliverables and quality reports. Figure 8-2 (verified): Plan Quality Management sends the quality management plan and quality metrics to Manage Quality; OPA quality templates also feed Manage Quality; Integration supplies deliverables and work performance data to Control Quality; Manage Quality sends test and evaluation documents and quality reports to Control Quality and quality reports to other processes; Control Quality returns quality control measurements and work performance information to Manage Quality, and sends verified deliverables to Validate Scope. Key concepts: applies to all projects; measures are deliverable-specific (software vs nuclear plant); failure has consequences (overworking the team, rushing inspections). Quality = 'the degree to which a set of inherent characteristics fulfill requirements' (ISO 9000, as quoted in the Guide); grade = a category for deliverables with the same functional use but different technical characteristics. Low quality is always a problem; low grade may not be (a low-grade, high-quality product may suit its purpose; a high-grade, low-quality product is a problem). The PM manages quality/grade trade-offs. Prevention is preferred over inspection - design quality in; preventing mistakes costs less than correcting them. Pairs to know: prevention (keep errors out of the process) vs inspection (keep errors out of the customer's hands); attribute sampling (conforms or not) vs variable sampling (continuous scale of conformity); tolerances (specified range of acceptable results) vs control limits (boundaries of common variation in a statistically stable process). Cost of quality (COQ): all costs over the product life for preventing nonconformance, appraising conformance and failing requirements (rework); failure costs are internal (found by the team) or external (found by the customer), a.k.a. cost of poor quality; life-cycle COQ decisions often belong to program/portfolio management, the PMO or operations. Five levels of increasingly effective quality management: let the customer find defects (most expensive: warranty, recalls, reputation, rework); detect and correct before delivery via quality control (appraisal and internal failure costs); quality assurance to correct the process itself; build quality into planning and design; create an organisation-wide culture committed to quality. Trends: customer satisfaction (conformance to requirements plus fitness for use; agile stakeholder engagement); continual improvement (PDCA cycle - Shewhart, modified by Deming; TQM, Six Sigma, Lean Six Sigma); management responsibility (all team members participate; management provides suitable resources at adequate capacity); mutually beneficial partnership with suppliers (long-term cooperative relationships over short-term gains). Tailoring: policy compliance and auditing, standards and regulatory compliance, continuous improvement level, stakeholder engagement. Agile: frequent quality and review steps throughout rather than at the end; recurring retrospectives check quality process effectiveness, find root causes and trial new approaches, later keeping, adjusting or dropping them; small batches uncover inconsistencies early when change is cheaper. ITTOs for 8.1-8.3 recorded in ittos.json from Figure 8-1.

r-9.1-plan-resource.title: 9.1 Plan Resource Management: OBS, RBS, RAM/RACI, organisational theory, resource management plan, team charter
r-9.1-plan-resource.notes: Agile context: in high-variability projects collaborative teams are critical (less time for central tasking); resource planning is less predictable, so fast-supply agreements and lean methods are critical for cost and schedule. Process: define how to estimate, acquire, manage and use team and physical resources; key benefit: approach and level of management effort based on project type and complexity; once or at predefined points. Ensures sufficient resources, considering availability of and competition for scarce resources, internal or procured; competing projects may affect cost, schedule, risk and quality. Inputs: charter (description, requirements, key stakeholders, summary milestones, preapproved financial resources); plan (quality management plan - resources needed for the quality level and metrics; scope baseline - deliverables drive resource types and quantities); documents (project schedule - timeline for resources; requirements documentation; risk register; stakeholder register - stakeholders interested in resources or able to influence resource choice); EEFs (culture and structure, geographic distribution, existing competencies and availability, marketplace); OPAs (HR policies, physical resource policies, safety and security policies, templates, historical information). Tools: expert judgment (negotiating for the best resources, talent management, preliminary effort level, reporting requirements, acquisition lead times, acquisition/retention/release risks, government and union regulations, seller and logistics management); data representation - goal: each work package has an unambiguous owner and everyone understands their role; hierarchical charts: WBS (deliverables to work packages, high-level areas of responsibility), organisational breakdown structure (OBS - arranged by existing departments, units or teams with their work packages listed, so a department sees all its project responsibilities), resource breakdown structure (hierarchical list of team and physical resources by category and type for planning, managing and controlling work); responsibility assignment matrix (RAM - resources assigned to each work package; high-level RAMs for groups per WBS component, lower-level ones for specific activities; shows all activities for one person and all people for one activity; ensures only one person is accountable for any task); RACI chart (responsible, accountable, consult, inform; useful with internal and external resources; Figure 9-4 verified: Create charter - Ann A, Ben R, Carlos I, Dina I, Ed I; Collect requirements - Ann I, Ben A, Carlos R, Dina C, Ed C; Submit change request - Ann I, Ben A, Carlos R, Dina R, Ed C; Develop test plan - Ann A, Ben C, Carlos I, Dina I, Ed R - note exactly one A per activity while R can be shared); text-oriented formats (position descriptions, role-responsibility-authority forms; reusable templates); organisational theory (how people, teams and units behave; can shorten planning time and effort; may recommend a flexible leadership style adapting to the team's maturity across the life cycle; organisation structure and culture shape the project organisation); meetings. Outputs: resource management plan (how resources are categorised, allocated, managed and released; may split into team management and physical resource management plans): identification of resources; acquiring resources; roles and responsibilities - role (function, e.g., civil engineer, business analyst, testing coordinator), authority (rights to apply resources, make decisions, sign approvals, accept deliverables, influence others - members work best when authority matches responsibility), responsibility (assigned duties and work), competence (skill and capacity; mismatches handled by training, hiring, schedule or scope changes); project organisation charts (team members and reporting relationships, detail scaled to the project - e.g., a 3,000-person disaster response team vs a 20-person internal project); project team resource management (define, staff, manage, release); training strategies; team development methods; resource control (physical resources available as needed, acquisition optimised, inventory, equipment, supplies); recognition plan (which rewards and when). Team charter: team values, communication guidelines, decision-making criteria and process, conflict resolution process, meeting guidelines, team agreements; sets expectations of acceptable behaviour; early commitment reduces misunderstandings and raises productivity; works best when the team develops or contributes to it; all members share responsibility for following it; reviewed periodically and used to orient new members. Document updates: assumption log (physical resource availability, logistics, location; team skills and availability), risk register. Data flow: charter from 4.1.

r-9.2-estimate-resources.title: 9.2 Estimate Activity Resources: resource calendars, estimating methods, resource requirements, RBS
r-9.2-estimate-resources.notes: Estimate team resources and the type and quantities of materials, equipment and supplies; key benefit: type, quantity and characteristics of resources required; periodically as needed. Closely coordinated with Estimate Costs (e.g., hire a consultant for local building codes vs internal labour; get automated assembly know-how via consultant, seminar or a manufacturing team member). Inputs: plan (resource management plan - how to identify and quantify resources per activity; scope baseline); documents (activity attributes - primary data source: resource requirements, imposed dates, location, assumptions, constraints; activity list; assumption log - productivity, availability, costs, approaches; cost estimates - affect quantity and skill choices; resource calendars - working days, shifts, business hours, weekends, holidays and periods when each resource is available, with experience, skill level and location; risk register); EEFs (resource location, availability, team skills, culture, published estimating data, marketplace); OPAs (staffing policies, supplies and equipment policies, historical resource information). Tools: expert judgment; bottom-up estimating (estimate at activity level and aggregate to work packages, control accounts and project); analogous estimating (quick, from a similar project, when only the top WBS levels are known); parametric estimating (e.g., 4,000 hours of coding to finish in 1 year at 2,000 hours per person per year = 2 coders); alternatives analysis (skill levels, machine sizes or types, manual vs automated tools, make-rent-buy); PMIS (resource management software for pools, RBS, availability, rates, calendars); meetings (with functional managers on resources per activity, level of effort, skill level, material quantities). Outputs: resource requirements (types and quantities per work package or activity, aggregated up the WBS, with assumptions); basis of estimates (method, sources, assumptions, constraints, range, confidence, risks); resource breakdown structure (hierarchical representation of resources by category - labour, material, equipment, supplies - and type - skill level, grade, certifications; guided categorisation in planning, now a completed document used to acquire and monitor resources; Figure 9-7 generic example: project -> personnel/material/equipment -> roles/levels/grades); document updates (activity attributes, assumption log - types and quantities and constraints such as collective bargaining agreements, continuous hours of operation, planned leave; lessons learned).

r-9.3-acquire-resources.title: 9.3 Acquire Resources: negotiation, pre-assignment, virtual teams, selection criteria, assignments and resource calendars
r-9.3-acquire-resources.notes: Obtain team members, facilities, equipment, materials, supplies and other resources; key benefit: guides selection and assignment of resources to activities; periodically as needed. Internal resources are assigned by functional or resource managers; external ones come through procurement. The PM team may lack direct control over selection (collective bargaining, subcontractor personnel, matrix environment, reporting relationships). Considerations: negotiate and influence those who provide resources; failing to acquire them affects schedule, budget, satisfaction, quality and risk, and may cancel the project; if unavailable, alternative resources with different competencies or costs may be used provided no legal, regulatory or mandatory criteria are violated - plan for this and document impacts on schedule, budget, risk, quality, training and other plans. Inputs: plan (resource management plan; procurement management plan - resources from outside and integration of procurement; cost baseline - overall budget); documents (project schedule - when resources are needed; resource calendars - availability, time zones, work hours, vacations, local holidays, maintenance schedules, other commitments; progressively elaborated; resource requirements; stakeholder register - expectations for specific resources); EEFs (resource availability, competence, experience and costs; marketplace; structure; geography); OPAs (acquisition and assignment policies, historical information). Tools: decision making - multicriteria decision analysis with weighted selection criteria (availability, cost, ability; for team members also experience, knowledge of the customer and environment, skills with project tools, attitude to teamwork, international factors such as location, time zone and communication capability); interpersonal skills - negotiation with functional managers (best resources for the needed time), other project teams (share scarce or specialised resources) and external organisations and suppliers (respect their policies and legal criteria); ability to influence and organisational politics matter (e.g., stressing project visibility to a functional manager); pre-assignment (resources determined in advance - named in a competitive proposal, project depends on specific experts, or assigned during chartering before the resource plan exists); virtual teams (groups with a shared goal who spend little or no time face to face; enable geographically spread teams, remote experts, home-based workers, different shifts, people with mobility limitations or disabilities, projects otherwise stopped by travel cost, savings on offices and equipment; communication planning becomes more important - time to set expectations, facilitate communication, conflict protocols, inclusive decisions, cultural understanding, shared credit). Outputs: physical resource assignments (material, equipment, supplies, locations); project team assignments (members, roles and responsibilities, team directory, names in org charts and schedules); resource calendars; change requests; plan updates (resource management plan, cost baseline); document updates (lessons learned, project schedule, RBS, resource requirements, risk register, stakeholder register); EEF updates (resource availability, consumable resources used); OPA updates (acquisition and assignment documentation). Data flow: change requests to 4.6.

r-9.4-develop-team.title: 9.4 Develop Team: high-performing team behaviours, Tuckman ladder, colocation, team building, recognition, training, assessments
r-9.4-develop-team.notes: Improve competencies, team interaction and the team environment; key benefit: improved teamwork, interpersonal skills and competencies, motivated employees, reduced attrition, better performance; performed throughout. Developing effective teams is a primary PM responsibility: create an environment for teamwork; motivate with challenges and opportunities, timely feedback and support, recognition and rewards. High performance via open and effective communication, team-building opportunities, trust, constructive conflict management, collaborative problem solving and decision making. Global, culturally diverse teams (multiple languages, a 'team language'): capitalise on cultural differences, sustain the team, work interdependently with mutual trust. Objectives: improve knowledge and skills (lower cost, shorter schedule, better quality); improve trust and agreement (morale up, conflict down, more teamwork); create a dynamic, cohesive, collaborative culture (productivity, spirit, cross-training and mentoring); empower the team to make decisions and own solutions. Tuckman ladder - five stages, usually in order but teams can get stuck, regress or skip if they worked together before: forming (meet, learn roles; independent and less open), storming (address work, technical decisions and approach; can be counterproductive without openness), norming (adjust habits to support the team; trust develops), performing (well-organised, interdependent, resolve issues smoothly), adjourning (work done, team released, e.g., at Close Project or Phase); stage length depends on dynamics, size and leadership. Inputs: resource management plan (rewards, feedback, training, discipline, team performance assessment criteria); documents (lessons learned, project schedule - when to train and build competencies, project team assignments, resource calendars - when members can join development activities, team charter); EEFs (HR policies - hiring, termination, reviews, training records, recognition; team skills and knowledge; geographic distribution); OPAs (historical information, lessons learned). Tools: colocation (place the most active members in one location - temporary or whole project; team meeting room, shared schedule boards - sometimes called a 'war room' in practice, though the Guide doesn't use that term here); virtual teams (more skilled resources, lower cost, less travel and relocation, proximity to suppliers or customers; online team environment with file storage, threads, calendar); communication technology (shared portal, video conferencing, audio conferencing, email/chat); interpersonal and team skills - conflict management (timely and constructive), influencing (gather relevant information, reach agreement while keeping trust), motivation (providing a reason to act; empower decision making and independent work), negotiation (consensus on project needs), team building (activities that enhance social relations and cooperation, from a 5-minute agenda item to a facilitated offsite; valuable for remote teams; essential early but continuous); recognition and rewards (plan made in Plan Resource Management; effective only if they satisfy a need the individual values; consider culture; intangible rewards can be as effective as money - growth, accomplishment, appreciation, challenge; recognise throughout, not just at the end); training (formal or informal: classroom, online, computer-based, on-the-job, mentoring, coaching; scheduled per the resource plan or unplanned after observation and appraisals; cost may be in the project budget or borne by the organisation if skills are reusable); individual and team assessments (attitudinal surveys, specific assessments, structured interviews, ability tests, focus groups - preferences, aspirations, information processing, decision making, interaction; build understanding, trust, commitment, communication); meetings (orientation, team-building, team development). Outputs: team performance assessments (formal or informal; indicators - improved individual skills, improved team competencies, reduced turnover, increased cohesiveness; identify training, coaching, mentoring, assistance or changes and the resources needed); change requests; plan updates (resource management plan); document updates (lessons learned, project schedule, project team assignments, resource calendars, team charter); EEF updates (employee development plan records, skill assessments); OPA updates (training requirements, personnel assessment).

r-9.5-manage-team.title: 9.5 Manage Team: conflict sources and five resolution techniques, decision making, emotional intelligence, influencing, leadership
r-9.5-manage-team.notes: Track team member performance, give feedback, resolve issues and manage team changes; key benefit: influences behaviour, manages conflict, resolves issues; performed throughout. Requires management and leadership skills with emphasis on communication, conflict management, negotiation and leadership; give challenging assignments and recognition; adapt style to members' willingness and ability (low-skill members need more intensive oversight). Inputs: resource management plan (how team resources are managed and released); documents (issue log - who resolves what by when; lessons learned; project team assignments; team charter - how the team decides, meets, resolves conflict); work performance reports (from schedule control, cost control, quality control and scope validation - inform resource needs, rewards and plan updates); team performance assessments (ongoing, to resolve issues, modify communication, address conflict, improve interaction); EEFs (HR policies); OPAs (certificates of appreciation, corporate apparel, other perquisites). Tools: interpersonal and team skills - conflict management: conflict is inevitable; sources include scarce resources, scheduling priorities and personal work styles; ground rules, group norms, communication planning and role definition reduce it; managed well it increases creativity and better decisions; team members are initially responsible for resolving their conflicts; if it escalates, the PM facilitates; address early, usually in private, directly and collaboratively; persistent disruptive conflict may need formal procedures including discipline. Factors in choosing a method: importance and intensity, time pressure, relative power, importance of the relationship, motivation for a long- or short-term solution. Five techniques: withdraw/avoid (retreat or postpone to prepare or let others resolve); smooth/accommodate (emphasise agreement, concede to maintain harmony); compromise/reconcile (some satisfaction for all, temporary or partial; occasionally lose-lose); force/direct (push one view at others' expense, win-lose, usually via power to resolve an emergency); collaborate/problem solve (incorporate multiple viewpoints, cooperative attitude and open dialogue leading to consensus and commitment; can be win-win). Decision making (here the ability to negotiate and influence; guidelines: focus on goals, follow a process, study environmental factors, analyse information, stimulate creativity, account for risk). Emotional intelligence (identify, assess and manage one's own, others' and groups' emotions; reduce tension, increase cooperation, anticipate actions, acknowledge concerns, follow up issues). Influencing (critical in a matrix with little direct authority: persuasiveness, clear articulation, active and effective listening, awareness of perspectives, gathering information while maintaining trust). Leadership (lead and inspire the team throughout the life cycle; use styles suited to situation; communicate the vision). PMIS (resource or scheduling software to coordinate members). Outputs: change requests (e.g., staffing changes - reassignments, outsourcing, replacing leavers - can cause schedule slips or overruns); plan updates (resource management plan, schedule baseline, cost baseline); document updates (issue log, lessons learned, project team assignments); EEF updates (input to organisational performance appraisals, personnel skill). Data flow: work performance reports from 4.5; team performance assessments from 9.4; change requests to 4.6.

r-9.6-control-resources.title: 9.6 Control Resources: physical resource control, problem-solving steps, outputs
r-9.6-control-resources.notes: Ensure physical resources assigned and allocated are available as planned, monitor planned vs actual utilisation and take corrective action; key benefit: resources available at the right time and place and released when no longer needed; performed continuously in all phases. Concerns physical resources (equipment, materials, facilities, infrastructure) - team members are handled in Manage Team. Concerned with: monitoring resource expenditures; identifying and dealing with shortage/surplus in time; using and releasing resources per plan; informing stakeholders of issues; influencing factors that change utilisation; managing actual changes. Schedule or cost baseline changes only via Perform Integrated Change Control. Inputs: resource management plan; documents (issue log - lack of resources, delayed or low-grade raw material; lessons learned; physical resource assignments - expected utilisation, type, amount, location, internal or outsourced; project schedule; RBS - reference for replacing or reacquiring; resource requirements; risk register); work performance data (number and type of resources used); agreements (basis for all external resources; define procedures for new unplanned resources or issues); OPAs (resource control and assignment policies, escalation procedures, lessons learned). Tools: data analysis - alternatives analysis (e.g., pay overtime or add resources vs late or phased delivery), cost-benefit analysis, performance reviews (planned vs actual utilisation; cost and schedule information), trend analysis (resources needed for upcoming stages); problem solving - problems from inside (machines not released by another department, materials damaged by bad storage) or outside (supplier bankruptcy, weather damage); steps: identify the problem, define it (break into smaller problems), investigate (collect data), analyse (find root cause), solve (choose a suitable solution), check the solution; interpersonal skills - negotiation (additional or changed physical resources, costs), influencing; PMIS (monitor utilisation - right resources on right activities at the right time and place). Outputs: work performance information (requirements and allocation vs utilisation; availability gaps); change requests; plan updates (resource management plan, schedule baseline, cost baseline); document updates (assumption log, issue log, lessons learned - logistics, scrap, utilisation variances, corrective actions; physical resource assignments - dynamic; RBS; risk register). Data flow: WPD from 4.3; agreements from 12.2; WPI to 4.5; change requests to 4.6.

r-leadership-qualities.title: Leadership skills, dealing with people and qualities of a leader
r-leadership-qualities.notes: Leadership = ability to guide, motivate and direct a team (negotiation, resilience, communication, problem solving, critical thinking, interpersonal skills). People are the common denominator - 'people can be counted, but they are not numbers'. Study behaviours and motivations; lead all stakeholders including steering team and sponsors. Qualities: visionary; optimistic; collaborative; managing relationships and conflict (trust, satisfying concerns, consensus, balancing goals, persuasion, negotiation, compromise, conflict resolution, networks, long-term view, political acumen); communicating (top PMs spend about 90% of their time communicating; manage expectations; accept feedback graciously; give it constructively; ask and listen); respectful, courteous, honest, trustworthy, loyal, ethical; integrity, cultural sensitivity, courage, problem solving, decisiveness; giving credit; life-long learner, results- and action-oriented; focusing on the important (continuous prioritisation, strategic vs tactical priorities, vigilance on primary constraints, sifting information); holistic and systemic view; critical thinking and being a change agent; building effective teams, service orientation, humour.

r-leadership-vs-management.title: Leadership vs management; leadership styles; personality
r-leadership-vs-management.notes: Management directs a person from one point to another using known expected behaviours; leadership works with others through discussion or debate to guide them. Table 3-1: management directs using positional power, maintains, administrates, focuses on systems and structure, relies on control, near-term goals, asks how and when, focuses on bottom line, accepts the status quo, does things right, focuses on operational issues and problem solving. Leadership guides, influences and collaborates using relational power, develops, innovates, focuses on relationships, inspires trust, long-range vision, asks what and why, focuses on the horizon, challenges the status quo, does the right things, focuses on vision, alignment, motivation, inspiration. PMs need both; the skill is the balance. Style factors: leader, team member, organisational and environmental characteristics. Styles: laissez-faire (hands-off), transactional (goals, feedback, rewards; management by exception), servant leader (serve first; others' growth, autonomy, well-being; leadership emerges after service), transformational (idealised attributes, inspirational motivation, innovation, individual consideration), charismatic, interactional (mix of transactional, transformational, charismatic). Personality traits: authentic, courteous, creative, cultural, emotional, intellectual, managerial, political, service-oriented, social, systemic; emphasis varies by situation.

r-performing-integration.title: Performing integration at process, cognitive and context levels; complexity
r-performing-integration.notes: Two-fold integration role: work with the sponsor to align project objectives with portfolio, program and business strategy; and guide the team to focus on what is essential by integrating processes, knowledge and people. Process level: processes overlap and recur (e.g., a requirement change affecting scope, schedule or budget raises a change request handled through Control Scope and Perform Integrated Change Control, which runs throughout); failing to integrate interacting processes leaves little chance of meeting objectives. Cognitive level: method depends on size, complexity and culture; PM becomes proficient in all Knowledge Areas and applies experience, insight, leadership, technical and business skills. Context level: new technologies, social networks, multicultural aspects, virtual teams and new values; consider them in communications planning and knowledge management. Complexity (Navigating Complexity practice guide) arises from system behaviour (interdependencies of components and systems), human behaviour (interplay of individuals and groups) and ambiguity (uncertainty of emerging issues, confusion). Complexity is a perception; a project 'contains' complexity. Properties: multiple parts, many connections, dynamic interactions, emergent behaviour not explained by the sum of the parts.

r-pm-definition-sphere.title: Project manager defined; sphere of influence (project, organisation, industry, profession, across disciplines)
r-pm-definition-sphere.notes: Conductor analogy continued: neither leader must play every instrument/role but needs domain knowledge, and both lead, plan and coordinate through written (scores/plans) and real-time (baton/meetings, verbal and nonverbal cues) communication. Definition: the PM is the person assigned by the performing organisation to lead the team responsible for achieving project objectives - distinct from a functional manager (oversight of a functional/business unit) and an operations manager (efficient operations). Sphere of influence (Figure 3-1): project team, sponsors, governing bodies, steering committees, PMOs, portfolio/program/project managers, resource managers, other stakeholders, suppliers, customers, end users. The project: lead the team, balance competing constraints with resources, communicate between sponsor, team and stakeholders, present the vision of success, use soft skills to reach consensus (relevant stakeholders support decisions even without 100% agreement). Research: the top 2% of PMs show superior relationship and communication skills and a positive attitude. Communication practices: multiple methods; create and follow communications plans; predictable, consistent; understand needs (communication may be the only deliverable some stakeholders get until the end); concise, clear, complete, simple, relevant, tailored; include positive and negative news; feedback channels; relationship skills and networks - informal networks matter more than formal ones. The organisation: interact with other PMs (shared resources, funding priorities, deliverable hand-offs, goal alignment); advocacy role; work with sponsor on internal political/strategic issues; build PM competency; tacit and explicit knowledge transfer; demonstrate value of PM, raise acceptance, advance the PMO; may report to a functional manager, PMO, portfolio or program manager; may be an external consultant. The industry: stay informed on product/technology development, market niches, standards, support tools, economic forces, discipline influences, process improvement and sustainability. Professional discipline: contribute knowledge (communities of practice) and keep learning in PM, related and other professions. Across disciplines: act as informal ambassador for the value of PM (timeliness, quality, innovation, resource management).

r-pm-role-overview.title: The project manager's role and the orchestra-conductor analogy
r-pm-role-overview.notes: The PM leads the team to achieve project objectives, often from initiation to closing, sometimes also in pre-project evaluation (advising executives on strategy, business analysis, business case, portfolio aspects) and follow-on benefits realisation. The role is tailored to the organisation as processes are tailored to the project. Analogy with a conductor: membership and roles (100+ members in sections like orchestra sections representing business units); responsibility for the team's product, taking a holistic view, aligning with organisational vision, mission and objectives and using that interpretation to communicate and motivate. (Continues on PDF 89.)

r-politics-power.title: Politics, power and getting things done: forms of power
r-politics-power.notes: Politics involves influence, negotiation, autonomy and power and is neither good nor bad in itself. The PM observes the project and organisational landscape, reviews data in context and selects the right kind of power to influence and negotiate, while respecting others and maintaining their autonomy. Power may stem from individual or organisational traits and is supported by others' perception. Forms: positional (formal, authoritative, legitimate), informational, referent (respect/admiration, credibility), situational (e.g., crisis), personal or charismatic, relational (networks, alliances), expert, reward-oriented, punitive or coercive, ingratiating, pressure-based, guilt-based, persuasive, avoiding. Top PMs are proactive and intentional: they acquire the power and authority they need within organisational policies rather than wait for it to be granted.

r-resource-overview.title: Project Resource Management overview: six processes, team vs physical resources, trends (EI, self-organising, virtual teams), tailoring, agile
r-resource-overview.section: 9 intro, key concepts, trends, tailoring, agile (Figure 9-1)
r-resource-overview.notes: Identify, acquire and manage resources needed for success; right resources at the right time and place. Processes: 9.1 Plan Resource Management (how to estimate, acquire, manage and utilise physical and team resources); 9.2 Estimate Activity Resources (team resources and type and quantities of material, equipment, supplies); 9.3 Acquire Resources (obtain team members, facilities, equipment, materials, supplies); 9.4 Develop Team (improve competencies, team interaction and environment); 9.5 Manage Team (track performance, give feedback, resolve issues, manage team changes); 9.6 Control Resources (ensure physical resources are available as planned, monitor planned vs actual use, take corrective action). Physical resources = equipment, materials, facilities, infrastructure; team resources = personnel (varied skills, full- or part-time, added or removed over time). Overlaps with Stakeholder Management; Section 9 covers the team subset of stakeholders. Key concepts: the team = individuals with assigned roles working toward a shared goal; invest effort in acquiring, managing, motivating and empowering it; involving all members in planning and decisions adds expertise and commitment; the PM is both leader and manager and responsible for forming an effective group, aware of team environment, geographic locations, communications, organisational change management, internal and external politics, cultural issues and organisational uniqueness; develops skills and competencies while keeping satisfaction and motivation; upholds professional and ethical behaviour. Physical resource management: allocate and use material, equipment and supplies efficiently; needs data on demand, configurations and supply; poor control is a risk (late critical equipment delays production; low-quality material causes recalls or rework; too much inventory raises costs, too little fails demand). Trends: shift from command and control to collaborative, supportive management empowering teams; optimise utilisation; resource management methods (lean, just-in-time manufacturing, Kaizen, total productive maintenance, theory of constraints) - adapt to what the organisation uses; emotional intelligence (inbound: self-management and self-awareness; outbound: relationship management; emotionally competent teams are more effective and have lower turnover); self-organising teams (agile, no centralised control; the PM - who may not be called that - provides environment and support and trusts the team; generalised specialists who adapt and accept feedback); virtual/distributed teams (enabled by email, audio and video conferencing, social media, web meetings; advantages - expertise from anywhere, home-based staff, people with mobility limitations or disabilities; challenges - isolation, knowledge-sharing gaps, tracking progress and productivity, time zones, culture). Tailoring: diversity, physical location, industry-specific resources, acquisition of team members (full/part-time), team development and special needs, life cycle approach. Agile: high-variability projects benefit from self-organising teams of generalising specialists; collaboration boosts productivity and innovative problem solving, integration, communication, knowledge sharing and flexible assignments. ITTOs for 9.1-9.6 recorded in ittos.json from Figure 9-1.

r-talent-triangle.title: PMI Talent Triangle: technical project management, leadership, strategic and business management
r-talent-triangle.notes: Based on the Project Manager Competency Development (PMCD) Framework. Technical project management = knowledge, skills and behaviours for specific domains of project, program and portfolio management. Leadership = guide, motivate and direct a team to help the organisation achieve business goals. Strategic and business management = industry and organisational expertise that enhances performance and delivers business outcomes. Technical skills alone are not enough; organisations want leadership and business intelligence; PMs need a balance of all three. Top PMs: focus on critical technical elements and have key artefacts at hand (critical success factors, schedule, selected financial reports, issue log); tailor traditional and agile tools; plan thoroughly and prioritise; manage schedule, cost, resources, risks; rely on expert judgment and know where to find expertise. Strategic/business skills: see the high-level organisation, negotiate and implement decisions supporting alignment and innovation; working knowledge of finance, marketing, operations; domain knowledge; explain the business aspects of the project, develop a delivery strategy with sponsor, team and SMEs, implement it to maximise business value; consult operational managers. Be able to explain strategy, mission, goals, products/services, operations, market and competition; apply strategy, mission, goals, priority, tactics and products to the project; weigh risks and issues, financial implications, cost vs benefit (NPV, ROI), business value, benefits realisation, scope/budget/schedule/quality; keep business and project strategies aligned with the sponsor as conditions change.

s-5.1-plan-scope.title: 5.1 Plan Scope Management: scope management plan and requirements management plan
s-5.1-plan-scope.notes: Create a scope management plan documenting how project and product scope will be defined, validated and controlled; key benefit: guidance on how scope will be managed; performed once or at predefined points. Begins with analysis of the charter, latest approved subsidiary plans, historical information (OPAs) and EEFs. Inputs: charter (purpose, high-level description, assumptions, constraints, high-level requirements); plan (quality management plan - quality policy shapes scope management; project life cycle description; development approach - waterfall, iterative, adaptive, agile or hybrid); EEFs (culture, infrastructure, personnel administration, marketplace); OPAs (policies and procedures, historical information and lessons learned). Tools: expert judgment (previous similar projects, industry/discipline/application area information); data analysis - alternatives analysis of ways to collect requirements, elaborate scope, create the product, validate and control scope; meetings (PM, sponsor, selected team members and stakeholders, owners of scope processes). Outputs: scope management plan - processes for preparing the scope statement, creating the WBS from the detailed scope statement, approving and maintaining the scope baseline, and obtaining formal acceptance of completed deliverables; formal or informal, broad or detailed. Requirements management plan (some call it a business analysis plan) - how requirements activities are planned, tracked and reported; configuration management activities (how changes are initiated, impacts analysed, traced, tracked, reported, and authorisation levels to approve); prioritisation process; metrics and rationale; traceability structure reflecting attributes captured in the traceability matrix. Data flow: charter from 4.1 and plan components in; both plans out to the project management plan.

s-5.2-collect-requirements.title: 5.2 Collect Requirements: elicitation techniques, requirements documentation, traceability matrix
s-5.2-collect-requirements.notes: Determine, document and manage stakeholder needs and requirements to meet objectives; key benefit: the basis for defining product and project scope; performed once or at predefined points. The Guide does not address industry-specific product requirements. Success depends on active stakeholder involvement in discovering and decomposing needs and on care in determining, documenting and managing requirements. Requirements are quantified, documented needs and expectations of sponsor, customer and other stakeholders, detailed enough for the scope baseline and to be measured during execution; they are the foundation of the WBS, and cost, schedule, quality planning and procurement are based on them. Inputs: charter (high-level description and requirements); plan (scope management plan, requirements management plan, stakeholder engagement plan - to adapt to stakeholders' participation level); documents (assumption log, lessons learned register - effective elicitation techniques especially for iterative/adaptive work, stakeholder register - who can provide requirements); business documents (business case - required, desired, optional criteria); agreements (may contain project and product requirements); EEFs (culture, infrastructure, personnel administration, marketplace); OPAs (policies, historical information). Tools (part 1): expert judgment (business analysis, elicitation, analysis, documentation, previous projects, diagramming, facilitation, conflict management); data gathering - brainstorming; interviews (formal or informal, prepared and spontaneous questions, individual or multiple participants; useful for confidential information); focus groups (prequalified stakeholders and SMEs, trained moderator, conversational); questionnaires and surveys (many respondents quickly; varied audiences, quick turnaround, geographically dispersed, statistical analysis); benchmarking (compare products, processes and practices with comparable internal or external organisations to find best practices, ideas and a performance basis); data analysis - document analysis (agreements, business plans, process/interface documentation, business rules repositories, current process flows, marketing literature, problem/issue logs, policies, regulatory documentation, RFPs, use cases); decision making - voting (unanimity: everyone agrees; majority: more than 50%, an odd group size avoids ties; plurality: largest block decides even without a majority, used with more than two options), autocratic (one person decides for the group), multicriteria decision analysis (decision matrix with criteria such as risk, uncertainty, valuation to rank ideas); data representation - affinity diagrams (classify many ideas into groups), mind mapping (consolidate individual brainstorming into one map showing commonalities, differences and new ideas). (Continued in batch B08.) Data flow (Figure 5-5, verified): inputs from 4.1 (charter), plan, documents, business documents, 12.2 (agreements), enterprise; outputs requirements documentation and RTM to project documents.

s-5.2-requirements-techniques-outputs.title: 5.2 Collect Requirements (continued): nominal group, observation, facilitation (JAD, QFD, user stories), context diagram, prototypes, requirement classes, RTM
s-5.2-requirements-techniques-outputs.notes: Nominal group technique: structured brainstorming with voting in four steps - question posed and each person silently writes ideas; moderator records all ideas on a flip chart; each idea is discussed until understood; individuals vote privately (usually 1-5, 5 highest), possibly in several rounds, and top-scoring ideas are selected. Observation/conversation ('job shadowing'): watch people do their jobs - useful when users find it hard or are reluctant to articulate requirements; a participant observer performs the process to uncover hidden requirements. Facilitation: focused workshops bring key stakeholders together to define cross-functional requirements quickly and reconcile differences; builds trust and consensus, surfaces issues earlier; JAD (joint application design/development - software; business SMEs with the development team), QFD (quality function deployment - manufacturing; starts with the voice of the customer, sorts and prioritises needs, sets goals), user stories (short text of required functionality: role who benefits, goal, motivation/benefit), often written in requirements workshops. Context diagram: a scope model showing the business system and how actors (people, other systems) interact with it - inputs, who provides them, outputs, who receives them. Prototypes: early feedback through a model (small-scale product, 2D/3D models, mock-ups, simulations); support progressive elaboration through cycles of mock-up, experimentation, feedback and revision until requirements are complete enough for design/build; storyboarding shows sequence or navigation through images (film, advertising, instructional design, software UI). Outputs: requirements documentation - how individual requirements meet the business need; progressively detailed; before baselining requirements must be unambiguous (measurable and testable), traceable, complete, consistent and acceptable to key stakeholders. Classes: business requirements (organisation-level needs and reasons for the project); stakeholder requirements; solution requirements - functional (behaviours: actions, processes, data, interactions) and nonfunctional (environmental conditions or qualities: reliability, security, performance, safety, level of service, supportability, retention/purge); transition and readiness requirements (temporary capabilities such as data conversion and training to move from as-is to to-be); project requirements (milestone dates, contractual obligations, constraints); quality requirements (conditions to validate completion, e.g., tests, certifications, validations). Requirements traceability matrix (RTM): a grid linking product requirements from their origin to the deliverables that satisfy them; ensures each requirement adds business value; tracks requirements through the life cycle; structures product scope change management. Traces to business needs and objectives, project objectives, scope/WBS deliverables, product design, development, test strategy and scenarios, and high-level to detailed requirements. Attributes: unique ID, description, rationale, owner, source, priority, version, status (active, cancelled, deferred, added, approved, assigned, completed), status date; plus stability, complexity, acceptance criteria.

s-5.3-define-scope.title: 5.3 Define Scope: product analysis, project scope statement, charter vs scope statement
s-5.3-define-scope.notes: Develop a detailed description of the project and product; key benefit: describes product, service or result boundaries and acceptance criteria. Not every collected requirement is included - Define Scope selects the final project requirements; builds on major deliverables, assumptions and constraints from initiation; analyses risks, assumptions and constraints for completeness; can be highly iterative (in iterative life cycles a high-level vision for the whole project, detailed scope one iteration at a time). Inputs: charter (high-level description, product characteristics, approval requirements); scope management plan; documents (assumption log, requirements documentation, risk register - responses such as reducing or changing scope to avoid or mitigate a risk); EEFs; OPAs (scope statement templates, previous project files, lessons learned).
