Tools: expert judgment; alternatives analysis (ways to meet requirements and charter objectives); multicriteria decision analysis (decision matrix with criteria such as requirements, schedule, budget, resources to refine scope); facilitation (workshops to reach cross-functional common understanding of deliverables and boundaries); product analysis (ask questions about the product to describe its use and characteristics; translate high-level descriptions into deliverables; product breakdown, requirements analysis, systems analysis, systems engineering, value analysis, value engineering). Outputs: project scope statement - description of project scope, major deliverables, assumptions and constraints; documents entire scope (project and product); common understanding; may list explicit exclusions; enables detailed planning, guides execution, baseline for judging whether requested work is in or out of scope. Contents: product scope description (progressively elaborated), deliverables (including ancillary results like reports and documentation), acceptance criteria (conditions to be met before deliverables are accepted), project exclusions (explicitly out of scope; manages expectations and reduces scope creep). Table 5-1: charter = high-level (purpose, measurable objectives and success criteria, high-level requirements, description/boundaries/key deliverables, overall risk, summary milestones, preapproved financial resources, key stakeholders, approval requirements, exit criteria, assigned PM and authority, sponsor name and authority); scope statement = detailed (scope description, deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions). Document updates: assumption log, requirements documentation, RTM, stakeholder register.

s-5.4-create-wbs.title: 5.4 Create WBS: decomposition, work packages, control accounts, planning packages, 100 percent rule, WBS dictionary, scope baseline
s-5.4-create-wbs.notes: Subdivide deliverables and work into smaller, more manageable components; key benefit: a framework of what has to be delivered; once or at predefined points. The WBS is a hierarchical decomposition of the total scope of work to accomplish objectives and create deliverables; represents the approved scope statement; planned work sits in the lowest components, work packages, where activities are grouped and scheduled, estimated, monitored and controlled. 'Work' in the WBS means work products or deliverables, not activities. Inputs: scope management plan (how the WBS is created from the scope statement); documents (scope statement, requirements documentation); EEFs (industry-specific WBS standards); OPAs (WBS policies, procedures and templates, previous project files, lessons learned). Tools: expert judgment; decomposition - dividing scope and deliverables into smaller parts until the work package level, where cost and duration can be estimated and managed; level guided by needed control and project size and complexity. Steps: identify and analyse deliverables and work; structure and organise the WBS; decompose upper levels; develop and assign identification codes; verify the degree of decomposition is appropriate. Approaches: top-down, organisation-specific guidelines, WBS templates; bottom-up to group subcomponents. Forms: phases at level 2 with deliverables at level 3 (Figure 5-13, software release example); major deliverables at level 2 (Figure 5-14, aircraft system example); subcomponents from outside organisations with a seller-developed contract WBS. In agile, epics decompose into user stories. Representations: outline, organisation chart or other hierarchy. Verify that lower-level components are necessary and sufficient for their parent. Different deliverables may need different depths. More detail improves planning and control, but excessive decomposition wastes management effort and resources, lowers efficiency and makes aggregation hard. Far-future deliverables may not be decomposable yet - rolling wave planning. The WBS includes all product and project work including project management; lower levels roll up so nothing is left out and nothing extra is done - the 100 percent rule. Output: scope baseline = approved scope statement + WBS + WBS dictionary, changed only via formal change control, a plan component. Work package: lowest level, unique identifier; identifiers form a code of accounts for hierarchical summation of cost, schedule and resource information; each work package belongs to exactly one control account. Control account: management control point where scope, budget and schedule are integrated and compared to earned value; has two or more work packages. Planning package: below the control account and above the work package; known work content but no detailed schedule activities. WBS dictionary: detailed deliverable, activity and scheduling information for each WBS component - code of account identifier, description of work, assumptions and constraints, responsible organisation, milestones, associated activities, resources, cost estimates, quality requirements, acceptance criteria, technical references, agreement information (much added later by other processes). Document updates: assumption log, requirements documentation. Figures 5-12 to 5-14 are illustrative WBS examples only.

s-5.5-validate-scope.title: 5.5 Validate Scope: formal acceptance by customer or sponsor; Validate Scope vs Control Quality
s-5.5-validate-scope.notes: Formalise acceptance of completed deliverables; key benefit: objectivity in acceptance and higher probability of final acceptance by validating each deliverable; performed periodically as needed. Verified deliverables from Control Quality are reviewed with the customer or sponsor for formal acceptance, using planning outputs (requirements documentation, scope baseline) and work performance data. Validate Scope is about acceptance; Control Quality is about correctness and meeting quality requirements; Control Quality is generally performed first, though they may run in parallel. Inputs: plan (scope management plan - how acceptance is obtained; requirements management plan - how requirements are validated; scope baseline); documents (lessons learned register, quality reports, requirements documentation, RTM - how each requirement will be validated); verified deliverables (completed and checked for correctness via Control Quality); work performance data (degree of compliance, number and severity of nonconformities, validation cycles). Tools: inspection (measuring, examining, validating against requirements and acceptance criteria; also called reviews, product reviews, walkthroughs); decision making - voting when validation is by team and stakeholders. Outputs: accepted deliverables (formally signed off by customer or sponsor; documentation forwarded to Close Project or Phase); work performance information (which deliverables were accepted or not, and why); change requests (non-accepted deliverables documented with reasons; may need defect repair); document updates (lessons learned register, requirements documentation - especially results better than required or waived requirements, RTM - validation method and outcome). Data flow (Figure 5-16, verified): in from 4.3 (WPD), 8.3 (verified deliverables), plan and documents; out to 4.7 (accepted deliverables), 4.6 (change requests), 4.5 (WPI), documents.

s-5.6-control-scope.title: 5.6 Control Scope: maintaining the scope baseline, scope creep, variance and trend analysis
s-5.6-control-scope.notes: Monitor the status of project and product scope and manage changes to the scope baseline; key benefit: scope baseline maintained throughout; performed throughout. Ensures all requested changes and recommended corrective/preventive actions go through Perform Integrated Change Control; manages actual changes when they occur; integrated with other control processes. Scope creep = uncontrolled expansion of product or project scope without adjustments to time, cost and resources. Change is inevitable, so some change control process is mandatory on every project. Inputs: plan (scope, requirements, change and configuration management plans; scope baseline; performance measurement baseline); documents (lessons learned register, requirements documentation, RTM); work performance data; OPAs. Tool: data analysis (variance analysis, trend analysis). Outputs: work performance information; change requests; plan updates (scope management plan, scope baseline, schedule baseline, cost baseline, performance measurement baseline); document updates (lessons learned register, requirements documentation, RTM). Data flow (Figure 5-18, verified): WPD from 4.3; WPI to 4.5; change requests to 4.6. (Continued on PDF 206.)

s-5.6-control-scope-detail.title: 5.6 Control Scope (continued): inputs, variance and trend analysis, baseline revisions
s-5.6-control-scope-detail.notes: Inputs detail: scope management plan (how scope is controlled), requirements management plan, change management plan (process for managing change), configuration management plan (configurable items, items needing formal change control, the control process), scope baseline and performance measurement baseline (compared with actual results, the latter when using earned value), lessons learned register, requirements documentation (detect deviation from agreed scope), RTM (impact of changes/deviations on objectives; requirement status), work performance data (number of change requests received and accepted, deliverables verified, validated and completed), OPAs (scope control policies, monitoring and reporting methods and templates). Variance analysis compares baseline to actual and decides whether the variance is within threshold or needs corrective/preventive action; trend analysis checks whether performance is improving or deteriorating over time; key aspects: the cause and degree of variance relative to the scope baseline and whether action is needed. WPI: correlated and contextualised scope performance vs baseline - categories of changes, scope variances and causes, schedule/cost impact, forecast scope performance. Change requests may target scope and schedule baselines or other components. Plan updates: scope management plan; scope, schedule, cost and performance measurement baselines updated in response to approved changes - and when variances are so severe that a revised baseline is needed to give a realistic basis for performance measurement. Document updates: lessons learned (causes of variances and corrective actions chosen), requirements documentation, RTM.

s-scope-overview.title: Project Scope Management overview: six processes, product vs project scope, predictive vs adaptive scope, requirements, business analysis
s-scope-overview.section: 5 intro, key concepts, trends, tailoring, agile considerations (Figure 5-1)
s-scope-overview.notes: Ensure the project includes all the work required, and only the work required; mainly defining and controlling what is and is not included. Processes: 5.1 Plan Scope Management (scope management plan for defining, validating, controlling scope); 5.2 Collect Requirements (determine, document, manage stakeholder needs and requirements); 5.3 Define Scope (detailed description of project and product); 5.4 Create WBS (subdivide deliverables and work into smaller manageable components); 5.5 Validate Scope (formalise acceptance of completed deliverables); 5.6 Control Scope (monitor scope status and manage changes to the scope baseline). Product scope = features and functions characterising the product, service or result; project scope = the work performed to deliver it (sometimes viewed as including product scope). Completion of project scope is measured against the project management plan; completion of product scope against the product requirements. Requirement = a condition or capability required to be present to satisfy an agreement or formally imposed specification. Predictive: deliverables defined at the start, changes progressively managed; Collect Requirements, Define Scope and Create WBS done early and updated through integrated change control; Validate Scope with each deliverable or phase review; Control Scope ongoing; scope baseline = approved scope statement + WBS + WBS dictionary, changed only via formal change control. Adaptive/agile: detailed scope defined and approved per iteration; overall scope decomposed into a product backlog; team pulls the highest-priority items it can deliver; Collect Requirements, Define Scope and Create WBS repeat each iteration, and so do Validate Scope and Control Scope; sponsor and customer representatives continuously engaged; backlogs (requirements, user stories) reflect current needs. Verified deliverables from Control Quality feed Validate Scope, which yields accepted deliverables signed off by the authorised stakeholder, who should be involved early. Trends: collaborating with business analysis professionals to determine problems and needs, recommend solutions, elicit, document and manage requirements, and facilitate implementation; requirements management starts with a needs assessment (portfolio, program or project) and ends with requirements closure (transition to the recipient to realise and sustain benefits); if a business analyst is assigned, requirements activities are that role's responsibility, while the PM ensures requirements work is in the plan, on time, on budget and delivering value - a collaborative partnership. Tailoring: knowledge and requirements management systems and reuse, validation and control policies, development approach, stability of requirements (unstable areas may need lean/agile until stable), governance. Agile: with evolving requirements, high risk or uncertainty, agile spends less time defining scope up front and more on a process for ongoing discovery and refinement; prototypes and releases close the gap between stated and real business requirements; scope is defined and redefined; requirements constitute the backlog. ITTOs for 5.1-5.6 recorded in ittos.json from Figure 5-1.

src-publication-structure.title: How the source publication is organised (Guide, Standard, Appendices; bundled Agile Practice Guide)
src-publication-structure.notes: Part 1 is the Guide (chapters 1-13): framework chapters 1-3 and ten Knowledge Area chapters 4-13. Part 2 is The Standard for Project Management (ANSI/PMI 99-001-2017), organised by the five Process Groups. Part 3 holds Appendices X1-X6, Glossary and Index. The Part 1 divider states that Part 1 is not an American National Standard and was not processed under ANSI's consensus requirements, whereas Part 2 is the ANSI standard. This PDF also bundles the Agile Practice Guide (PDF 794-976).

std-closing-group.title: Standard: Closing Process Group - purpose, single process, early closure; Close Project or Phase inputs and outputs
std-closing-group.notes: Closing = process(es) to formally complete or close a project, phase or contract; verifies that defined processes are completed within all Process Groups and formally establishes completion. Key benefit: phases, projects and contracts are closed out appropriately. Only one process (6.1 Close Project or Phase) but the term Process Group is kept because organisations may have their own closure processes. Also addresses early closure - aborted or cancelled projects. Inputs and outputs match Part 1 (verified); all plan components may be inputs; example documents: assumption log, basis of estimates, change log, issue log, lessons learned, milestone list, project communications, quality control measurements, quality reports, requirements documentation, risk register, risk report; document update: lessons learned register.

std-eef-opa-tailoring.title: Standard: EEFs and OPAs; tailoring the project artifacts; plan components vs project documents vs business documents
std-eef-opa-tailoring.notes: EEFs originate outside the project and often the enterprise; conditions not under the team's control that influence, constrain or direct the project; impact at enterprise, portfolio, program or project level; e.g., internal culture, structure and governance (vision, mission, values, beliefs, norms, hierarchy, authority relationships). OPAs are internal to the enterprise (from the enterprise, a portfolio, program, other project or combination): plans, processes, policies, procedures and knowledge bases used by the performing organisation; e.g., change control procedures, templates, previous project information, lessons learned repositories. 1.11: 'artifact' here includes processes, inputs, tools, techniques, outputs, EEFs and OPAs; selecting and adapting them is tailoring - needed because not every process or ITTO is required on every project. The project management plan is the most prevalent artifact (subsidiary management plans, baselines, life cycle description); identifying which components are needed is part of tailoring. The Standard lists plan components and project documents beneath each process's input/output table only as examples - not required and not exhaustive. Project documents are other documents not part of the plan; the PM is accountable for identifying which documents a process needs and updates. Table 1-2 repeats Part 1 Table 4-1 (18 plan components, 33 project documents). Business documents originate outside the project and are inputs to it (business case, benefits management plan); their use depends on company culture and the initiation process. EEFs and OPAs depend on the project and are not listed per process in the Standard.

std-executing-group.title: Standard: Executing Process Group - purpose, budget consumption, change requests; inputs and outputs of the 10 executing processes (4.1-4.9)
std-executing-group.notes: Executing = processes performed to complete the work defined in the project management plan to satisfy requirements: coordinating resources, managing stakeholder engagement, integrating and performing activities per the plan. Key benefit: the work needed to meet requirements and objectives is performed according to plan. A large portion of the project budget, resources and time is expended in Executing. Executing processes may generate change requests; if approved they may trigger planning processes producing a modified plan, documents and possibly new baselines. Figure 4-1 groups the ten executing processes: Integration - Direct and Manage Project Work, Manage Project Knowledge; Quality - Manage Quality; Resource - Acquire Resources, Develop Team, Manage Team; Communications - Manage Communications; Risk - Implement Risk Responses; Procurement - Conduct Procurements; Stakeholder - Manage Stakeholder Engagement. Sections 4.1-4.9 restate definitions, key benefits, frequency and input/output lists (Direct and Manage Project Work, Manage Project Knowledge, Manage Quality, Acquire Resources, Develop Team, Manage Team, Manage Communications, Implement Risk Responses, Conduct Procurements) with example components and documents - all matching Part 1 ITTOs (verified). (4.10 Manage Stakeholder Engagement continues on PDF 646.)

std-executing-group-2.title: Standard: Conduct Procurements (end) and Manage Stakeholder Engagement inputs and outputs
std-executing-group-2.notes: Example documents and plan/document updates for Conduct Procurements and the full input/output list for Manage Stakeholder Engagement (increase support, minimise resistance), all matching Part 1 (verified).

std-initiating-group.title: Standard: Initiating Process Group - purpose, project boundaries, revisiting at each phase; Develop Project Charter and Identify Stakeholders inputs and outputs
std-initiating-group.notes: Initiating = processes to define a new project or phase by obtaining authorisation. Purpose: align stakeholders' expectations with the project purpose, inform them of scope and objectives, and discuss how their participation helps meet their expectations. The initial scope is defined, initial financial resources committed, stakeholders identified, the PM appointed if not already, captured in the charter and stakeholder register; charter approval officially authorises the project and the PM's authority to apply resources. Key benefits: only projects aligned with strategic objectives are authorised; business case, benefits and stakeholders are considered from the start. In some organisations the PM helps develop the business case and benefits and writes the charter; elsewhere pre-project work is done by the sponsor, PMO, portfolio steering committee or others; the Standard assumes the sponsor or governing body approved the project after reviewing business documents. Figure 2-1 (project boundaries): the sponsor and business documents sit outside the boundary and feed Initiating; within the boundary, Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling and Closing processes interact; deliverables go out to end users and project records to OPAs. In phased projects, Initiating information is re-examined at each phase start - charter, business documents and success criteria verified; stakeholders' influence, drivers, expectations and objectives reviewed - keeping focus on the business need; involving sponsors, customers and stakeholders in initiation creates shared understanding of success criteria and raises acceptance and satisfaction. Processes: 2.1 Develop Project Charter (Integration) and 2.2 Identify Stakeholders (Stakeholder) - definitions, key benefits and frequency as in Part 1; inputs and outputs match Part 1 figures (verified); example plan components for 2.2: communications management plan, stakeholder engagement plan; documents: change log, issue log, requirements documentation; plan updates: requirements, communications, risk, stakeholder engagement plans; document updates: assumption log, issue log, risk register.

std-intro-and-projects.title: The Standard for Project Management: purpose and relationship to the Guide; projects and project management; competing constraints
std-intro-and-projects.notes: Part 2 is The Standard for Project Management (ANSI/PMI 99-001-2017). A standard is a document established by an authority, custom or general consent as a model or example; developed on consensus, openness, due process and balance; describes processes considered good practice on most projects most of the time, organised by Process Group; defines key concepts (relationship to strategy and objectives, governance, portfolio and program management, project environment, success), life cycles, stakeholders and the PM's role. Section 1 gives key concepts; Sections 2-6 define each Process Group and describe its processes with key benefits, inputs and outputs (tools and techniques are left to the Guide). The Standard is the foundation and framework for the Guide, which adds context, environment, influences, ITTO descriptions, tools and techniques, key concepts and trends per Knowledge Area. 1.1: a project is a temporary endeavour to create a unique product, service or result; temporary means a definite beginning and end, not necessarily short; ends when objectives are achieved, or it is terminated because objectives will not or cannot be met or the need no longer exists; termination requires approval by an appropriate authority (a point stated in the Standard). Project management = applying knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to meet requirements, through applying and integrating the processes. Managing a project typically includes identifying requirements; addressing stakeholders' needs, concerns and expectations; active communication; managing resources; balancing competing constraints - scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources and risk. Circumstances influence how processes are implemented and constraints prioritised.

std-life-cycle-stakeholders-pm.title: Standard: project life cycle and phases, impact of variables over time, stakeholders, role of the project manager, Knowledge Areas
std-life-cycle-stakeholders-pm.notes: 1.5: life cycle = series of phases from start to completion; phase = logically related activities culminating in deliverables; sequential, iterative or overlapping; names, number and duration set by management and control needs, nature of the project and application area; phases are time bound with a control point (phase review, phase gate, control gate) where the charter and business documents are re-examined and performance compared to the plan to decide whether to change, terminate or continue. Influenced by organisation, industry, development method or technology. Generic structure (Figure 1-2): starting the project, organizing and preparing, carrying out the work, closing (labelled 'ending') the project. Generic characteristics (Figure 1-3): cost and staffing low at the start, rise during the work and drop rapidly near closure; risk greatest at the start and decreasing as decisions are made and deliverables accepted; stakeholders' ability to influence the product's final characteristics without significant cost or schedule impact is highest at the start and decreases; the cost of making changes and correcting errors increases substantially toward completion. 1.6: stakeholder = individual, group or organisation that may affect, be affected by, or perceive itself to be affected by a decision, activity or outcome; internal or external; actively involved, passively involved or unaware; positive or negative impact. Internal examples: sponsor, resource manager, PMO, portfolio steering committee, program manager, other PMs, team members; external: customers, end users, suppliers, shareholders, regulatory bodies, competitors (Figure 1-4 mirrors the sphere of influence figure). Involvement ranges from surveys and focus groups to full sponsorship and changes over the life cycle, so identification, analysis, engagement and expectation management throughout are critical. 1.7: the PM is assigned by the performing organisation to lead the team; reporting relationships follow structure and governance; attributes: knowledge (PM, business environment, technical), skills (lead, coordinate, collaborate, solve problems, decide), abilities (develop and manage scope, schedules, budgets, resources, risks, plans, presentations, reports), other attributes (personality, attitude, ethics, leadership). Interpersonal skills: leadership, team building, motivating, communicating, influencing, decision making, political and cultural awareness, negotiating, facilitating, managing conflict, coaching. Success = objectives achieved plus stakeholder satisfaction; tailor approach, life cycle and processes. 1.8: Knowledge Areas are fields or areas of specialisation commonly employed; a Knowledge Area is a set of processes associated with a topic; ten used on most projects most of the time, others may be needed; definitions repeat Part 1 Section 1.2.4.6.

std-monitoring-controlling-group.title: Standard: Monitoring and Controlling Process Group - monitoring vs controlling, what the group involves; inputs and outputs of the 12 M&C processes
std-monitoring-controlling-group.notes: M&C = processes to track, review and regulate progress and performance, identify needed plan changes and initiate them. Monitoring = collecting project performance data, producing performance measures, and reporting and disseminating performance information. Controlling = comparing actual with planned performance, analysing variances, assessing trends to effect process improvements, evaluating alternatives and recommending corrective action as needed. Key benefit: performance is measured and analysed at regular intervals, appropriate events or exception conditions to identify and correct variances from the plan. Also involves: evaluating change requests and deciding responses; recommending corrective or preventive action in anticipation of problems; monitoring ongoing activities against the plan and baselines; influencing factors that could circumvent change control so only approved changes are implemented. Continuous monitoring gives insight into status and areas needing attention; M&C covers each Knowledge Area, each Process Group, each life cycle phase and the project as a whole. Figure 5-1 groups the 12 processes: Integration - Monitor and Control Project Work, Perform Integrated Change Control; Scope - Validate Scope, Control Scope; Schedule - Control Schedule; Cost - Control Costs; Quality - Control Quality; Resource - Control Resources; Communications - Monitor Communications; Risk - Monitor Risks; Procurement - Control Procurements; Stakeholder - Monitor Stakeholder Engagement. Sections 5.1-5.12 restate definitions, key benefits, frequency (Control Procurements: throughout the project when procurements are active) and input/output lists with example components - all matching Part 1 (verified). Note: the Standard's definition of Perform Integrated Change Control includes managing changes to organisational process assets as well as deliverables, documents and the plan (consistent with the Part 1 chapter introduction).

std-planning-group.title: Standard: Planning Process Group - purpose, progressive elaboration, baselines; inputs and outputs of the 24 planning processes (part 1: 3.1-3.13)
std-planning-group.notes: Planning = processes that establish the total scope of the effort, define and refine objectives and develop the course of action; they develop the plan components and project documents. Repeated feedback loops may be needed; significant changes may require revisiting planning and possibly initiating processes. Ongoing refinement of the plan is progressive elaboration - planning and documentation are iterative or ongoing. Key benefit: defines the course of action to complete the project or phase successfully. The team seeks input and involvement from relevant stakeholders. When initial planning is complete, the approved plan is considered a baseline; M&C processes compare performance to baselines. Figure 3-1 groups the 24 planning processes by Knowledge Area (Integration: Develop Project Management Plan; Scope: Plan Scope Management, Collect Requirements, Define Scope, Create WBS; Schedule: Plan Schedule Management, Define Activities, Sequence Activities, Estimate Activity Durations, Develop Schedule; Cost: Plan Cost Management, Estimate Costs, Determine Budget; Quality: Plan Quality Management; Resource: Plan Resource Management, Estimate Activity Resources; Communications: Plan Communications Management; Risk: Plan Risk Management, Identify Risks, Perform Qualitative and Quantitative Risk Analysis, Plan Risk Responses; Procurement: Plan Procurement Management; Stakeholder: Plan Stakeholder Engagement - labelled 'Plan Stakeholder Management' in the figure, a naming slip in the source). Sections 3.1-3.13 restate definitions, key benefits, frequency and input/output lists for Develop Project Management Plan through Determine Budget, with example plan components and documents; all inputs/outputs match the Part 1 ITTO figures recorded in ittos.json (verified item by item). Create WBS note: scope baseline = approved scope statement, WBS and WBS dictionary. The Standard lists inputs and outputs only; tools and techniques are in the Guide.

std-planning-group-2.title: Standard: planning processes 3.14-3.24 (quality, resource, communications, risk, procurement, stakeholder planning) - inputs, outputs and example components
std-planning-group-2.notes: Restates definitions, key benefits, frequency and input/output lists for Plan Quality Management, Plan Resource Management, Estimate Activity Resources, Plan Communications Management, Plan Risk Management (all available plan components should be considered so risk management fits project needs), Identify Risks, Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis, Perform Quantitative Risk Analysis, Plan Risk Responses, Plan Procurement Management and Plan Stakeholder Engagement, with example plan components and documents that match Part 1. Note: the Standard's 3.22.2 lists project team assignments as a Plan Risk Responses input, consistent with Part 1 Figure 11-16 (supporting the choice made where Figure 11-17 differs). All inputs and outputs verified against ittos.json.

std-ppp-governance-success.title: Standard: portfolios, programs and projects; OPM as a strategy execution framework; organisational vs project governance; project success and benefits management
std-ppp-governance-success.notes: 1.2: portfolio = projects, programs, subsidiary portfolios and operations managed in a coordinated manner to achieve strategic objectives; portfolio management = centralised management of one or more portfolios, ensuring performance consistent with objectives and optimising resource allocation; may include operational work. Program = related projects, subsidiary programs and program activities managed in a coordinated manner for benefits not otherwise available; includes program-related work outside discrete projects and possibly operational work; program management supports strategy by authorising, changing or terminating projects and managing interdependencies: resolving resource constraints and conflicts, aligning with strategy, managing issues and change in shared governance, addressing risks affecting components, managing benefits realisation by analysing, sequencing and monitoring interdependencies. A project can be stand-alone, within a program or within a portfolio. Figure 1-1: strategy drives portfolios, programs and projects with shared resources and stakeholders; relationships are not always strictly hierarchical. OPM is described here as a strategy execution framework using portfolio, program and project management to deliver strategy consistently and predictably for better performance, results and sustainable competitive advantage. 1.3: types of governance - organisational, OPM, portfolio, program, project. Organisational governance = structured direction and control through policies and processes to meet strategic and operational goals, typically by a board of directors for accountability, fairness and transparency; it influences lower levels by enforcing legal, regulatory, standards and compliance requirements, defining ethical, social and environmental responsibilities and specifying operational, legal and risk policies. Project governance = framework, functions and processes guiding project management activities; at project level: guiding and overseeing work, ensuring adherence to policies and standards, establishing governance roles, responsibilities and authorities, decisions on risk escalations, changes and resources, ensuring stakeholder engagement, monitoring performance. Project governance framework elements: stage gate or phase reviews; identifying, escalating and resolving risks and issues; roles, responsibilities and authorities; knowledge management and lessons learned; decision making, problem solving and escalation beyond the PM's authority; reviewing and approving project and product changes beyond the PM's authority. 1.4: projects realise business opportunities aligned with strategy; a business case often precedes initiation (objectives, investment, financial and qualitative success criteria) and is the basis for measuring success. Strategic considerations initiating projects: market demand, strategic opportunity/business need, social need, environmental consideration, customer request, technological advancement, legal or regulatory requirement, existing or forecasted problem. Benefits management plan: target benefits, strategic alignment, timeframe, benefits owner, metrics, risks. Success is measured against objectives and success criteria; product success (market share, operating cost, new product success) may only be known after transition, so the PMO, portfolio steering committee or another business function evaluates later. Business case and benefits management plan are developed before initiation and referenced after completion, so they are business documents - not project documents or plan components - though they may be inputs (e.g., to Develop Project Charter).

std-process-groups.title: Standard: the five Process Groups, process frequency categories, Process Group interactions and phases
std-process-groups.notes: Process Group definitions repeat Part 1 (Initiating - define a new project or phase by obtaining authorisation; Planning - establish scope, refine objectives, define the course of action; Executing - complete the planned work to satisfy requirements; Monitoring and Controlling - track, review and regulate progress and performance, identify needed plan changes and initiate them; Closing - formally complete or close a project, phase or contract). Process Groups are independent of application areas (marketing, information services, accounting) and industry focus (construction, aerospace, telecommunications). Individual processes are often iterated before a phase or project completes. Frequency categories: once or at predefined points (charter, close); periodically as needed (acquire resources, conduct procurements); continuously (define activities with rolling wave or adaptive approaches; most M&C processes). Outputs of one process generally become inputs to another or deliverables (e.g., the plan and documents such as the risk register and responsibility assignment matrix from Planning are used and updated in Executing). Figure 1-5 shows Process Groups overlapping over time within a project or phase with varying level of effort (Initiating first, Planning and Executing peaks, Monitoring and Controlling spanning the whole duration, Closing last). Process Groups are not phases: within a phased project, processes of all Process Groups may be repeated in each phase (concept development, feasibility, design, prototype, build, test) until the phase completion criteria are satisfied. Table 1-1 maps the 49 processes to Process Groups and Knowledge Areas - identical to Part 1 Table 1-4 (see process-map.json).

t-6.1-plan-schedule.title: 6.1 Plan Schedule Management: the schedule management plan contents
t-6.1-plan-schedule.notes: Establish policies, procedures and documentation for the schedule; key benefit: guidance on how the schedule will be managed; once or at predefined points. Inputs: charter (summary milestone schedule); plan (scope management plan; development approach - shapes scheduling approach, estimating techniques, tools, control techniques); EEFs (culture and structure, team and physical resource availability and skills, scheduling software, tailoring guidelines, commercial databases such as standardised estimating data); OPAs (historical information and lessons learned, schedule policies and procedures, templates and forms, monitoring and reporting tools). Tools: expert judgment (schedule development, management and control; methodologies; software; industry); alternatives analysis (which methodology or combination, how detailed, rolling-wave wave length, review frequency - balancing detail against update effort); meetings. Output: schedule management plan (formal or informal, detailed or broad, with control thresholds), establishing: schedule model development (methodology and tool); release and iteration length (time-boxed periods in adaptive life cycles - time-boxing minimises scope creep by forcing essential features first); level of accuracy (acceptable range for realistic duration estimates, may include contingency); units of measure per resource (staff hours, days, weeks; metres, litres, tons, cubic yards); organisational procedures links (the WBS is the framework, giving consistency with estimates and schedules); schedule model maintenance (how status and progress are recorded during execution); control thresholds (agreed variation, typically % deviation from the baseline, before action is needed); rules of performance measurement (rules for percent complete, EVM techniques such as baselines, fixed-formula, percent complete; schedule measures such as SV and SPI); reporting formats and frequency.

t-6.2-define-activities.title: 6.2 Define Activities: decomposition into activities, rolling wave planning, activity list, attributes, milestones
t-6.2-define-activities.notes: Identify and document the specific actions to produce deliverables; key benefit: decomposes work packages into schedule activities as the basis for estimating, scheduling, executing, monitoring and controlling; performed throughout. Inputs: schedule management plan (methodology, rolling-wave wave duration, level of detail); scope baseline (WBS, deliverables, constraints, assumptions); EEFs (culture and structure, commercial databases, PMIS); OPAs (lessons learned with activity lists from similar projects, standardised processes, activity list templates, activity planning policies). Tools: expert judgment; decomposition - activities represent the effort to complete a work package; Define Activities produces activities whereas Create WBS produces deliverables; the activity list, WBS and WBS dictionary can be developed sequentially or concurrently; involving team members improves accuracy; rolling wave planning - iterative technique where near-term work is planned in detail and future work at a higher level; a form of progressive elaboration for work packages, planning packages and release planning in agile or waterfall; meetings. Outputs: activity list (all schedule activities with an identifier and a scope-of-work description; updated periodically under rolling wave or agile); activity attributes (evolve over time: initially ID, WBS ID, name; later description, predecessors, successors, logical relationships, leads and lags, resource requirements, imposed dates, constraints, assumptions, location, calendar, type of effort; used for scheduling and sorting in reports); milestone list (significant points or events, each mandatory - e.g., contractual - or optional - e.g., historical; milestones have zero duration); change requests (elaborating deliverables into activities after baselining may reveal work outside the baselines, processed via 4.6); plan updates (schedule baseline, cost baseline).

t-6.3-network-diagrams.title: 6.3 Sequence Activities (continued): lags, network diagrams, path convergence and divergence
t-6.3-network-diagrams.notes: Lag = time a successor is delayed relative to its predecessor (editing starts 15 days after writing starts = SS with 15-day lag). Network diagrams show lags as e.g. SS+10 even without a timescale. The team decides which dependencies need leads or lags; leads and lags must not replace schedule logic; duration estimates never include leads or lags; document activities and assumptions. PMIS scheduling software sequences activities, inserts relationships, leads and lags, and distinguishes dependency types. Output: project schedule network diagram - graphical representation of logical relationships (dependencies), manual or software-produced, detailed or with summary activities, often with a narrative explaining unusual sequences. Path convergence = an activity with multiple predecessors; path divergence = an activity with multiple successors; both carry greater risk. Figure 6-11 (visually verified) example: Begin feeds A, H and K; A->B; B->C is SS; C->D->E; B->E; H->C; H->F; F->G is FS+15; H->I is SS+10; K->I; K->L; I->J; L->J is FF; E, G and J feed End. Activity I is a convergence (H and K); K is a divergence (I and L). Document updates: activity attributes, activity list, assumption log, milestone list.

t-6.3-sequence-activities.title: 6.3 Sequence Activities: PDM relationship types, dependency types, leads and lags
t-6.3-sequence-activities.notes: Identify and document relationships among activities; key benefit: the logical sequence of work for the greatest efficiency given all constraints; performed throughout. Every activity except the first and last should have at least one predecessor and one successor with an appropriate logical relationship; leads/lags may be needed for a realistic schedule; converts the activity list into a diagram as a first step to the schedule baseline. Inputs: schedule management plan (method, accuracy); scope baseline; documents (activity attributes, activity list, assumption log - may create schedule risks, milestone list); EEFs (standards, PMIS, scheduling tools, work authorisation systems); OPAs (portfolio and program plans and dependencies, policies, network templates, lessons learned). Tools: precedence diagramming method (PDM) - activities are nodes linked by logical relationships; predecessor comes before a dependent activity, successor comes after. Finish-to-start (FS): successor cannot start until predecessor finishes (install OS after assembling the PC) - most common. Finish-to-finish (FF): successor cannot finish until predecessor finishes (editing finishes after writing finishes). Start-to-start (SS): successor cannot start until predecessor starts (level concrete after pouring begins). Start-to-finish (SF): successor cannot finish until predecessor starts (new payables system must start before the old one can shut down) - very rarely used. Two relationships between the same pair (e.g., SS and FF) are possible but not recommended - pick the highest-impact one; closed loops not recommended. Dependency determination and integration - four attributes combinable in pairs: mandatory (legally/contractually required or inherent in the work; physical limits; 'hard logic'; not to be confused with schedule constraints in the tool; technical dependencies are not necessarily mandatory) vs discretionary (preferred/preferential/soft logic based on best practice or a desired sequence, e.g., electrical after plumbing to reduce risk; document fully because they can create arbitrary total float and limit options; review when fast tracking); external (project activities vs non-project activities, usually outside team control - hardware delivery, government hearings) vs internal (between project activities, inside team control). Leads and lags: lead = time a successor can be advanced relative to its predecessor (landscaping starts 2 weeks before punch list completion = FS with a 2-week lead; often shown as negative lag in software). (Continued on PDF 230.)

t-6.4-estimate-durations.title: 6.4 Estimate Activity Durations: effort vs duration factors, analogous, parametric, three-point, bottom-up, reserves
t-6.4-estimate-durations.notes: Estimate the number of work periods needed for each activity with estimated resources; key benefit: how long each activity takes; performed throughout. Uses scope of work, resource types/skills, quantities and resource calendars; also constraints (fixed duration, fixed effort, fixed number of resources) and the network analysis technique. Inputs come from the people most familiar with the work; estimates are progressively elaborated as data improves. Estimates effort and available resources, then converts to work periods using project and resource calendars; changing a driving resource usually changes duration, but not linearly; some work takes a fixed time regardless (24-hour stress test). Factors: law of diminishing returns; number of resources (doubling people rarely halves time - risk, knowledge transfer, learning curve, coordination); advances in technology; staff motivation - Student Syndrome (procrastination until the deadline) and Parkinson's Law (work expands to fill the time available). Document all data and assumptions. Inputs: schedule management plan (method, accuracy); scope baseline (WBS dictionary technical details); documents (activity attributes, activity list, assumption log, lessons learned, milestone list, project team assignments, RBS, resource calendars, resource requirements - lower-skilled or extra resources may lengthen duration via communication/training/coordination, risk register); EEFs (duration estimating databases, productivity metrics, published commercial information, team location); OPAs (historical durations, project calendars, estimating policies, scheduling methodology, lessons learned). Tools: expert judgment; analogous estimating (uses actual values - duration, budget, size, weight, complexity - of a similar past activity/project; gross value, adjusted for known differences; used when detail is limited; cheaper and quicker but less accurate; most reliable when past work is similar in fact, not just appearance, and estimators have expertise); parametric estimating (algorithm/statistical relationship between historical data and variables, e.g., quantity x labour hours per unit: 1,000 m of cable at 25 m/hour = 40 hours; accuracy depends on the model); three-point estimating (most likely tM, optimistic tO, pessimistic tP; triangular distribution tE = (tO + tM + tP) / 3 used with insufficient history or judgmental data; gives expected duration and range of uncertainty. NOTE: the Guide states only the triangular formula in 6.4; the beta distribution formula (cO + 4cM + cP) / 6 is stated in Cost 7.2.2.5 (PDF 282, confirmed in batch B12), so lessons present beta for durations as the same weighting applied to tO, tM, tP and cite 7.2.2.5); bottom-up estimating (decompose an activity that cannot be estimated confidently and aggregate the detailed estimates; document resource dependencies); data analysis - alternatives analysis (resource capability/skill levels, compression techniques, manual vs automated tools, make/rent/buy) and reserve analysis (contingency reserve = schedule reserve inside the schedule baseline for identified, accepted risks - known-unknowns; may be a % of duration or fixed work periods; may be aggregated; used, reduced or removed as information improves; clearly identified. Management reserve = withheld for management control for unforeseen in-scope work - unknown-unknowns; not in the schedule baseline but part of overall duration requirements; using it may require a baseline change depending on contract terms); decision making - voting incl. fist of five (closed fist = no support to five fingers = full support; anyone showing fewer than three fingers discusses objections; repeat until everyone shows three or more or the team moves on); meetings - in agile, sprint/iteration planning on the first day with product owner, Scrum team and PM: discuss prioritised backlog items, commit, break stories into tasks estimated in hours, validate against capacity; outputs iteration backlog, assumptions, concerns, risks, dependencies, decisions, actions. Outputs: duration estimates (quantitative assessments of likely work periods; exclude lags; may show a range - '2 weeks +/- 2 days' = 8 to 12 days on a 5-day week - or a probability - '15% probability of exceeding 3 weeks' = 85% probability of 3 weeks or less); basis of estimates (how derived, assumptions, constraints, range such as +/-10%, confidence level, individual risks); document updates (activity attributes, assumption log, lessons learned).

t-6.5-develop-schedule.title: 6.5 Develop Schedule: inputs, schedule network analysis, critical path method, float
t-6.5-develop-schedule.notes: Analyse activity sequences, durations, resource requirements and schedule constraints to create the schedule model; key benefit: a model with planned dates; performed throughout. Iterative: may revise duration, resource estimates and schedule reserves to reach an approved schedule that becomes the baseline. Key steps: define milestones, identify and sequence activities, estimate durations; then assigned staff review their dates against resource calendars and other commitments; analyse logic conflicts and need for resource leveling before approval and baselining; maintain a realistic model throughout. Inputs: schedule management plan (method, tool, how calculated); scope baseline; documents (activity attributes, activity list, assumption log, basis of estimates, duration estimates, lessons learned, milestone list, network diagrams, project team assignments, resource calendars, resource requirements, risk register - schedule-relevant risk reflected in schedule reserves using expected/mean impact); agreements (vendors' input on how they will meet commitments); EEFs (standards, communication channels); OPAs (scheduling methodology, project calendars). Schedule network analysis: the overarching technique generating the schedule model, using CPM, resource optimisation and modelling; also assess whether to aggregate schedule reserves where paths converge or diverge, and review whether the critical path has high-risk or long-lead items needing reserves or risk responses; iterate until viable. Critical path method: estimates minimum project duration and schedule flexibility; computes early start (ES), early finish (EF), late start (LS) and late finish (LF) by forward and backward pass, ignoring resource limits. Critical path = sequence of activities forming the longest path through the project, which determines the shortest possible project duration; it has the least total float, usually zero. Early/late dates are not the schedule itself but windows in which activities could occur. Total float = how long an activity can be delayed or extended from its early start without delaying the project finish or violating a constraint. Critical paths may have positive, zero or negative total float depending on constraints: positive when the backward pass starts from a constraint later than the forward-pass early finish; negative when a late-date constraint is violated by duration and logic; negative float analysis finds ways to accelerate a delayed schedule. Networks may have near-critical paths. To get zero or positive float, adjust durations (more resources or less scope), discretionary logic, leads and lags or constraints. Free float = how long an activity can be delayed without delaying the early start of any successor or violating a constraint. Figure 6-16 (visually verified; day-1 convention, i.e., EF = ES + duration - 1 and the successor's ES = predecessor's EF + 1): A (ES1, dur 5, EF5; LS1, TF0, LF5); B (6, 5, 10; 11, TF5, 15); C (6, 10, 15; 6, 0, 15); D (16, 15, 30; 16, 0, 30). Path A-B-D = 25, path A-C-D = 30 = critical path. Free float of B = 5 days.

t-6.5-optimisation-compression.title: 6.5 Develop Schedule (continued): resource leveling vs smoothing, what-if, Monte Carlo, crashing vs fast tracking
t-6.5-optimisation-compression.notes: Resource optimisation adjusts start/finish dates so planned resource use is at or below availability. Resource leveling: adjusts dates based on resource constraints to balance demand with supply - used when shared or critical resources are available only at certain times or in limited quantities, are over-allocated (Figure 6-17: Sue assigned 16 hours on one day across A and B; after leveling her work spreads over two days), or to keep usage constant; uses available float and can change (often lengthen) the critical path. Resource smoothing: keeps resource requirements within predefined limits without changing the critical path or delaying completion - activities move only within free and total float; may not optimise all resources. Data analysis: what-if scenario analysis ('what if scenario X happens?' - e.g., late component delivery, longer engineering, strike, permit changes - computed on the schedule to test feasibility and prepare reserves and response plans); simulation (models combined effects of individual risks and other uncertainty; most common is Monte Carlo analysis, which calculates possible project outcomes from probability distributions; Figure 6-18: 10% probability of finishing by the 13 May target, 90% by 28 May). Leads and lags are refinements used in limited circumstances during network analysis. Schedule compression shortens duration without reducing scope to meet constraints, imposed dates or objectives; negative float analysis helps. Crashing: shorten duration for the least incremental cost by adding resources (overtime, extra resources, paying to expedite) - only works on critical path activities where more resources actually shorten duration; may increase risk and/or cost. Fast tracking: activities or phases normally done in sequence are done in parallel for at least part of their duration (e.g., foundation before all architectural drawings are complete) - may cause rework, increase risk and possibly cost; only works where activities can overlap on the critical path; using leads increases coordination effort and quality risk. Figure 6-19 compares normal, crashing (higher cost) and fast tracking (higher risk). (Continued on PDF 253.)

t-6.5-outputs.title: 6.5 Develop Schedule (continued): agile release planning, schedule baseline, schedule presentations, schedule data, calendars
t-6.5-outputs.notes: PMIS scheduling software generates start and finish dates from activities, network diagrams, resources and durations. Agile release planning: a high-level summary timeline of the release schedule (typically 3 to 6 months) based on the product roadmap and vision; determines the number of iterations or sprints in the release; lets the product owner and team decide how much to build and how long until a releasable product, given business goals, dependencies and impediments; features represent customer value, so the timeline shows which features will be available at the end of each iteration. Figure 6-20 hierarchy: product vision drives the product roadmap; the roadmap drives release plans; a release plan establishes the iterations; iteration plans schedule feature development; prioritised features are delivered by user stories estimated in story points; tasks to deliver stories are estimated in hours. Outputs: schedule baseline - approved version of the schedule model with baseline start and finish dates, changed only via formal change control, compared to actuals during M&C, a plan component. Project schedule - output of the schedule model presenting linked activities with planned dates, durations, milestones and resources; at minimum planned start and finish for each activity; preliminary until resource assignments are confirmed (usually no later than completion of the project management plan); a target schedule may also exist; summary (master/milestone schedule) or detailed. Presentations: bar (Gantt) charts - activities on the vertical axis, dates on the horizontal axis, bars for durations; easy to read; summary activities for control communications; milestone charts - only start/completion of major deliverables and key external interfaces; project schedule network diagrams - activity-on-node without time scale ('pure logic diagram') or time-scaled ('logic bar chart'/time-scaled logic diagram) showing logic and critical path. Figure 6-21 shows a milestone schedule, a summary schedule and a detailed schedule for 'New Product Z' with a data date. Schedule data - at minimum milestones, activities, activity attributes and documented assumptions and constraints; often resource histograms, alternative schedules (best/worst case, leveled or not, with or without imposed dates), applied schedule reserves, cash-flow projections, order and delivery schedules. Project calendars - working days and shifts available; a model may need several. Change requests (incl. preventive actions to reduce the probability of negative schedule variance). Plan updates: schedule management plan, cost baseline. Document updates: activity attributes, assumption log, duration estimates, lessons learned, resource requirements (leveling may change them), risk register.

t-6.6-control-schedule.title: 6.6 Control Schedule: predictive and agile control, burndown charts, variance on critical vs non-critical paths, schedule forecasts
t-6.6-control-schedule.notes: Monitor project status to update the schedule and manage changes to the schedule baseline; key benefit: baseline maintained; performed throughout. Updating the model requires actual performance; any change to the schedule baseline must be approved through Perform Integrated Change Control. Concerns: current schedule status; influencing factors that create schedule changes; reconsidering schedule reserves; determining if the schedule has changed; managing actual changes. Agile: compare total work delivered and accepted with estimates for the elapsed cycle; retrospectives (scheduled reviews recording lessons to correct and improve processes); reprioritise the backlog; determine velocity (rate deliverables are produced, validated and accepted per iteration of agreed length, typically 2 weeks or 1 month); determine changes; manage changes. For contracted work, regular and milestone status updates from contractors plus status reviews and walkthroughs to verify contractor reports. Inputs: plan (schedule management plan - update frequency, reserve use, control approach; schedule baseline; scope baseline; performance measurement baseline); documents (lessons learned, project calendars, project schedule - latest version with notations, resource calendars, schedule data); work performance data (activities started, progress - actual duration, remaining duration, physical percent complete - and finished); OPAs (schedule control policies, tools, monitoring and reporting methods). Tools: data analysis - earned value analysis (SV and SPI), iteration burndown chart (tracks work remaining in the iteration backlog against an ideal diagonal burndown from iteration planning; plot daily actual remaining work; a trend line forecasts completion and likely variance), performance reviews (actual start/finish dates, percent complete, remaining duration vs baseline), trend analysis, variance analysis (planned vs actual dates, durations and float; cause and degree of variance; implications for remaining work; e.g., a long delay on a non-critical activity may matter little while a short delay on a critical or near-critical activity may need immediate action), what-if scenario analysis guided by risk outputs; critical path method (progress on the critical path determines status; critical-path variance directly affects the end date; near-critical paths reveal schedule risk); PMIS; resource optimisation; leads and lags (e.g., increase lead so landscaping starts before exterior work finishes; remove lag so editing starts right after writing); schedule compression (fast tracking or crashing remaining work). Source note: Figure 6-22 numbers the tools .1-.4 then .6-.7 (no .5) - a numbering gap in the source figure; the overview Figure 6-1 lists the same six tools. Outputs: work performance information (variances in dates and durations at work package and control account level; SV and SPI for work performance reports); schedule forecasts (estimates or predictions of future conditions based on current knowledge, past performance and expected corrective/preventive actions; can include EV indicators and schedule reserve information); change requests; plan updates (schedule management plan; schedule baseline - for approved changes in scope, resources or duration estimates, or changes caused by compression or performance issues; cost baseline; performance measurement baseline); document updates (assumption log, basis of estimates, lessons learned, project schedule, resource calendars, risk register - risks from compression, schedule data - possibly a new target schedule when delays are severe). Data flow: WPD from 4.3; WPI and schedule forecasts to 4.5; change requests to 4.6.

t-schedule-overview.title: Project Schedule Management overview: six processes, scheduling method/tool/model, trends, tailoring, agile
t-schedule-overview.section: 6 intro, key concepts, trends, tailoring, agile (Figures 6-1, 6-2)
t-schedule-overview.notes: Processes to manage timely completion. 6.1 Plan Schedule Management (policies, procedures and documentation for planning, developing, managing, executing and controlling the schedule); 6.2 Define Activities (identify and document specific actions to produce deliverables); 6.3 Sequence Activities (identify and document relationships among activities); 6.4 Estimate Activity Durations (number of work periods to complete activities with estimated resources); 6.5 Develop Schedule (analyse sequences, durations, resource requirements and constraints to create the schedule model); 6.6 Control Schedule (monitor status, update the schedule, manage changes to the schedule baseline). Key concepts: the schedule is a detailed plan of how and when the project will deliver its scope, a communication tool, a way to manage expectations and a basis for performance reporting. The team selects a scheduling method (e.g., critical path or an agile approach), enters project-specific data (activities, dates, durations, resources, dependencies, constraints, calendars, milestones, lags) into a scheduling tool to create a schedule model, which generates the project schedule and presentations such as network diagrams, bar charts and activity lists (Figure 6-2). On small projects 6.2-6.5 are so tightly linked they act as one process done by one person quickly; presented separately because their tools differ. Keep the detailed schedule flexible for knowledge gained, risk understanding and value-added activities. Trends: adaptive planning; iterative scheduling with a backlog (rolling wave on adaptive life cycles; user stories prioritised and refined just before construction; time-boxed work; delivers incremental value; good when many teams build features with few dependencies; welcomes change); on-demand scheduling (Kanban; theory of constraints and lean pull concepts; limit work in progress to balance demand with throughput; pull from a backlog/queue as resources free up; suits incremental evolution in operational or sustainment settings with similarly sized tasks). Tailoring: life cycle approach; resource availability and productivity; project dimensions (complexity, technological uncertainty, novelty, pace, progress tracking such as EV, percent complete, stop-light indicators); technology support. Agile: short cycles with review and adaptation; large organisations may need long-term roadmaps and scaling factors (team size, geography, regulation, organisational and technical complexity), combining predictive, adaptive or hybrid techniques; the PM's role does not change, but the PM must know adaptive tools and techniques. ITTOs for 6.1-6.6 recorded in ittos.json from Figure 6-1.

x1-sixth-edition-changes.title: Appendix X1: Sixth Edition changes - ITTO conventions, tool-and-technique groups, new and renamed processes, Knowledge Area front matter
x1-sixth-edition-changes.notes: Scope of update: review deferred material and feedback on the Fifth Edition, align with ISO 21500, harmonise with other PMI standards, consider the PM role delineation study and research; focus on consistency and clarity of processes and ITTOs. Glossary rule: terms in both the Guide and PMI Lexicon use the Lexicon definition; terms in other PMI standards should be identical or are escalated to the Lexicon team. Input/output rules: inputs are documents key to the process; outputs should become inputs elsewhere unless terminal or embedded; inputs come from another process's output unless from outside the project. Project documents: listed specifically the first time created, then as 'project documents updates'; as inputs, listed as 'project documents' with specifics in the narrative. Plan: planning processes creating a subsidiary plan list the charter first and the project management plan second; the creating process lists the component specifically, later as 'plan updates'. Sequencing: charter first; plan components ordered by the section that produces them, then baselines, then other plans; project documents alphabetical; EEFs then OPAs last; updates ordered plan updates, project documents updates, OPA updates. Tools and techniques were reduced to those used on most projects most of the time; described the first time and referenced afterwards; grouped by intent: data gathering, data analysis, data representation, decision-making, communication skills, interpersonal and team skills (Appendix X6 indexes them). Plan components created within Develop Project Management Plan: change management plan, configuration management plan, performance measurement baseline, project life cycle, development approach, management reviews. Section 1 rewritten (life cycles, phases, gates, development approaches; business documents); Section 2 rewritten (governance, management elements, structure types); Section 3 new (PM role, sphere of influence, Talent Triangle, leadership styles, personality, integration). Agile: 'Considerations for Adaptive Environments' added to Sections 4-13; agile tools such as sprint/iteration planning introduced; Appendix X3 explains agile, adaptive, iterative and hybrid approaches. Knowledge Area front matter standardised: key concepts (compiled in X4), trends and emerging practices (not necessarily practised on most projects - the Guide describes good practice, it does not lead the industry), tailoring considerations (compiled in X5), agile/adaptive considerations. Knowledge Area renames: Project Time Management -> Project Schedule Management (the schedule, not time, is managed); Project Human Resource Management -> Project Resource Management (team and physical resources). Process changes: added Manage Project Knowledge (4.4), Control Resources (9.6), Implement Risk Responses (11.6); moved Estimate Activity Resources from Schedule to Resource; eliminated Close Procurements (12.4) - closure evaluation of deliverables absorbed into Control Procurements, administrative/communications/records into Close Project or Phase, because few PMs actually have authority to close procurements. Renames: Perform Quality Assurance -> Manage Quality (quality managed through the plan; many QA tools little used); Plan Human Resource Management -> Plan Resource Management; Acquire Project Team -> Acquire Resources; Develop Project Team -> Develop Team; Manage Project Team -> Manage Team; Control Communications -> Monitor Communications; Control Risks -> Monitor Risks; Plan Stakeholder Management -> Plan Stakeholder Engagement; Control Stakeholder Engagement -> Monitor Stakeholder Engagement - research shows PMs monitor, facilitate and manage rather than control, especially with people; risks cannot be controlled, only monitored; stakeholders cannot be controlled. Section notes: Integration - lessons learned register emphasises continuous learning; business documents as inputs to Develop Project Charter and Close Project or Phase. Scope - aligned with The Standard for Business Analysis. Schedule - agile concepts in Develop Schedule. Communications - 'communication' = the act (facilitating, informing, listening); 'communications' = the artefacts (memos, presentations, emails). Risk - emphasis on overall project risk; new 'escalate' response. Procurement - more global perspective. Stakeholder - focus on engagement rather than management. Glossary updated for clarity and translation; unused terms removed. x3-life-cycle-continuum.title: Appendix X3: continuum of life cycles (predictive, iterative, incremental, agile), iteration-based and continuous overlapping phases
x3-life-cycle-continuum.notes: Explores how the Process Groups are performed across environments and life cycles; the life cycle must be flexible because projects evolve as information becomes available - especially with high change, uncertainty or varied stakeholder expectations. Development life cycles: predictive (plan-driven), adaptive (agile), iterative, incremental, hybrid. Figure X3-1 continuum: Predictive - requirements defined up front before development; deliver plans for the eventual deliverable then a single final product at the end; change constrained as much as possible; key stakeholders involved at specific milestones; risk and cost controlled by detailed planning of mostly knowable considerations. Iterative - requirements elaborated at periodic intervals during delivery; delivery can be divided into subsets; change incorporated at periodic intervals; stakeholders regularly involved; risk and cost controlled by progressively elaborating plans with new information. Incremental - (shares the middle of the continuum with iterative; figure groups iterative/incremental characteristics). Agile - requirements elaborated frequently during delivery; frequent delivery of customer-valued subsets; change incorporated in real time; stakeholders continuously involved; risk and cost controlled as requirements and constraints emerge. Predictive: emphasis on specifying requirements and detailed planning early; M&C focuses on constraining changes to scope, schedule, budget. Agile: progressive elaboration through short planning and executing cycles; continuous stakeholder feedback enables faster response to change and better quality. Middle of the continuum: risk and cost reduced by iterative evolution of plans; more stakeholder involvement opportunities than milestone-based predictive; projects lean predictive or agile depending on requirements, risk/cost handling and stakeholder involvement and may use hybrid methods; different phases of one project (or projects in a program) may use different life cycles. Phases: Process Group processes repeat in each phase until completion criteria are met. Sequential iteration-based phases: adaptive projects decomposed into timeboxed iterations of consistent, pre-agreed duration creating a predictable cadence; repeating Process Groups each iteration adds overhead, accepted for high complexity, uncertainty and change (Figure X3-2: each iteration contains initiating, planning, executing, M&C and closing effort). Continuous overlapping phases: highly adaptive projects perform all Process Groups continuously ('continuous and adaptive planning', inspired by lean); aggressively refine plans beyond iteration checkpoints; continuously pull tasks from a prioritised list, removing iteration start/end overhead - 'microiterations' maximising execution time, still needing their own planning, tracking and adjustment mechanisms (Figure X3-3).

x3-process-groups-adaptive.title: Appendix X3: Process Groups in adaptive environments (initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling via a backlog, closing)
x3-process-groups-adaptive.notes: Initiating: adaptive projects revisit and revalidate the charter frequently because priorities and dynamics may make constraints and success criteria obsolete; rely heavily on a knowledgeable customer or designated customer representative giving continuous feedback - identify them early; an initiating process is typically conducted each iterative cycle. Planning: predictive projects (few scope changes, high stakeholder alignment) benefit from detailed up-front planning; adaptive projects develop high-level plans for initial requirements and progressively elaborate them per planning cycle - they differ in how much planning is done and when; under complexity and uncertainty involve as many team members and stakeholders as possible in planning. Executing: work directed through short fixed iterations ending with a demonstration of functionality or design, then a retrospective with stakeholders and team; demonstrations check progress against plan, decide scope/schedule/process changes and manage engagement; retrospectives surface execution issues and improvements and are a primary tool to manage project knowledge and develop the team; iteration-level trends (development speed, spend, defect rates, team capacity) are summed and extrapolated to track project completion; highly adaptive teams self-organise tasks to meet higher-level objectives rather than the PM selecting and sequencing work - practical plans with high buy-in; junior teams need coaching and assignments first and are reviewed in retrospectives for readiness. Monitoring and controlling: progress regulated through a backlog prioritised by a business representative with the team estimating and flagging technical dependencies; work pulled from the top by business priority and team capacity; change requests and defect reports are evaluated and prioritised into the same backlog - a single list of work and changes that originated where change rates overwhelmed separate change control; this one backlog is where stakeholders manage work, perform change control and validate scope; frequent sampling yields capacity, progress against original scope, change impacts and defect remediation effort, enabling cost, schedule and scope estimates from real rates; shared through trend graphs ('information radiators') to communicate progress, share issues, drive improvement and manage expectations. Closing: highest-value items are done first, so premature closure is likely to have already produced business value - less a sunk-cost failure, more an early benefit realisation, quick win or proof of concept.
